s: Holy brothers and sisters, you remember that we usually preach on the Gospel of John, as it is read to us in order, lesson by lesson. But now the holy festival days have come in between. On these days certain readings must be read in the Church. They come around every year, and they cannot be anything other than what they are. So for a little while we have to interrupt the order we started. We are not dropping it completely.

So I was thinking about what part of the Scriptures I could preach on with you this week, as the Lord gives me grace. I wanted something that fits the joy of these days, and something we could finish in these seven or eight days. Then the letter of blessed John came to my mind. We have stopped reading his Gospel for a while, but by preaching on his letter we will not leave his side. There is another good reason too. This letter is very sweet to everyone whose heart has a healthy taste for the Bread of God. It is very much worth remembering in God’s holy Church. And above all, it praises love.
He says many things, and nearly all of them are about love.
If someone already has inside him what he is about to hear, he cannot help being glad when he hears it.
For that person, this reading will be like oil poured on a flame. If there is something there to feed, it gets fed, and it grows, and it lasts.
For others, it should be like a flame put to wood. If someone was not burning before, the words he hears may set him on fire.
In some people, what is already there gets fed. In others, it gets lit, if it was not there before. And so we can all be glad together in one love.
But where there is love, there is peace. And where there is humility, there is love.
Now let us listen to John himself. And whatever the Lord puts in our minds as we hear his words, let us tell you that too, so that you can understand it well.

“What was there from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our own eyes, what our hands have touched—this is about the Word of life. The life appeared. We have seen it, and we are witnesses to it. We announce to you that eternal life, which was with the Father and appeared to us. We tell you what we have seen and heard, so that you also can share in fellowship with us. And we want our fellowship to be with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ.
We write these things to you so that your joy may be complete.
This is the message we have heard from Him, and we pass it on to you: God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all.

If we say we have fellowship with Him but keep walking in darkness, we are lying, and we are not doing what is true. But if we walk in the light, as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another. And the blood of His Son Jesus Christ will wash us clean from all sin.
If we say we have no sin, we are lying to ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
If we confess our sins, He can be trusted, and He is just. He will forgive our sins and wash away all our wrongdoing.
If we say we have not sinned, we make Him out to be a liar, and His word is not in us.
My little children, I write these things to you to keep you from sinning.

But if anyone sins, we have a defender who speaks for us to the Father: Jesus Christ, the righteous one. He is the sacrifice that wins forgiveness for our sins. And not just for ours, but also for the sins of the whole world.
This is how we know Him: if we keep His commandments.
Whoever says he knows Him but does not keep His commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him.
But whoever keeps His word truly has the love of God made complete in him.
This is how we know that we are in Him: if we are perfect in Him.
Whoever says he stays in Him ought to walk just the way He walked.
Beloved, the commandment I am writing to you is not new. It is an old commandment, one you have had since the beginning.
The old commandment is the message you have heard.
Then again, I am writing you a new commandment. It is true in Him and in you. For the darkness is gone, and now the true light shines.
Whoever says he is in the light but hates his brother is still in darkness, even now.
Whoever loves his brother stays in the light, and there is nothing in him that makes anyone stumble.
But whoever hates his brother is in darkness and walks around in darkness. He does not know where he is going, because the darkness has made his eyes blind.”
1. “What was there from the beginning, what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what our hands have touched—this is about the word of life.”
Who could touch the Word with his hands? It was only possible because “the Word became flesh and lived in us.”
This Word became flesh so that He could be touched. He began to be flesh from the Virgin Mary. But the Word Himself did not begin then. For the apostle says, “What was there from the beginning.”
See how his letter backs up his Gospel. You heard it read recently: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.”
Someone might think that “about the word of life” is just a way of speaking about Christ. He might think it does not mean the actual body of Christ that hands touched.
But look at what comes next: “And the Life appeared.”
So Christ is “the word of life.”
And how did it appear? It was there “from the beginning,” but it had not yet been shown to human beings. It had been shown to the angels, though. They saw it and fed on it as their bread.
But what does the Scripture say?
“Human beings ate the bread of angels.”
So “the Life appeared” in the flesh. It was put out in the open, so that something that can only be seen with the heart could also be seen with the eyes. And the purpose was to heal our hearts.
The Word can only be seen with the heart. But flesh can be seen with our physical eyes too.
We had eyes that could see flesh, but we had nothing that could see the Word. So “the Word became flesh,” something we could see. That way, the part of us that could see the Word would be healed.
2. “And we have seen and are witnesses.”

Some of our brothers and sisters do not know Greek. So maybe they do not know what the Greek word for “witnesses” is. Yet it is a word everyone uses, and people say it with deep respect. What we call “witnesses” in our language is “martyrs” in Greek.

Is there anyone who has not heard of martyrs? Is there any Christian who does not say the word “martyrs” every day? If only it lived in our hearts as well as on our lips! Then we would copy the sufferings of the martyrs instead of persecuting them with our drinking cups!
So “We have seen and are witnesses” means the same as “We have seen and are martyrs.”

The martyrs bore witness to what they had seen. They also bore witness to what they had heard from those who had seen. Their testimony made the people they spoke against angry. That is why the martyrs suffered everything they suffered.
The martyrs are God’s witnesses.
God was pleased to have human beings as His witnesses, so that human beings could also have God as their witness.
“We have seen,” he says, “and are witnesses.”
Where did they see?
Out in plain view. What does “in plain view” mean?
In the sun—that is, in this daylight.

But how could the One who made the sun be seen in the sun? Only in the way the Scripture says: “He set His tent in the sun. And He Himself came out like a bridegroom from his room, and rejoiced like a giant to run His race.”

He existed before the sun, and He made the sun. He existed before the morning star, before all the stars, before all the angels. He is the true Creator (“for all things were made by Him, and without Him nothing was made”). He wanted to be seen by human eyes, the eyes that see the sun. So He set His tent in the sun. That is, He showed His flesh out in plain view, in this daylight. And the Bridegroom’s room was the Virgin’s womb. For in that virgin womb two were joined together, the Bridegroom and the bride. The Bridegroom was the Word, and the bride was the flesh. As it is written, “And the two shall become one flesh.” And the Lord says in the Gospel, “So they are no longer two, but one flesh.
And Isaiah knows very well that they are two. Speaking as Christ, he says, “He put a headdress on me like a bridegroom, and decorated me with jewelry like a bride.”
One person seems to be speaking, and yet He makes Himself both Bridegroom and Bride. That is because they are “not two, but one flesh.” It is because “the Word became flesh and lived in us.”
The Church is joined to that flesh. And so the whole Christ is formed, Head and body together.
3. “And we are witnesses, and we announce to you that eternal life which was with the Father and was shown to us.” That means it was shown among us. Or, to say it more plainly, it was shown to us.
So, “what we have seen and heard, we announce to you.”
They saw the Lord Himself there in the flesh. They heard words from the Lord’s own mouth. And they told them to us.
So we too have heard, but we have not seen.
Does that make us less happy than those who saw and heard?
Then how can he add, “So that you also can share in fellowship with us”?
They saw, and we have not seen. Yet we are their partners, because we share the same faith.

There was one disciple who did not believe even when he saw. He insisted on touching, so that he could believe. He said, “I will not believe unless I push my fingers into the place of the nails and touch His scars.”
The Lord always lets the angels see Him. But for a short time He let human hands touch Him. That disciple did touch Him, and he cried out, “My Lord and my God!”
He touched the Man, and so he confessed the God.

And the Lord wanted to comfort us. Now that He sits in heaven, we cannot touch Him with our hands. We can only reach Him by faith. So He said to that disciple, “You believe because you have seen. Blessed are those who have not seen and still believe.”
That describes us. We are the ones He meant.
So let that blessing come true in us, just as the Lord said it would. Let us hold firmly to what we do not see, because those who did see have told us.
“So that you also,” he says, “can share in fellowship with us.”
But is it such a great thing to have fellowship with human beings?
Do not look down on it. See what he adds: “and so that our fellowship may be with God the Father and with Jesus Christ His Son.
We write these things to you,” he says, “so that your joy may be complete.”
He means complete joy in that fellowship, in that love, in that unity.
4. “And this is the message we have heard from Him, and we announce it to you.”
What is this message? These same people saw the Word of life and touched Him with their hands. He “was there from the beginning.” For a time He was made visible and touchable—the only Son of God.
Why did He come? What new thing did He tell us?
What did He want to teach?
Why did He do what He did? Why did the Word become flesh? Why did “God over all things” put up with insults from people? Why did He let Himself be slapped in the face by hands He Himself had made?
What did He want to teach?
What did He want to show?
What did He want to announce?

Let us listen. If we do not get the fruit of His teaching, then hearing the story of how Christ was born and how Christ suffered is just entertainment for the mind. It does not make the mind stronger.
What great thing are you hearing?
Make sure you hear it in a way that bears fruit.
What did He want to teach?
What did He want to announce? Listen. “God is light,” he says, “and there is no darkness in Him at all.”
So far he has named the light, but his words are still dark. It would be good for us if the very light he named would shine into our hearts, so that we could see what he means.
This is what we announce: “God is light, and there is no darkness in Him at all.”
Who would dare to say there is darkness in God?
But what is this light?
And what is this darkness? We must not think he is talking about the kind of things these eyes of ours can see.
“God is light.” Someone will say, “The sun is light too. The moon is light too. A candle is light.”
But this light must be something far greater than these, far better, far higher.
God is far above what He created. The Maker is far above what He made. Wisdom is far above the things Wisdom made. In the same way, this light must be far above everything.

And maybe we will come near to it if we learn what this light is and draw close to it, so that it can shine on us. In ourselves we are darkness. Only when it shines on us can we become light. Then it will not put us to shame, the way we are put to shame by ourselves.
Who is put to shame by himself?
The person who knows he is a sinner.
Who is not put to shame by the light?
The person the light shines on.
What does it mean to have the light shine on you?

It means this. A person now sees that sin has made him dark. He wants the light to shine on him, so he comes close to it. That is why the Psalm says, “Come close to Him, and let His light shine on you, and your faces will not be ashamed.”

The light will show you to yourself, and you will see how dirty you are. If your own dirtiness then displeases you, the light will not put you to shame. And you will be able to see how beautiful it is.
This is what He wanted to teach.
5. But are we saying this too quickly?
Let the apostle himself make it clear in what comes next.
Remember what I said at the start: this letter praises love. “God is light,” he says, “and there is no darkness in Him at all.”
And what did he say before that?
“So that you can have fellowship with us, and our fellowship may be with God the Father and with His Son Jesus Christ.”

So think about it. “God is light, and there is no darkness in Him at all, and we must have fellowship with Him.” Then the darkness must be driven out of us too, so that light can be created in us. For darkness cannot have fellowship with light.
That is why he goes on: “If we say we have fellowship with Him but walk in darkness, we are lying.”
The apostle Paul says it too: “What fellowship can light have with darkness?”
You say you have fellowship with God, but you walk in darkness. “And God is light, and there is no darkness in Him at all.” So how can light and darkness have fellowship?
At this point a person might say to himself: What am I going to do? How can I become light?
I live in sin and wrongdoing.
A kind of hopelessness and sadness creeps over him.
There is no salvation except in fellowship with God.
“God is light, and there is no darkness in Him at all.”
But sins are darkness. The apostle says this about the devil and his angels: they are “rulers of this darkness.”
He would not call them rulers of darkness unless he meant rulers of sins, who have power over wicked people.
So what are we to do, my brothers and sisters?

We must have fellowship with God. There is no other hope of eternal life. But “God is light, and there is no darkness in Him at all.” And our sins are darkness. Our sins weigh us down, so that we cannot have fellowship with God. So what hope do we have?
Didn’t I promise that during these days I would say something that would make you glad?
If I don’t keep that promise, this is sad.
“God is light, and there is no darkness in Him at all.” Sins are darkness. What will happen to us?
Let us listen and see if He will comfort us, lift us up, and give us hope, so that we do not give up on the way.
For we are running, and we are running home to our own country. If we give up hope of getting there, that very hopelessness will make us fail.
But He wants us to get there, so that He can keep us safe in our own land. So He feeds us along the way.
So let us listen: “If we say we have fellowship with Him but walk in darkness, we are lying, and we are not doing what is true.”
Let us not claim to have fellowship with Him if we are walking in darkness.
“If we walk in the light, as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another.”
Let us walk in the light, as He is in the light, so that we can have fellowship with Him.
But what are we to do about our sins?
Listen to what comes next: “And the blood of His Son Jesus Christ will wash us clean from all sin.”
What great confidence God has given us!
We have good reason to celebrate the Passover, when the Lord’s blood was shed! By that blood we are made clean “from all sin”!
We can be sure of this. The devil held “the written record that was against us,” the contract that made us slaves. But the blood of Christ has wiped it out.
“The blood of His Son,” he says, “will wash us clean from all sin.”
What does “from all sin” mean?
Look! Just now, in the name of Christ, all the sins of these people here have been washed away. They have just confessed Christ, and they are called “infants.”
They came in old, and they went out new.
What do I mean, they came in old and went out new?
They came in as old men, and they went out as babies.
The old life is old age, with all its foolishness. But the new life is the babyhood of being born again.
But what are we to do?

Our past sins have been forgiven—not only theirs, but ours too. But after all our sins were forgiven and wiped away, we have gone on living in this world, surrounded by temptations. So perhaps we have picked up some new sins.
So let each person do what he can. Let him admit what he is, so that he can be healed by the One who always is what He is. For He always was and always is. We once did not exist, and now we do.
6. For look at what He says: “If we say we have no sin, we are lying to ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
So if you have admitted that you are a sinner, the truth is in you. For the Truth itself is light.
Your life does not yet shine with perfect brightness, because there are sins in you. But you have already started to be lit up, because you confess your sins.
For look at what comes next: “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just. He will forgive us our sins and wash us clean from all wrongdoing.”
This means not only our past sins, but also any we may have picked up in this life. For as long as a person lives in this body, he cannot avoid having at least some light sins.
But these sins that we call light—do not take them lightly.
If you think little of them when you weigh them, be afraid when you count them.
Many light sins add up to one huge sin. Many drops fill a river. Many grains make a heap.
So what hope is there?
First of all, confession. No one should think he is righteous. God sees what truly is. A human being once did not exist, and now he does. So he must not proudly lift up his neck before God’s eyes.
So first, confession. Then, love. For what is said about love?
“Love covers a great many sins.”
Now let us see whether he praises love because of the sins that catch up with us later. For only love puts out sins.
Pride puts out love. So humility makes love strong. And love puts out sins.

Humility goes together with confession. It is the humility that makes us admit we are sinners. This is humility: not saying it with our tongue as if only to avoid looking proud, so that people won’t be annoyed with us if we say we are righteous.
That is what ungodly people do, people who have lost their senses. They say, “I know I am righteous, but what should I say in front of people?
If I call myself righteous, who will put up with it? Who will stand it? Let God know that I am righteous. But I will say I am a sinner, just so people won’t hate me for being proud.”
Tell people what you are. Tell God what you are. For if you do not tell God what you are, God will condemn what He finds in you.
Do you want Him not to condemn you?
Then condemn yourself. Do you want Him to forgive you? Then admit your sin, so that you can say to God, “Turn Your face away from my sins.”
Say to Him also these words from the same Psalm: “For I admit my wrongdoing.”
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just. He will forgive us our sins and wash us clean from all wrongdoing.
If we say we have not sinned, we make Him out to be a liar, and His word is not in us.”
If you say, “I have not sinned,” you make Him a liar, while you are trying to make yourself truthful.
How could God be a liar and a human being be truthful? The Scripture says the opposite: “Every human being is a liar; God alone is true.”
So God is true by Himself. You are true through God. By yourself you are a liar.

7. Someone might think he had given people permission to sin without punishment, because he said, “He is faithful and just to wash us clean from all wrongdoing.” Then people might say to themselves from now on, “Let’s sin! Let’s do whatever we want without worrying! Christ washes us clean. He is faithful and just. He washes us clean from all wrongdoing.” So He takes away your bad feeling of safety and puts in a fear that is good for you.
You would like to feel safe, but it would hurt you. You need to be careful and concerned.
For “He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins” only if you always stay unhappy with yourself and keep changing until you are made perfect.
So what comes next? “My little children, I write these things to you to keep you from sinning.”
But maybe sin catches up with us because of this mortal life. What should we do then?
What? Should we give up hope now?
Listen: “And if anyone sins, we have a defender with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous one. He is the one who wins forgiveness for our sins.”

So He is the defender. You do your best not to sin. But if sin catches you because this life is weak, deal with it right away. Right away, be unhappy with it. Right away, condemn it. And when you have condemned it, you can come to the Judge with confidence.
There you have your defender. Don’t be afraid that confessing will make you lose your case.
In this life, people often hand their case over to a skilled speaker, and they don’t lose. You are handing yourself over to the Word. Will you lose?
Cry out, “We have a defender with the Father!”
8. Look how humble John himself is.

He was certainly a righteous and great man. From the Lord’s chest he drank in the secrets of His mysteries. By drinking from the Lord’s chest he wrote about His divine nature: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.” Yet even a man like this does not say, “You have a defender with the Father.” Instead he says, “If anyone sins, we have a defender.”
He does not say “you have.” He does not say “you have me.” He does not even say “you have Christ Himself.” He puts Christ forward, not himself. And he says “we have,” not “you have.”

He preferred to count himself among the sinners, so that he could have Christ as his defender. He did not want to put himself in Christ’s place as the defender, and be found among the proud people who will be condemned.
Brothers and sisters, it is Jesus Christ the righteous one whom we have as our defender with the Father. “He,” He Himself, “is the sacrifice that wins forgiveness for our sins.”
Whoever holds on to this has not started a heresy. Whoever holds on to this has not caused a split in the Church.
Where did splits come from?
They came when people said, “We are righteous.” When people said, “We make the unclean holy. We make the ungodly righteous. We ask, and we receive.”
But what does John say?
“And if anyone sins, we have a defender with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous one.”
But someone will say, “Then don’t the saints pray for us?
Don’t bishops and leaders pray for the people?”
Yes, they do. But look at the Scriptures. You will see that leaders also ask the people to pray for them.
That is why the apostle says to the church, “Pray for us too.”
The apostle prays for the people, and the people pray for the apostle.
We pray for you, brothers and sisters. But you must pray for us too.
Let all the members pray for each other. And let the Head plead for everyone.
So it is no surprise that he goes on here to shut the mouths of those who divide the Church of God.

He has just said, “We have Jesus Christ the righteous one, and He is the sacrifice that wins forgiveness for our sins.” He was thinking of people who would split themselves off and say, “Look, here is Christ! Look, there He is!” They would try to show Him in just one part, though He bought the whole and owns the whole. So he goes right on to say, “Not only for our sins, but also for the sins of the whole world.”
What does this mean, brothers and sisters?
Certainly “we have found it in the fields of the forest.” We have found the Church in all nations.
Look! Christ “is the sacrifice that wins forgiveness for our sins, and not only ours, but also the sins of the whole world.”
Look, you have the Church all over the world. Do not follow false people who claim they make others righteous. The truth is, they cut people off.

Stay on that mountain that has filled the whole earth. For “Christ is the sacrifice that wins forgiveness for our sins, and not only ours, but also the sins of the whole world.” He bought that world with His blood.
9. “And this is how we know Him,” he says: “if we keep His commandments.”
Which commandments? “Whoever says, ‘I know Him,’ but does not keep His commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him.”
But you are still asking, “Which commandments?”
“But whoever keeps His word,” he says, “truly has the love of God made complete in him.”
Let us see whether this very commandment is called love.
We were asking, “Which commandments?” And he says, “But whoever keeps His word truly has the love of God made complete in him.”
Look at the Gospel and see whether this is the commandment. “I give you a new commandment,” says the Lord: “love one another.” “This is how we know that we are in Him: if we are made perfect in Him.”
He calls them people made perfect in love. What is perfect love?
It is loving even your enemies, and loving them with this goal: that they may become your brothers.
For our love should not be an earthly, fleshly love.
It is good to wish someone well in this passing life. But even if that fails, let the soul be safe.
Do you wish life to someone who is your friend?
That is good. Are you glad when your enemy dies?
That is wrong. But maybe the life you want for your friend is not good for him. And maybe the death you are glad about was actually good for your enemy.
No one can be sure whether this present life is good for a person or not. But the life that is with God is good, without any doubt.
So love your enemies in a way that wishes for them to become your brothers. Love your enemies in a way that invites them into your fellowship.
That is how He loved. As He hung on the cross, He said, “Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing.”
He did not say, “Father, let them live a long time. They are killing Me, but let them live.”
He was driving out of them the death that lasts forever and ever. He did it by His most merciful prayer and by His power, which is greater than all.
Many of them came to believe, and they were forgiven for shedding the blood of Christ.
At first they shed it in their rage. Later they drank it as believers.
“This is how we know that we are in Him: if we are made perfect in Him.”
The Lord spoke about this very perfection of loving our enemies. He urged us, “So be perfect, as your Father in heaven is perfect.”
“So whoever says he stays in Him ought to walk just the way He walked.”
How should we do this, brothers and sisters? What is he telling us to do?
“Whoever says he stays in Him”—that is, in Christ—“ought to walk just the way He walked.”
Does this mean we should walk on the sea?
Of course not!
No, it means we should walk in the way of righteousness.
What way is that? I have already told you.
He was nailed to the cross, and yet He was walking in this very way. This way is the way of love: “Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing.”
So if you have learned to pray for your enemy, you are walking in the Lord’s way.
10. “My dear ones, I am not writing you a new commandment, but the old commandment you had from the beginning.”
Which commandment does he call “old”?
The one “you had,” he says, “from the beginning.”
So it is “old” in this sense: you have already heard it. Otherwise he would be contradicting the Lord, who says, “I give you a new commandment: love one another.”
But why is it an “old” commandment?
Not because it belongs to the old self.
Then why? “Which you had from the beginning.
The old commandment is the message you have heard.”
So it is old in this sense: you have already heard it.
And he shows that this same commandment is new. He says, “Then again, I am writing you a new commandment.”
It is not a different one. The same commandment he called old is also new.
Why? “It is true in Him and in you.”
Why is it old? You have already heard: because you already knew it.
But why is it new? “Because the darkness is gone, and now the true light shines.”
See, this is why it is new. The darkness belongs to the old self, but the light belongs to the new self.
What does the apostle Paul say?
“Take off the old self, and put on the new.”
And what else does he say?
“Once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”
11. “Whoever says he is in the light”—now he is making clear everything he has been saying—“whoever says he is in the light but hates his brother is still in darkness, even now.”
What is this, my brothers and sisters? How long will we have to tell you, “Love your enemies”?
Look and see whether you are doing something even worse: hating your brothers.
If you loved only your brothers, you would not yet be perfect. But if you hate your brothers, what are you? Where are you?
Let each of you look into his own heart. Do not hold on to hatred against your brother because of some harsh word. Do not fight over earthly things and so become earth yourself.
Whoever hates his brother must not say that he walks in the light.
“Whoever says he is in the light but hates his brother is still in darkness, even now.”

For example, take a man who was a pagan and has become a Christian. Pay attention. Look, he was in darkness while he was a pagan. Now, from here on, he has become a Christian. Everyone happily says, “Thanks be to God!” The apostle’s words are read, where he joyfully says, “For once you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”
He used to worship idols; now he worships God. He used to worship things he had made; now he worships the One who made him.
He has changed. “Thanks be to God!” say all the Christians, as they joyfully welcome him.
Why? Because from now on he worships the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. And he hates demons and idols.
But John is still worried about our new convert. Many people welcome him with joy, but John still looks at him with concern.
Brothers and sisters, let us be glad for a mother’s worried care.
The mother has good reason to worry about us even while others are celebrating. By “the mother” I mean love. She lived in John’s heart when he spoke these words.
Why would he worry, unless there is something in us that he is afraid of, even while people now welcome us with joy?
What is he afraid of?
“Whoever says he is in the light”—what does this mean?
It means whoever says he is now a Christian—“but hates his brother is still in darkness, even now.”
This needs no explaining. We only need to be glad if it is not true of us, or to weep over it if it is.

12. “Whoever loves his brother stays (manet) in the light, and there is nothing in him that makes anyone stumble.” I beg you by Christ: God is feeding us. Soon we will go and refresh our bodies with food, in the name of Christ. In a good measure both have already been fed, and both will be fed again. So now let your mind be fed.

I am not saying this because I plan to preach for a long time. Look, the reading is almost finished. I say it so that we don’t get tired and listen less carefully than we should to something very important. “Whoever loves his brother stays in the light, and there is no scandal in him”—or, “nothing in him that makes anyone stumble.”
Who are the people who stumble, or who make others stumble?
They are people who take offense at Christ, and at the Church.
Those who take offense at Christ are like people burned by the sun. Those who take offense at the Church are like people burned by the moon.

But the Psalm says, “The sun will not burn you by day, and the moon will not burn you by night.” This means: if you hold on to love, you will not stumble over Christ or over the Church. You will not leave Christ, and you will not leave the Church.
For if someone leaves the Church, how can he be in Christ, when he is not among Christ’s members?
How can someone be in Christ if he is not in Christ’s body?
So the people who stumble, or fall, are the ones who leave Christ or the Church.
But how do we know what the Psalm means when it says, “The sun will not burn you by day, nor the moon by night”? How do we know that the “burning” means stumbling, or taking offense?
First of all, look at the picture itself.

Think of someone who is being burned by something. He says, “I can’t stand it! I can’t take it!” and he pulls back. It is the same with people who can’t stand certain things in the Church. They pull away, either from the name of Christ or from the Church. Those people are stumbling.

Look how some people stumbled, as if the sun had burned them. They were people who thought only in earthly ways. Christ was telling them about His flesh. He said, “Whoever does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink His blood will have no life in him.”
About seventy people said, “This teaching is hard.” They turned back and left Him, and only the twelve stayed.
The sun burned all of those people. They turned back because they could not bear the power of the Word.
So the twelve stayed.

People might imagine that they are doing Christ a favor by believing in Him, when really He is the one doing them a favor. So that no one would think that, the Lord spoke to the twelve who were left. He said to them, “Are you going to leave too?”
In other words: so that you may know that you need Me, not that I need you.
But the ones the sun had not burned answered through Peter. He said, “Lord, You have the word of eternal life. Where would we go?”
But who are the people that the Church burns at night, like the moon?
The ones who have caused splits in the Church.
Listen to the very word the apostle uses: “Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?”
So what does it mean that there is nothing to stumble over in the person who loves his brother?
It means this: the one who loves his brother puts up with everything for the sake of unity. For love between brothers lives in the unity of love.
Maybe someone offends you. I don’t know who. Maybe he really is a bad man. Maybe you only think he is bad. Or maybe you just pretend he is bad. And because of him, will you leave so many good people?
What kind of brotherly love have these people shown?
They accuse the Africans, and meanwhile they have left the whole world!
What? Were there no holy people anywhere in the whole world?
Or could you really condemn them without even hearing them?
Oh, if only you loved your brothers! Then there would be nothing in you that makes you stumble.
Listen to what the Psalm says: “Those who love Your law have great peace, and nothing makes them stumble.”
The Psalm says there is great peace for those who love God’s law. That is why nothing makes them stumble.
So people who stumble, or take offense, destroy peace.
And who does he say neither stumble nor make others stumble?
Those who love God’s law.
So they are living in love.
But someone will say, “He said that about people who love God’s law, not about loving our brothers.”
Then listen to what the Lord says: “I give you a new commandment: love one another.”
What is the Law, if not a commandment?
Besides, why is it that they do not stumble? Because they put up with one another.
As Paul says, “Put up with one another in love. Work hard to keep the unity of the Spirit, tied together by peace.”
And to show that this is Christ’s law, listen to the same apostle praising this very law.
He says, “Carry one another’s burdens. That is how you will keep the law of Christ.”
13. “For whoever hates his brother is in the dark. He walks in the dark, and he does not know where he is going.”
This is important, my brothers and sisters. Please pay attention to it.
“Whoever hates his brother walks in the dark and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has made his eyes blind.”
Who could be more blind than people who hate their brothers?
Here is how you can tell they are blind: they have tripped over a Mountain.
I say the same things often so that you won’t forget them.
The Stone that was “cut out of the Mountain without hands”—isn’t that Christ? He came from the kingdom of the Jews without any human being doing the work.
Hasn’t that Stone smashed all the kingdoms of the earth to pieces? That means all the power of idols and demons.
Hasn’t that Stone grown into a great mountain that fills the whole earth?
Do we have to point at this Mountain with our finger, the way people point at the moon when it is three days old?

For example, when people want others to see the new moon, they say, “Look, the moon! Look, there it is!” If some people there can’t see well and ask, “Where?” then someone points a finger so they can see it.
Sometimes people are embarrassed to seem blind, so they say they saw it when they really didn’t.
My brothers and sisters, do we have to point out the Church like that?
Isn’t it out in the open?
Isn’t it plain to see?
Hasn’t it spread through all nations?
Hasn’t the promise made to Abraham so many years before come true—that all nations would be blessed through his offspring?
The promise was made to one believer, and now the world is full of thousands of believers.
Look! Here is the mountain that covers the whole face of the earth!
Look! Here is the city described in these words: “A city built on a mountain cannot be hidden!”
But those people trip over the mountain. When someone tells them, “Go up,” they say, “There is no mountain.” They would rather bang their heads against it than look for a home there.

Isaiah was read yesterday. Some of you were awake—not only with your eyes but with your ears, and not just the ears of your body but the ears of your heart. You noticed this: “In the last days the mountain of the Lord’s house will be plain to see, set up on the top of the mountains.”
What is easier to see than a mountain?
But there are also mountains that people don’t know about, because they are in just one part of the world.
Which of you knows Mount Olympus?
In the same way, the people who live there don’t know our Giddaba.
These mountains are in different parts of the world.
But that Mountain is not like that. It has filled the whole face of the earth. It is the one described as “set up on the top of the mountains.”
It is a Mountain higher than the tops of all the other mountains.
He says, “And all nations will gather to it.”
Who could miss this Mountain?
Who would break his head by tripping over it?
Who doesn’t know about the city built on a mountain?
But don’t be surprised that people who hate their brothers don’t know it. They walk in the dark and don’t know where they are going, because the darkness has made their eyes blind.
They don’t see the Mountain. I don’t want you to be surprised: they have no eyes.
Why do they have no eyes?
Because the darkness has blinded them.
How can we prove this?

Because they hate their brothers. They are offended at some Africans, and so they cut themselves off from the whole world. For the sake of Christ’s peace, they will not put up with the people they slander. Yet for the sake of Donatus, they do put up with the people they condemn.
“I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven through His name.
I am writing to you, fathers, because you have known the One who is from the beginning.
I am writing to you, young men, because you have beaten the evil one.
I am writing to you, children, because you have known the Father.
I am writing to you, fathers, because you have known the One who is from the beginning.
I am writing to you, young men, because you are strong. The word of God lives in you, and you have beaten the evil one.
Do not love the world or the things in the world.
If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love is not in him.
For everything in the world is the desires of the body, the desires of the eyes, and pride in this life. These things do not come from the Father. They come from the world.
The world is passing away, and so are its desires. But whoever does what God wants will last forever (just as God also lasts forever).”
1. Everything read from the Holy Scriptures is there to teach us and to save us. So we should listen to all of it very carefully.
But we must remember most of all the parts that are strongest against heretics. Heretics never stop setting sly traps for anyone who is weaker or careless.
Remember that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ died for us and rose again. He died for our sins, and He rose again to make us right with God.

You just heard about the two disciples He met on the road. “Their eyes were kept from recognizing Him.” He found them with no hope left that Christ would set them free. They thought He had suffered and died like any man. They did not think that, as the Son of God, He lives forever. They also thought He was so dead in His body that He would never come back to life, just like one of the prophets. Those of you who were paying attention just heard their own words.

Then “He explained the Scriptures to them, starting with Moses.” He went through all the prophets. He showed them that everything He had suffered had been predicted. He did this so that they would not be even more shaken when the Lord rose again. If those things had not been told ahead of time, they might have found it even harder to believe Him.
For our faith is made firm by this: everything that happened to Christ was predicted.
So the disciples did not recognize Him until “the breaking of the bread.”
And truly, whoever does not eat and drink judgment on himself in the breaking of the bread does know Christ.
Later those eleven also “thought they were seeing a spirit.”

So He let them touch Him. He is the same One who let Himself be crucified. He let enemies crucify Him, and He let friends touch Him. But He is the Doctor who heals everyone: He healed the enemies of their wickedness and the friends of their unbelief.
You heard in the reading from the Acts of the Apostles how many thousands of the people who killed Christ came to believe.
If people who had killed Him believed later on, shouldn’t those believe who had doubted only for a little while?

And yet, even for them—and you should especially notice this and remember it—touching Him was not enough. (God chose to put into the Scriptures the things that make us strong against sly errors. And no one who wants to look like a Christian at all dares to speak against the Scriptures.) So after He let them touch Him, He did not stop there. He also wanted to make the hearts of believers strong by using the Scriptures. He was looking ahead to us, who would come later. For we have nothing of Him that we can touch, but we do have something we can read.
For if those disciples believed only because they held Him and touched Him, what are we supposed to do?
Christ has now gone up into heaven. He will not come back until the end, when He comes to judge the living and the dead.
So how will we believe? By the same thing He wanted to use to make even those who touched Him strong.
For He explained the Scriptures to them. He showed them that Christ had to suffer. He showed them that everything written about Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms had to come true.
In what He said, He covered the whole of the ancient Scriptures.
Everything in those older Scriptures speaks about Christ—but only if there are ears to hear it.
He also “opened their minds so they could understand the Scriptures.”
So we too must pray that He will open our minds.
2. But what did the Lord show them was written about Him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms?
What did He show them?
Let Him tell us Himself. The Gospel writer put it briefly, so that we would know what to believe and understand out of all the huge amount of Scripture.
There are certainly many pages and many books. But all of them are summed up in what the Lord told His disciples in a few words.
What is it? That “Christ had to suffer and rise again on the third day.”
So now you have what was said about the Bridegroom: “Christ had to suffer and rise again.” The Bridegroom has been shown to us.
Now let’s see what He says about the Bride. Then, when you know both the Bridegroom and the Bride, you will have good reason to come to the wedding.
For every celebration is a wedding celebration: we are celebrating the wedding of the Church.
The King’s Son is about to get married, and that King’s Son is a King Himself. And the guests who crowd into the wedding are themselves the Bride.

In an ordinary human wedding, some people are guests and someone else is the bride. It is not like that in the Church. In the Church, those who come as guests—if they come with the right heart—become the Bride.
For the whole Church is Christ’s Bride. Its beginning and first fruit is the flesh of Christ. That is where the Bride was joined to the Bridegroom in the flesh.
That is why, when He wanted to point to that same flesh, He broke bread. And that is why, “in the breaking of the bread,” the eyes “of the disciples were opened, and they recognized Him.”
So then, what did the Lord say was written about Him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms?
That “Christ had to suffer.”
If He had not added, “and rise again,” those whose eyes were kept from seeing might well have been sad. But “rising again” was also predicted.
Why was that? Why did Christ have to suffer and rise again?
Because of the Psalm we especially asked you to pay attention to last week, on the fourth day, at the first station.
Why did Christ have to suffer and rise again?
For this reason: “All the ends of the earth will remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations will worship before Him.”
So that you would know that Christ had to suffer and rise again, what did He add here too? After showing us the Bridegroom, He also wanted to show us the Bride.
He says, “And in His name, turning from sin and forgiveness of sins must be preached to all nations, starting at Jerusalem.”
You have heard it, brothers and sisters. Hold on to it.
No one should doubt that the Church is “in all nations.” No one should doubt that it started at Jerusalem and has filled all nations.
We know the field where the Vine was planted. But now that the Vine has grown, we can’t see the field anymore, because the Vine has covered all of it.
Where did it start?
“At Jerusalem.” How far has it reached?
To “all nations.” A few are left, but it will take over all of them.
Meanwhile, as it spreads to all of them, the Gardener has decided to cut off some useless branches. Those branches have started heresies and splits.
Don’t let the branches that were cut off talk you into being cut off too. Instead, urge those who were cut off to be grafted back in.
It is clear that Christ suffered, rose again and went up into heaven. The Church is clear to see too, because “turning from sin and forgiveness of sins are preached in His name to all nations.”
Where did it start?

“Starting at Jerusalem.” A man hears this, and he is foolish and empty-headed and—how can I put it?—worse than blind! Such a huge mountain, and he doesn’t see it! A lamp set on a lampstand, and he shuts his eyes to it!

3. We say to them, “If you are Catholic Christians, join in fellowship with the Church from which the Gospel has spread over the whole earth. Join in fellowship with Jerusalem.” When we say this, they answer, “We will not share fellowship with the city where our King was killed, where our Lord was killed.” They act as if they hate the city where our Lord was killed.
The Jews killed Him when they found Him on earth. These people mock Him while He sits in heaven!
Who is worse? Those who looked down on Him because they thought He was just a man? Or those who mock the sacraments of the One they now say is God?
But they say they hate the city where their Lord was killed!
What holy and kind people! They are very sad that Christ was killed—and yet they kill Christ in people!
But He loved that city and felt sorry for it. He commanded that the preaching about Him should start there: “starting at Jerusalem.”
He had the preaching of His name begin there. And you shudder at the idea of sharing fellowship with that city!
No wonder you hate the root, now that you have been cut off.
What did He say to His disciples?
“Stay in the city, because I am sending My promise on you.”
Look what kind of city it is that they hate!
Maybe they would love it if Christ’s murderers still lived there.
For it is well known that all of Christ’s murderers—that is, the Jews—have been driven out of that city.
The city that once held people who raged against Christ now holds people who worship Christ.
So that is why these men hate it: because Christians live there.
That is where He wanted His disciples to wait. That is where He wanted to send them the Holy Spirit.
Where did the Church begin? It began where the Holy Spirit came from heaven and filled the hundred and twenty people who were sitting together in one place.
The number twelve had been multiplied by ten.

A hundred and twenty people were sitting there. Then the Holy Spirit came, “and filled the whole place. There came a sound like a powerful wind rushing in, and there were tongues that looked like fire, split apart.”
You have heard the Acts of the Apostles. It was today’s reading: “They began to speak in languages, as the Spirit gave them the words.”

Everyone who was there—Jews who had come from many different nations—each recognized his own language. They were amazed. Those men had no schooling and no learning, and yet suddenly they had learned not just one or two languages, but the languages of every nation.
So in that place, where all the languages were heard, it was a sign that people of every language would believe.

But these men love Christ so much that they refuse to share fellowship with the city that killed Christ. And they honor Christ by claiming that He has only two languages left, Latin and Punic, that is,
African. Imagine Christ owning only two languages!
For those are the only two languages on Donatus’s side. They have no others.

Let’s wake up, my brothers and sisters! Let’s look instead at the gift of God’s Spirit. Let’s believe what was said ahead of time about Him, and let’s see the words of the Psalm come true: “There are no speeches or words where their voices are not heard among them.”

Someone might think that all the languages came together to one place, instead of Christ’s gift going out to all languages. So listen to what comes next: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”
Why is that? Because “He has set His tent in the sun”—that is, out in the open light.
His tent is His body. His tent is His Church. It is set “in the sun”—not in the night, but in the day.
So why don’t those people recognize it?

Go back to the reading where it stopped yesterday, and you will see why they don’t recognize it: “Whoever hates his brother walks in the dark and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has made his eyes blind.”
As for us, let’s look at what comes next, so that we are not in the dark.
How can we stay out of the dark?
By loving our brothers and sisters.
How can it be shown that we love the family of believers?
By not tearing apart our unity, and by holding on to love.
4. “I am writing to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven through His name.”
He calls you “little children” because you are born when your sins are forgiven.
But through whose name are sins forgiven?
Through Augustine’s name? No! So not through the name of Donatus either.
It is up to you to see who Augustine is, or who Donatus is. But sins are not forgiven through the name of Paul, or through the name of Peter.

Some people divided up the Church among themselves and tried to break unity into different groups. To them, Mother Love speaks through the apostle. She is like a mother in labor with her little ones. She shows them her very heart. With her words she almost tears open her chest. She weeps for her children, whom she sees being carried out dead. They insisted on having many names, and she calls them back to the one Name. She pushes them away from loving her, so that they will love Christ. And she says, “Was Paul crucified for you?
Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?”

What is he saying? “I don’t want you to belong to me—that way you can be with me. Be with me! We all belong to Him who died for us, who was crucified for us.” That is why it says here too, “Your sins are forgiven through His name”—not through the name of any human being.
5. “I am writing to you, fathers.”
Why does he call them sons first? “Because your sins are forgiven through His name.” You are born again into a new life, so you are sons.
Why fathers? “Because you have known the One who is from the beginning.” Being a father has to do with a beginning.
Christ is new in His human body, but ancient as God.
How ancient do we think He is? How many years old?
Do we think He is older than His mother?
He is certainly older than His mother, for “all things were made through Him.”
If He made all things, then the Ancient One made the very mother from whom the New One would be born.
Do we think He existed only before His mother?
In fact, He is even older than His mother’s ancestors.
His mother’s ancestor was Abraham. And the Lord says, “Before Abraham, I am.”
Do we say, “Before Abraham”?
Heaven and earth were made before there were any people.
The Lord existed before these. Better still, He simply is.
That is why He puts it so perfectly. He does not say, “Before Abraham I was,” but, “Before Abraham I Am.”
For what we say “was” does not exist anymore, and what we say “will be” does not exist yet. But He knows only how to be.
As God, He knows “to be.” He does not know “was” and “will be.”
There, it is one day—but a day that lasts forever and ever.
That day is not stuck between a yesterday and a tomorrow. Here, when “yesterday” is over, “today” begins, and then “today” is ended by the coming “tomorrow.”
That one day there is a day with no darkness, no night, no gaps, no measuring, no hours.
Call it whatever you like. If you like, it is a day. If you like, it is a year. If you like, it is years.
For Scripture says about it, “And Your years will never run out.”
But when is it called a day?
When these words are said to the Lord: “Today I have fathered You.”
He is born of the eternal Father. He is born from eternity, born in eternity. He has no beginning, no limit, no stretch of space. That is because He is the One who is. He Himself is “He Who Is.”
He told Moses this name of His: “Tell them, ‘He Who Is has sent me to you.’”
So why just say “before Abraham”? Why not before Noah? Why not before Adam?
Listen to the Scripture: “Before the morning star I fathered You.”
In short, before heaven and earth.
Why? Because “all things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made.”
This is how you can tell who the “fathers” are: they become fathers by recognizing “the One who is from the beginning.”
6. “I am writing to you, young men.”
There are sons, there are fathers, and there are young men. They are sons because they have been born. They are fathers because they recognize the Beginning. Why are they young men?
“Because you have beaten the evil one.”
In the sons, we see birth. In the fathers, we see great age. In the young men, we see strength.
If the evil one is “beaten” by the young men, that means he fights against us.
He fights, but he doesn’t win.
Why not? Is it because we are strong? Or is it because He is strong in us—the One who was found weak in the hands of those who persecuted Him?
He made us strong—He who did not fight back against the people who persecuted Him.
“For He was crucified because of weakness, but He is alive by the power of God.”
7. “I am writing to you, children.”
Why children? “Because you have known the Father.
I am writing to you, fathers.” He stresses this and says it again: “Because you have known the One who is from the beginning.”
Remember that you are fathers. If you forget “the One who is from the beginning,” you have lost your fatherhood.
“I am writing to you, young men.”
Think about it again and again: you are young men. Fight, so that you can win. Win, so that you can be crowned. Stay humble, so that you don’t fall in the fight.
“I am writing to you, young men, because you are strong. The word of God lives in you, and you have beaten the evil one.”

8. My brothers and sisters, think about all these things: “because we have known the One who is from the beginning, because we are strong, because we have known the Father.” In a way, they all praise knowledge. But don’t they also praise love?
If we know, then let’s love. For knowledge without love does not save anyone.
“Knowledge makes people proud, but love builds them up.”
If you want to confess Him but not love Him, you are starting to be like the demons.
The demons confessed that He was the Son of God. They said, “What do we have to do with You?” And they were driven away.
Confess Him and hold Him close. The demons were afraid because of their sins. But you, love Him who forgives your sins.
But how can we love God if we love the world?
So He gets us ready for love to live in us.

There are two loves: love of the world and love of God. If love of the world lives in you, love of God has no way to get in. Let love of the world move out, and let love of God move in. Let the better love have the room.

You used to love the world. Stop loving the world. When you have emptied your heart of earthly love, you will drink in God’s love. From then on, love begins to live in you, and nothing evil can come from it.
So listen to his words. See how he works like someone clearing land.
He comes to people’s hearts like a field he wants to take over. But what shape does he find it in?
If he finds a forest, he pulls it up by the roots. If he finds the field already cleared, he plants it.
He wants to plant a tree there: love.
And what is the forest he wants to pull up?
Love of the world.
Listen to him, the one who pulls up the forest!
“Do not love the world,” (this is what comes next) “or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love is not in him.”
9. You have heard it: “If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love is not in him.”

Brothers and sisters, no one should say in his heart that this is not true. God says it. The Holy Spirit has spoken through the apostle. Nothing is truer: “If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love is not in him.”
Do you want the Father’s love, so that you can share the inheritance with the Son?
Then don’t love the world.
Shut out the bad love of the world, so that you can be filled with God’s love.
You are a container, but right now you are full.
Pour out what you have, so that you can receive what you don’t have.
Our brothers and sisters have just now been born again of water and the Spirit. Some years ago we too were born again of water and the Spirit.
It is good for us not to love the world. Otherwise the sacraments will stay in us to condemn us, instead of making us strong to be saved.
What makes us strong to be saved is having the root of love. It is having “the power of godliness,” not just “the outward form.”
The form is good. The form is holy. But what use is the form if it isn’t attached to the root?
When a branch is cut off, isn’t it thrown into the fire?
Have the form, but keep it in the root.
But how can you be rooted so that you won’t be pulled up?
By holding on to love. As the apostle Paul says, “rooted and firmly set in love.”
How can love take root there, in a heart that is an overgrown wilderness of love for the world?
Clear away the forest completely.
You are about to plant a mighty seed. Don’t let anything in the field choke it.
These are the words he spoke to pull things up by the roots: “Do not love the world or the things in the world.
If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love is not in him.”
10. “For everything in the world is the desires of the body, the desires of the eyes, and pride in this life.” He has named three things. They do not come from the Father, but from the world.
“The world is passing away, and so are its desires. But whoever does what God wants will last forever, just as He lasts forever.”
Why shouldn’t I love what God made?
What do you want? Do you want to love the things of time and pass away with time? Or do you want to stop loving the world and live forever with God?
The river of passing things sweeps people along. But our Lord Jesus Christ is like a tree that has grown up beside the river.
He took on a human body, died, rose again and went up into heaven.
In a way, He chose to plant Himself beside the river of passing things.
Are you being swept down the stream, rushing toward the deep?
Grab hold of the tree.
Is love of the world spinning you around?
Grab hold of Christ. For your sake He became part of time, so that you could become eternal. For He became part of time in such a way that He still stayed eternal.
Something from time was added to Him, but nothing was taken away from His eternity.
But you were born into time, and sin made you a creature of time. You were made part of time by sin. He was made part of time by mercy, to forgive sins.
Think how different two people in a prison can be—the criminal and the one who visits him!
Sometimes a person goes to see his friend and goes inside to visit him. Both of them seem to be in prison, but there is a huge difference between them.
One is held down by his crime. The other is brought there by kindness.
It is the same in this mortal life of ours. We were held tight by our guilt. He came down out of mercy. He came in to the prisoner as a Rescuer, not as an oppressor.
The Lord shed His blood for us. He bought us back. He changed our hope.
For now we still carry bodies that will die, and we trust that we will live forever in the future. We are tossed by the waves on the sea, but the anchor of our hope is already fixed on land.
11. But let’s “not love the world or the things in the world.
For the things in the world are the desires of the body, the desires of the eyes, and pride in this life.”
These are the three. He says this so that no one will say, “God made the things in the world: heaven and earth, the sea, the sun, the moon, the stars, and everything that decorates the sky.
What decorates the sea? All the creeping creatures.
What decorates the earth? Animals, trees and birds.
These are ‘in the world,’ and God made them.
So why shouldn’t I love what God has made?”
May God’s Spirit be in you, so that you can see that all these things are good. But how terrible for you if you love the things that were made and abandon the One who made them!
They are beautiful to you, but how much more beautiful is the One who formed them!

Pay close attention, dear friends. Examples can teach you. Otherwise Satan might sneak up on you and say what he usually says: “Enjoy the things God has created. Why else did He make them, if not for you to enjoy?”
And people get themselves drunk, and they are ruined, and they forget their own Creator. When they use created things with greed instead of self-control, the Creator is treated with contempt.
The apostle speaks about people like that: “They worshiped and served what He created, rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever.”
God does not forbid you to love these things. But you must not set your heart on them as if they could make you truly happy. Instead, value them and praise them, so that you will love your Creator.

My brothers and sisters, it is like this. Suppose a bridegroom made a ring for his bride. And suppose that after she received it, she loved the ring more than she loved the bridegroom who made it for her. Wouldn’t her heart be guilty of adultery in the very gift the bridegroom gave her? And that is true even though all she loved was his gift.
Of course she should love what the bridegroom gave her. But what if she said, “This ring is enough for me. I don’t want to see his face anymore”? What kind of woman would she be?
Who wouldn’t hate such foolishness? Who wouldn’t say she has an unfaithful heart?

You love the gold instead of the man. You love a ring instead of the bridegroom. Suppose that is true of you—you love a ring instead of your bridegroom and have no wish to see him. Then the gift he gave you as a promise is not tying you to him. It is turning your heart away from him!
The reason a bridegroom gives a promise-gift is so that he himself will be loved through it.
So then: God gave you all these things. Love the One who made them.
He wants to give you even more. He wants to give you Himself, the One who made these things.
But if you love these things—even though God made them—and ignore the Creator and love the world, won’t your love be counted as unfaithful, like adultery?

12. The word “world” doesn’t only mean the things God made—heaven and earth, the sea, things we can see and things we can’t. The people who live in the world are also called “the world.” It’s like the word “house.” We use it for the walls, and also for the people who live inside.
Sometimes we praise a house but find fault with the people who live in it.

We say, “That’s a good house,” because it has marble and beautiful ceilings. But we also say, “That’s a good house,” in another way. We mean that no one there is treated unfairly. No one there robs or bullies anyone.
Then we are praising the people who live in the building, not the building itself. Yet we call both of them a “house.”

All who love the world live in the world through their love. In the same way, some people live in heaven: their hearts are up there, even while their bodies walk on earth. So, as I said, all who love the world are called “the world.”
These people have only three things: “the desires of the body, the desires of the eyes, and empty pride in this life.”
They crave eating, drinking and sex. They want to enjoy these pleasures.
Surely it doesn’t mean there is no proper amount of these things. When it says, “Don’t love these things,” does that mean you must not eat, or drink, or have children?
That is not what it is saying.
Just keep a limit, for the Creator’s sake, so that these things don’t tie you down because you love them. Don’t love for pleasure the things you should only use.
But you are only really tested when two things are put in front of you and you must choose one: Do you want to do what is right, or do you want to make money?
“But I don’t have enough to live on. I don’t have enough to eat or drink.”
But what if the only way you can get these things is by doing wrong?
Isn’t it better to love what you can never lose than to lose yourself by doing wrong?
You see the gold you gain. You don’t see the faith you lose.
So this is what he tells us “the desires of the body” means: craving the things that belong to the body, like food and sex, and all other things like that.
13. “And the desires of the eyes.” By “the desires of the eyes” he means every kind of curiosity.
And curiosity reaches so far!
Curiosity is what is at work in public shows, in theaters, in the devil’s rituals, in magic, and in dealings with dark powers. It is nothing but curiosity.

Sometimes it even tempts God’s servants. They want to work a miracle, so to speak. They want to test God to see if He will answer their prayers by doing miracles. That is curiosity. That is “the desires of the eyes.” It “does not come from the Father.”
If God has given you the power, then do the miracle, because He has made it possible for you. But don’t think that people who have never done miracles won’t be part of God’s kingdom.
The apostles were once very happy that the demons obeyed them. What did the Lord say to them then?
“Don’t be happy about this. Be happy because your names are written in heaven.”
He wanted the apostles to be happy about the very same thing that makes you happy.
How terrible for you if your name is not written in heaven!
But is it terrible for you if you don’t raise the dead? Is it terrible for you if you don’t walk on the sea? Is it terrible for you if you don’t drive out demons?
If you have been given the power to do these things, use it humbly, not proudly.
The Lord even said that certain false prophets “will do signs and wonders.”
So don’t have “worldly ambition.” Ambitio saeculi means pride.
Such a man wants to make himself important through the honors he receives. He thinks he is great because he is rich or because he has some power.
14. There are these three things. You will not find anything that can tempt human desire except these three: the desires of the body, the desires of the eyes, and pride in this life.
The devil tempted the Lord with these same three things.
He was tempted with the desires of the body when He was hungry after His fast. The devil said to Him, “If You are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.”
But how did He push the tempter away? And how did He teach His soldier to fight?
Listen to what He said to him: “A person does not live on bread alone, but on every word of God.”

He was also tempted with the desires of the eyes, through a miracle. The devil said to Him, “Throw Yourself down. For it is written: He will give His angels orders to watch over You. They will hold You up in their hands, so that You never strike Your foot against a stone.”

He resisted the tempter. If He had done the miracle, it would only have looked as though He had given in, or had done it out of curiosity. For He did miracles whenever He wanted, because He is God—but He did them to heal the weak.
If He had done it at that moment, people might have thought He just wanted to perform a miracle.

So that no one would think that, listen to how He answered. And when you face a temptation like this, you say the same thing: “Get behind Me, Satan! For it is written: You must not test the Lord your God.” In other words: if I do this, I will be testing God.
He said what He wants you to say.
The enemy may whisper to you, “What kind of person are you? What kind of Christian are you?

Have you done even one miracle yet? Have your prayers raised anyone from the dead? Have you healed anyone with a fever? If you really mattered, you would do some miracle.” Then answer him: “It is written: You must not test the Lord your God.” So I will not test God. I will not act as if I belong to God only if I do a miracle, and don’t belong to Him if I don’t. Otherwise, what happens to His words, “Be happy because your names are written in heaven”?
How was the Lord tempted with “pride in this life”?
The devil took Him up to a high place and said to Him, “I will give You all of this if You will bow down and worship me.”
He wanted to tempt the King of all worlds with the greatness of an earthly kingdom. But the Lord who made heaven and earth crushed the devil under His feet.
Is it any great thing for the Lord to defeat the devil?
So what was He doing when He answered the devil? He was teaching you the answer He wants you to give.
“It is written: Worship the Lord your God, and serve Him alone.”

If you hold on to these things, you will not have the world’s cravings. And if you don’t have the world’s cravings, then the desires of the body, the desires of the eyes, and pride in this life will not rule over you. And you will make room for Love when she comes, so that you can love God.
For if love for the world is there, love for God will not be there.
Instead, hold on to the love of God. Then, just as God lasts forever and ever, you too can last forever and ever. For each person is like what he loves.
Do you love the earth? You will be earth.
Do you love God? What should I say—that you will be a god?
I don’t dare say that on my own. Let’s listen to the Scriptures: “I have said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.”
So if you want to be gods and sons of the Most High, then “don’t love the world or the things in the world.
If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.

For everything in the world—the desires of the body, the desires of the eyes, and pride in this life—does not come from the Father. It comes from the world.” That means it comes from people who love the world.
“And the world is passing away, and its desires with it. But whoever does the will of God lasts forever, just as God also lasts forever.”
“Children, it is the last hour. You have heard that the antichrist is coming, and even now many antichrists have appeared. That is how we know it is the last hour.

They went out from us, but they were not truly part of us. If they had been part of us, they would surely have stayed with us. But they went out so that it would become clear that not all of them were part of us.
But you have been anointed by the Holy One, and you know all things.
I am writing to you, not because you don’t know the truth, but because you do know it, and you know that no lie comes from the truth.
Who is a liar? Whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ.
[Whoever denies the Father and the Son is the antichrist.]
Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father or the Son. But whoever acknowledges the Son has both the Father and the Son.
So let what you heard from the beginning stay in you.
If what you heard from the beginning stays in you, you will also remain in the Son and in the Father.
And this is what He has promised us: eternal life.
I have written these things to you about those who are trying to lead you astray. I want you to know that you have an anointing, and that the anointing you received from Him should stay in you.
You don’t need anyone to teach you, because His anointing teaches you about all things.”
1. “Children, it is the last hour.”
In this reading he speaks to the children. He wants them to hurry up and grow, because “it is the last hour.”
You can’t choose how old or how tall your body is.
A person doesn’t grow physically whenever he wants, any more than he is born whenever he wants. But where being born depends on the will, growing depends on the will too.
No one is “born of water and the Spirit” unless he is willing.
So if he chooses, he grows and increases. If he chooses, he shrinks.
What does it mean to grow?
To move forward by making progress.
What does it mean to shrink?
To slide backward by falling short.
Whoever knows he has been born should understand that he is a baby. He should eagerly hold on to his mother’s breasts, and he will grow quickly.
His mother is the Church. Her breasts are the two Testaments of the holy Scriptures.

So he should drink the milk of all the things that happened in history for our eternal salvation, as signs of spiritual truths. Then, fed and made strong, he can go on to eat solid food. That solid food is this: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
Our milk is Christ in His humility. Our solid food is the very same Christ, equal with the Father.
He feeds you with milk so that later He can feed you with bread. For to touch Christ spiritually with your heart means to know that He is equal with the Father.
2. That is why He told Mary not to touch Him. He said to her, “Don’t touch Me, because I have not yet gone up to the Father.”
What does this mean? He let the disciples handle Him. Did He then avoid Mary’s touch?
Isn’t He the same one who said to the doubting disciple, “Put your fingers here, and feel the scars”?
Had He gone up to the Father by then?
Then why does He stop Mary and say, “Don’t touch Me, because I have not yet gone up to the Father”?
Or should we say that He wasn’t afraid of being touched by men, but was afraid of being touched by women?
His touch makes all flesh clean.
He chose to show Himself first to women. Was He afraid of being handled by them?
Wasn’t His resurrection announced to the men by women? That way the serpent would be defeated by a kind of counter-plan.
The serpent first brought news of death to man through a woman. So news of life was also brought to men through a woman.
Then why did He not want to be touched? Only because He wanted us to understand a spiritual kind of touch.
Spiritual touch comes from a pure heart.
A person touches Christ with a pure heart when he understands that Christ is fully equal with the Father.
But someone who does not yet understand that Christ is God reaches only His body. He does not reach His divine nature.
And what is so great about reaching only what the persecutors who crucified Him reached?

The great thing is this: to understand that the Word is God with God, in the beginning, and that all things were made through Him. That is how He wanted to be known when He said to Philip, “I have been with you such a long time, and you still don’t know Me, Philip?
Whoever sees Me also sees the Father.”
3. But in case anyone is lazy about moving forward, let him listen: “Children, it is the last hour.”
Move forward! Run! Grow! “It is the last hour.”
This last hour is long, but it is still the last.
He used the word “hour” to mean “the last time,” because our Lord Jesus Christ will come in the last times.
But some people will say, How can these be the last times? How can this be the last hour?
Surely the antichrist will come first, and after that the day of judgment will come.

John saw that people would think like this. He didn’t want them to feel too safe and think it wasn’t the last hour yet just because the antichrist was still to come. So he said to them, “You have heard that the antichrist is coming, and now many antichrists have come.”
Could there be many antichrists if it were not “the last hour”?
4. Who are the people he calls antichrists?
He goes on and explains it.
“That is how we know it is the last hour.”
How do we know? Because “many antichrists have come.
They went out from us.” Look—there are the antichrists!
“They went out from us.” So we grieve over losing them.
Now hear the comfort: “But they were not truly part of us.”
All heretics and all who split the Church went out from us. That means they leave the Church. But they would not leave if they were truly part of us.
So even before they left, they were not part of us.
And if they were not part of us even before they left, then many people are still inside. They have not left, but they are still antichrists.
We dare to say this. Why? So that no one who is inside will be an antichrist.
For he is about to describe the antichrists and point them out, and we will see them in a moment.
And each person should question his own conscience and ask whether he is an antichrist.
In our language, “antichrist” means “against Christ.”
Some people think the name means he will come ante Christum—“before Christ.” That is,
that Christ will come after him. But it doesn’t mean that, and that is not how it is written. It is written Antichristus, which means “against Christ.”
You already see from the apostle’s own explanation who is against Christ. You understand that only antichrists can go out. Those who are not against Christ can never go out.
Anyone who is not against Christ holds on firmly in His body and is counted as one of its parts.
The parts of a body never fight against each other.
The whole body is made up of all its parts.
And what does the apostle say about how the parts agree with each other?
