And what does this mean: “Do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing”? What else can it mean, except that the right hand stands for a pure conscience, and the left hand for the craving for worldly things?
Many people do many amazing things because they crave worldly things. Then the left hand is working, not the right.
The right hand should do the work, and without the left hand knowing. That way, the craving for worldly things will not even mix itself in when we do something good out of love.
And where do we find this out?
You are standing before God. Question your heart. Look at what you have done and what you were aiming for in it: your salvation, or the empty praise of people?
Look inside, because no person can judge someone he cannot see.
If “we reassure our heart,” let it be “before Him.”

Because “if our heart thinks badly of us”—that is, if it accuses us inside, telling us we did not do the thing with the attitude we should have—“God is greater than our heart, and He knows everything.”
You hide your heart from people. Hide it from God, if you can!
How will you hide it from Him? A sinner, full of fear and confessing, says to Him, “Where can I go to get away from Your Spirit? And where can I run from Your face?”
He looked for a way to run away and escape God's judgment, and he found none.
For where is God not?
“If I go up to heaven,” he says, “You are there. If I go down to hell, You are there.”
Where will you go? Where will you run?
Do you want some advice?
If you want to run from Him, run to Him.
Run to Him by confessing, not away from Him by hiding. You cannot hide, but you can confess.
Say to Him, “You are my place of safety.” And let love be fed in you, because love alone leads to life.
Let your conscience be your witness that your love comes from God.
If it comes from God, do not try to show it off to people. For people's praise does not lift you up to heaven, and their criticism does not pull you down from there.
Let Him see it—the One who gives you the crown. Let Him be your witness—the Judge who crowns you.
“God is greater than our heart, and He knows everything.”
4. “Dear friends, if our heart does not think badly of us, we can be confident before God.” What does “If our heart does not think badly of us” mean?

It means this: our heart tells us truthfully that we love, and that there is real love in us—not fake but sincere. It is a love that looks for a brother's salvation and expects to gain nothing from him except his salvation. Then “we can be confident before God, and whatever we ask for, we will receive from Him, because we keep His commandments.” So this is not in front of people, but where God Himself sees, in the heart. Then “we can be confident before God, and whatever we ask for, we will receive from Him”—but only because we keep His commandments.
What are “His commandments”?
Do we have to keep repeating it?
“I give you a new commandment: love one another.”
It is love itself that he is talking about. This is what he is pressing on us.

So suppose someone has love for his brothers and sisters, and has it before God, where God sees. And suppose his heart is questioned in a fair examination and gives him no other answer than this: the true root of love is there, and good fruit will come from it. That person can be confident before God. Whatever he asks for, he will receive from Him, because he keeps His commandments.

5. Here we run into a question. It is not about this person or that person, or about you or me. If I ask God for something and do not get it, anyone could easily say about me, “He does not have love.” That could easily be said about anyone living today. Let people think what they like—one person about another. No, the question is not really about us. It is about those people who, as everyone knows, were saints when they wrote, and who are now with God.

Who could have love, if Paul did not have it? He said, “We have spoken openly to you, Corinthians. Our heart is wide open. We are not holding back from you.” He also said, “I will gladly spend myself for your souls.” There was so much grace in him that it was clear he had love.
And yet we find that he asked for something and did not receive it.
What do we say to that, brothers and sisters?
It is a real question. Look carefully to God. This too is a big question.

Remember what was said about sin: “Anyone who is born of God does not sin.” We found that this sin meant breaking love. That was exactly what that passage meant. In the same way, we now ask what John means here.
If you look only at the words, the meaning seems clear. But if you think about real examples, it becomes hard to understand.
Nothing could be clearer than the words here.
“And we will receive from Him whatever we ask, because we keep His commands and do the things that please Him.”
“Whatever we ask,” he says, “we will receive from Him.”
He has put us in a very tight spot.

He would have put us in a tight spot in the other passage too, if he had meant every sin. But there we found a way to explain it. He meant one certain sin, not every sin. It was a sin that “anyone who is born of God does not commit.” And we found that this sin is nothing other than breaking love.
We also have a clear example from the Gospel. The Lord says, “If I had not come, they would not have had sin.”
What does that mean? Were the Jews innocent when He came to them, just because He talks like this?
If He had not come, would they have had no sin at all?
Did the Doctor’s visit make people sick instead of taking away their fever?
Who would be crazy enough to say that?
He came for one reason only: to cure and heal the sick.
So when He said, “If I had not come, they would not have had sin,” what did He want us to understand? He meant one particular sin.
There was one sin the Jews would not have had.
Which sin? That they did not believe in Him. When He came, they looked down on Him.

There He said “sin,” but that does not mean every sin, only a certain sin. It is the same here. John does not mean every sin. Otherwise it would go against the place where he says, “If we say that we have no sin, we fool ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” He means one particular sin: breaking love.

But in this passage he has tied us up even more tightly. He says, “If we ask”—“if our heart does not accuse us, but answers us before God that true love is in us”—then “we will receive from Him whatever we ask.”
6. Now then, my dear brothers and sisters, I have already told you: nobody should look to us.
After all, what are we? And what are you?
We are simply the Church of God, which everyone knows.
If it pleases God, we are in that Church. Those of us who stay in it through love should keep going there, if we want to show the love we have.
But what about the apostle Paul? What bad thing should we think about him?
Paul—not love his brothers and sisters? Impossible!
Paul—not have the witness of his conscience inside him before God? Impossible!
Paul—not have inside him that root of love from which all his good fruit grew? Impossible!
Who would be crazy enough to say that?
So where do we find that the apostle asked and did not receive?
He tells us himself: “So that I would not become too proud because of all the great things God showed me, I was given a thorn in my flesh. It was an angel of Satan sent to beat me.
I pleaded with the Lord three times to take it away from me.
And He said to me, My grace is enough for you, because strength is made complete in weakness.”
So you see, he prayed that the “angel of Satan” would be taken away from him, and that prayer was not answered.
Why not? Because it was not good for him.
So he was heard for his salvation, even though he did not get what he wanted.
My dear friends, understand this great mystery. We want you to think about it carefully so that you do not forget it when you are tempted.

God always hears the saints in a way that leads to their salvation. He always hears them in everything that has to do with their eternal salvation. That is what they really want, and in this their prayers are always answered.
7. But let us look at the different ways God answers prayer.
Some people do not get what they want, but they are heard for their salvation. And some people get what they want, but they are not heard for their salvation.
Notice this difference. Hold on to this example of a man who did not get what he wanted but was heard for his salvation.
Listen to the apostle Paul. God Himself showed him what it means to be heard for salvation. God said, “My grace is enough for you, because strength is made complete in weakness.”

You begged. You cried out. You cried out three times. I heard your cry once and for all. I did not turn My ears away from you. I know what I should do. You want Me to take away the thing that burns you, even though it is healing you. I know the weakness that weighs you down.
So here is a man who was heard for his salvation, even though he did not get what he wanted.
Where do we find people who got what they wanted but were not heard for their salvation?
Do you think we can find some wicked, ungodly person whom God gave what he wanted, but not in a way that led to his salvation?
If I gave you the example of some person, you might say to me, “You are the one calling him wicked. He was actually a good man. If he had not been good, God would not have answered his prayer.”
So the example I am going to give is someone whose wickedness and ungodliness nobody can doubt.
The devil himself. He asked for Job, and he got him.
Haven’t you also heard here about the devil, that “whoever commits sin is from the devil”?
That does not mean the devil created the sinner. It means the sinner copies the devil.
Isn’t it said about him, “He did not stand in the truth”?
Isn’t he also “that old serpent”? Through the woman he handed the first man a drink of poison.
And in Job’s case, didn’t he leave Job his wife, so that she would tempt her husband instead of comforting him?
The devil asked for a holy man so he could tempt him, and he got what he asked for. The apostle asked for the thorn in his flesh to be taken away, and he did not get it.
But the apostle was heard more than the devil.
The apostle was heard for his salvation, though not for what he wanted. The devil got what he wanted, but it led to his damnation.
Job was handed over to him to be tempted so that, when Job stood firm under the test, the devil would be tormented.
My brothers and sisters, we find this not only in the books of the Old Testament, but also in the Gospel.
When the Lord drove the demons out of a man, they begged Him to let them go into the pigs.
Didn’t the Lord have the power to tell them to stay away even from those animals?
If He had not wanted to allow it, they could never have rebelled against the King of heaven and earth.
But He let the demons go into the pigs because of a certain mystery, a deeper meaning. He wanted to show that the devil rules over people who live like pigs.
So the demons got what they asked for. Was the apostle not heard?
Or should we rather say—and this is more true—that the apostle was heard and the demons were not?
They got what they wanted. He got what was truly good for him, and it was made complete.
8. So we should understand this: even when God does not give us what we want, He gives us what we need for our salvation.
Suppose you ask for something that would hurt you, and the Doctor knows it would hurt you. What then?
We should not say that the doctor is not listening to you. Maybe you ask for cold water. If it is good for you, he gives it to you right away. If it is not good for you, he does not give it.
Was he refusing to listen to you? Or was he listening for your good, even when he said no to what you wanted?
So, my brothers and sisters, have love in you. Let love be in you, and then you can be at peace. Even when you do not get what you ask for, your prayer is answered. You just do not know it.
Many people have been left to have their own way, and it has hurt them. The apostle speaks about them: “God handed them over to the evil desires of their own hearts.”
Someone asks for a large amount of money. He gets it, and it hurts him.
When he did not have it, he had little to fear. But as soon as he had it, more powerful people went after him like hunters after prey.
Wasn’t that man’s prayer answered to his own harm? He insisted on having something that made robbers come looking for him. When he was poor, nobody came looking for him.
Learn to pray to God in a way that leaves it to the Doctor to do what He knows is best.
You admit that you are sick. Let Him choose the cure.
All you need to do is hold on to love.
He must cut, and He must burn. What if you cry out, and He does not spare you because of your crying while He cuts and burns and it hurts? Still, He knows how far the rot has spread.
You want Him to take His hands off you right now. But He is thinking only about how deep the wound is. He knows how far He needs to go.
He does not listen to you to give you what you want. But He does listen to you to make you well.

So, my brothers and sisters, be sure that what the apostle says is true: “We do not know what we ought to pray for as we should. But the Spirit Himself pleads for us with groans no one can put into words. He pleads for the saints.”
Why does it say, “The Spirit Himself pleads for the saints”? It means the love that the Spirit produces in you.
That is why the same apostle says, “The love of God is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, whom God gave to us.”
It is love that groans. It is love that prays. And the One who gave that love cannot close His ears to it.
So be at peace. Let love do the asking, and God’s ears are there listening.
What happens is not what you want, but what is good for you.

So John says, “Whatever we ask, we will receive from Him.” As I already said, if you take this to mean “for our salvation,” there is no problem. If you do not take it that way, there is a problem, and a big one. It is a problem that would make you accuse the apostle Paul.
“Whatever we ask, we receive from Him, because we keep His commands and do the things that please Him”—inside, where He sees.
9. And what are those commands?
“This,” he says, “is His command: that we believe in the name of His Son Jesus Christ and love one another.”
You see that this is the command. You see that anyone who goes against this command commits the sin from which “everyone who is born of God” is free.
“As He commanded us”: that we love one another.
“And whoever keeps His command”—you see that we are told to do nothing else but love one another—“whoever keeps His command will live in Him, and He in him.”
“And this is how we know that He lives in us: by the Spirit He has given us.
Isn’t it clear that this is what the Holy Spirit does in a person—He fills him with love and charity?
Isn’t it clear, as the apostle Paul says, that “the love of God is poured out in our hearts by the Holy Spirit, whom God gave to us”?
For [our apostle] was talking about love. He was saying that we should question our own heart before God.
“But if our heart does not think badly of us”—that is, if our heart admits that whatever good work we do comes from love for our brother.
Then, when he talks about the command, he also says this: “This is His command: that we believe in the name of His Son Jesus Christ and love one another, as He commanded us.”
“And whoever does what He commands lives in Him, and He in him.
This is how we know that He lives in us: by the Spirit He has given us.”
If you truly find that you have love, then you have the Spirit of God so that you can understand. And that is a very necessary thing.
10. In the very early days, “the Holy Spirit came down on those who believed, and they spoke in tongues”—languages they had never learned—“as the Spirit gave them the words.”
These were signs that fit that time.
There had to be this sign of the Holy Spirit in all languages. It showed that the Gospel of God would spread through every language over the whole earth.
That was done as a sign, and then it passed away.
Today, when we lay hands on people so that they may receive the Holy Spirit, do we expect them to speak in tongues?

When we laid our hands on these babies, did any of you watch to see if they would speak in tongues? And when you saw that they did not, did any of you get it so wrong as to say, “These babies have not received the Holy Spirit. If they had, they would speak in tongues, as people did back then”?
So if these miracles are no longer the proof that the Holy Spirit is present, what is the proof? How can someone know that he has received the Holy Spirit?
Let him ask his own heart.
If he loves his brother, the Spirit of God lives in him.
Let him look. Let him test himself before God’s eyes. Let him see if he loves peace and unity. Let him see if he loves the Church that is spread over the whole earth.
He should not be satisfied just with loving the brother he can see. We have many brothers and sisters we do not see, and we are joined to them in the unity of the Spirit.
Why be surprised that they are not here with us?
We are in one body. We have one Head, and He is in heaven.
Brothers and sisters, our two eyes cannot see each other. You could say they do not know each other.
But in the love that holds the body together, don’t they know each other?
Here is how you can tell that they know each other in the love that joins them: when both eyes are open, the right eye cannot rest on anything unless the left eye rests on it too.
Try to aim your right eye at something without the left, if you can.
They meet together on one thing. They point together at one thing. They have one aim, even though they are in different places.
So if everyone who loves God along with you has the same aim as you, don’t worry that your bodies are in different places. The eyes of your hearts are fixed together on the same light of truth.
So if you want to know whether you have received the Spirit, ask your heart. You might have the sacrament but not have the power of the sacrament.
Ask your heart. If love for your brothers and sisters is there, you can be at peace.
There cannot be love without the Spirit of God. Paul cries out, “The love of God is poured out in your hearts by the Holy Spirit, whom God gave to us.”
11. “Beloved friends, do not believe every spirit.”
He said this because he had just said, “This is how we know that He lives in us: by the Spirit He has given us.”
But how can we know this same Spirit? Listen: “Beloved friends, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they come from God.”
And who is able to test the spirits?
He has given us a hard task, my brothers and sisters!
It is good for us that he tells us himself how to tell them apart.
He is about to tell us, so do not be afraid. But first, look. Notice that this passage speaks of the very thing that empty-headed heretics mock us about.
Look closely at what he says: “Beloved friends, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they come from God.”
In the Gospel the Holy Spirit is called water. The Lord “cried out and said, If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink.
Whoever believes in Me, rivers of living water will flow from deep inside him.”
But the Gospel writer explains what He was talking about. He goes on to say, “He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him would receive.”
Why didn’t the Lord baptize many people?
But what does the Gospel writer say?
“The Holy Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

So those people had been baptized, but they had not yet received the Holy Spirit. The Lord sent the Spirit from heaven on the day of Pentecost. First they had to wait for the Lord to be glorified, and then the Spirit could be given.

Even before He was glorified and before He sent the Spirit, He still invited people to get ready to receive the water He spoke about: “Whoever is thirsty, let him come and drink.” And, “Whoever believes in Me, rivers of living water will flow from deep inside him.”
What does “rivers of living water” mean?
What is that water?
Don’t ask me. Ask the Gospel.
“He said this,” it says, “about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him would receive.”
So the water of the sacrament is one thing. The water that stands for the Spirit of God is another.
The water of the sacrament can be seen. The water of the Spirit cannot be seen.
The first washes the body, and it is a sign of what happens in the soul.
By this Spirit the soul itself is made clean and fed.
This is the Spirit of God. Heretics and all who cut themselves off from the Church cannot have Him.
Some people do not openly cut themselves off, but their wickedness cuts them off. They are inside, but they blow around like chaff and are not real grain. These people do not have this Spirit.
The Lord calls this Spirit by the name of water. We have heard this letter say, “Do not believe every spirit.” And the words of Solomon agree: “Stay far away from strange water.”
What does “water” mean here? The Spirit.
Does water always mean spirit?

Not always. In some places it means the Spirit. In some places it means baptism. In some places it means peoples. In some places it means wise advice. That is why you find it said in one place, “Wise advice is a fountain of life to those who have it.”
So in different places in the Scriptures, the word “water” means different things.

But here you have heard the word water used for the Holy Spirit. That is not our own explanation. The Gospel itself says so: “He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in Him would receive.”

So water stands for the Holy Spirit. And this letter tells us, “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they come from God.” So let us understand that this is what the saying is about: “Stay far away from strange water, and do not drink from a strange fountain.”
What does “Do not drink from a strange fountain” mean?
Do not believe a strange spirit.
12. So what is left is the test that proves it is the Spirit of God.
He has given us a sign, and it may be hard. But let us see.
We have to go back to that love. Love is what teaches us, because love is the anointing.
But what does he say here?
“Test the spirits to see whether they come from God, because many false prophets have gone out into this world.”
That includes all the heretics and all the people who split the Church.
So how am I supposed to test the spirit?
He goes on: “This is how the Spirit of God is known.”
Wake up the ears of your heart!
We did not know what to do. We were saying, “Who knows? Who can tell?”
Look, he is about to tell us the sign.

“This is how the Spirit of God is known: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. And every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not from God. This is the antichrist. You have heard that he was coming, and he is already in the world right now.”
Our ears, you might say, are wide awake to learn how to tell the spirits apart. But what we have been told does not help us tell them apart one bit.
What does he say?
“Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ came in the flesh is from God.”
Then is the spirit among the heretics from God? After all, they “confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.”

Yes, here they may rise up against us and say, “You do not have the Spirit from God. But we confess ‘that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.’ And the apostle said here that the people who do not have the Spirit of God are those who do not confess ‘that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.’”

Ask the Arians: they confess “that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.” Ask the Eunomians: they confess “that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.” Ask the Macedonians: they confess “that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.” Ask the Cataphryges: they confess “that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.” Ask the Novatians: they confess “that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.”
So do all these heresies have the Spirit of God?
Are they not false prophets, then?
Is there no lying there, no leading people astray?
Of course they are antichrists! For “they went out from us, but they were not truly part of us.”
13. So what should we do?
How can we tell them apart?
Pay close attention. Let us go together in our hearts and knock.
Love herself is keeping watch. She is the one who will knock, and she is the one who will open. Soon you will understand, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
You have already heard what was said earlier: “Whoever denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is an antichrist.”
There, too, we asked, “Who denies it?” We do not deny it, and they do not deny it either.
And we found that some people deny it by what they do. We gave proof from the apostle, who says, “They claim to know God, but by what they do they deny Him.”
So now, too, let us look for the answer in people’s actions, not in their words.
What is the spirit that is not from God?
The one “that denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.”
And what is the spirit that is from God?
The one “that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.”
Who is the one who confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh?
Now, brothers and sisters, let’s get to the point! Let us look at what people do, and not stop at the noise their tongues make.
Let us ask why Christ came in the flesh. Then we will find out who the people are who deny that He has come in the flesh.
If you only listen to what people say, you will hear many heresies confess that Christ has come in the flesh. But the truth proves them wrong.
Why did Christ come in the flesh?
Wasn’t He God?
Isn’t it written about Him, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”?
Wasn’t He the one who fed the angels? Isn’t He the one who still feeds the angels?
When He came here, didn’t He come without leaving heaven?
When He went back up, didn’t He go without leaving us?
So why did He come in the flesh?
Because we needed to be shown the hope of the resurrection.
He was God, and He came in a human body. God could not die, but a body could die. So He came in the flesh so that He could die for us.
But how did He die for us?
“No one has more love than this, that a person gives up his life for his friends.”
So it was love that brought Him into the flesh.
So whoever does not have love denies that Christ has come in the flesh.
Now you can question all the heretics.
Did Christ come in the flesh?
“Yes, He came. I believe this. I confess this.”
No, you deny it.
“How do I deny it?
You can hear me saying it!”
No, I can prove that you deny it.
You say it with your voice, but you deny it with your heart. You say it with words, but you deny it with your actions.
“How,” you ask, “do I deny it with my actions?”
Because the reason Christ came in the flesh was so that He could die for us.
He died for us because in doing that He taught us great love.
“No one has more love than this, that a person gives up his life for his friends.”
You do not have love, because you break up unity for the sake of your own honor.
So this is how you can tell the spirit that comes from God.
Tap the clay pots. Test them. See if they are cracked and make a dull sound. See if they ring out full and clear. See if love is there.
You pull yourself away from the unity of the whole world. You split the Church into groups. You tear apart the Body of Christ.
He came in the flesh to gather people into one. You shout and make trouble to scatter them.
So this is the Spirit of God: the one who says that Jesus has come in the flesh. He says it not with the tongue but with actions. He says it not by making noise but by loving.
And the spirit that denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not from God. Here too, it denies it not with the tongue but with its life, not with words but with actions.
So it is clear how we can recognize the brothers and sisters.
Many people who are inside the Church are only inside in a way. But nobody is outside unless he really is outside.
14. And so that you know he is talking about actions, he says, “And every spirit, qui solvit Christum, that undoes Christ, that He came in the flesh, is not from God.”
He means undoing Christ by what we do.
What has he shown you?
He shows what “denies” means when he says “undoes” (or “unmakes”).
He came to gather into one. You come to pull apart.
You want to tear the parts of Christ’s body away from each other.
You tear apart the Church of God that He gathered together. How can anyone say that you do not deny that Christ has come in the flesh?
So you are working against Christ. You are an antichrist.
Whether you are inside or outside, you are an antichrist. The only difference is this: when you are inside, you are hidden. When you are outside, everyone can see it.
You undo Jesus and deny that He came in the flesh. You are not from God.
That is why He says in the Gospel: “Whoever breaks one of these least commands, and teaches people to do so, will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.”
What is this breaking?
What is this teaching? It is breaking the command by what you do, and teaching, so to speak, by what you say.
“You preach that people should not steal. Do you steal?”

So the person who steals breaks or undoes the command by what he does, and in a way he teaches people to do so. “He will be called least in the kingdom of heaven”—that is, in the Church of this present time.
About such people it is said, “Do what they say, but do not do what they do.
But whoever does the commands, and teaches people to do so, will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

Notice that here He said fecerit, “will do.” In contrast, there He said solverit, which means non fecerit, “will not do, and will teach so.” So to break a command means not to do it. What is He teaching us? That we should look closely at what people do, and not just trust their words.

These things are hard to understand, and that forces us to speak for a long time. We do this mainly so that what the Lord is kind enough to reveal can reach even the brothers and sisters who understand more slowly. After all, all of them were bought with the blood of Christ.
And I am afraid we will not finish the letter itself during these days, as I promised. But as the Lord wills. It is better to save the rest for later than to overload your hearts with too much food.
“Now, little children, you come from God, and you have defeated him. For the One who lives in you is greater than the one who is in this world.
They come from the world. So they talk about the world, and the world listens to them.
We come from God. Whoever knows God listens to us. Whoever does not come from God does not listen to us.
This is how we can tell the spirit of truth from [the spirit] of error.
My dearly loved friends, let us love one another, because love comes from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.
Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.
This is how God’s love was shown in us: God sent His only Son into this world so that we might live through Him.
This is what love is: not that we loved, but that He loved us and sent His Son to be the One who makes up for our sins.
My dearly loved friends, if God loved us so much, then we too must love one another.
Nobody has ever seen God.”
1. For all believers who are looking for their true homeland, this world is like the desert was for the people of Israel.
They were still wandering and looking for their homeland. But with God as their guide, they could not get lost.
Their road was God’s command.
They wandered around for forty years, yet the journey itself has only a few stops, and everyone knows it.
They were slowed down because they were being trained, not because God had left them.

What God promises us is a sweetness and a goodness too great for words. The Scripture says so, and you have often heard us repeat it: it is what “the eye has not seen, the ear has not heard, and has never come into anyone’s heart.”
But for now we are put to work by the hard labors of this life, and we are trained by the temptations of this present life.
So if you don’t want to die of thirst in this desert, drink love.
Love is the fountain God was pleased to put here so that we do not faint on the way. And we will drink from it even more when we reach our own land.
The Gospel has just been read. Think about the very words at the end of that reading. What did you hear about, except love?
In our prayer we have made an agreement with our God. If we want Him to forgive our sins, then we must also forgive the sins others have done against us.
And the thing that forgives is nothing other than love.
Take love out of the heart, and hatred takes over. Then the heart does not know how to forgive.
Let love be there, and she forgives without fear, because she is not cramped or narrow.
And look at this whole letter we have started to explain to you. See if it praises anything else except this one thing: love.
We do not need to be afraid that if we talk about love a lot, people will start to hate it.
If love becomes hateful, what is left to love?
It is through love that we learn to love other things in the right way. So how much we must love love itself!
So what should never leave our hearts should not leave our tongues either.
2. “Now,” he says, “you come from God, little children, and you have defeated him.” Defeated whom? Who else but the Antichrist?
Earlier he had said, “Whoever undoes Jesus Christ and denies that He has come in the flesh is not from God.”
If you remember, we explained that everyone who breaks love denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

Jesus had no reason to come except love. The love we are praising is the same love the Lord Himself praises in the Gospel: “No one can have more love than this, that a person gives up his life for his friends.”
How could the Son of God give up His life for us without putting on a body in which He could die?
So whoever breaks love—no matter what he says with his tongue—his life denies that Christ has come in the flesh. He is an antichrist, wherever he may be, however he has gotten in.
But what does the apostle say to those who are citizens of that homeland we long for?
“You have defeated him.”
And how did they defeat him?
“Because the One who lives in you is greater than the one who is in this world.”

He did not want them to think they had won by their own strength. Then arrogant pride would defeat them—for the devil defeats everyone he makes proud. He wanted them to stay humble. So what does he say?
“You have defeated him.”
Now when anyone hears the words “You have defeated,” he lifts up his head, sticks out his neck, and wants to be praised.
Don’t puff yourself up. See who it is that won the victory in you.
Why did you win?
“Because the One who lives in you is greater than the one who is in the world.”
Be humble. Carry your Lord. Be the animal He rides on.
It is good for you that He is in control and that He guides you.

If you do not have Him riding on you, you may lift up your neck and kick up your heels. But how terrible for you if no one is in charge of you! That kind of freedom sends you out among the wild beasts to be eaten!
3. “These people come from the world.”
Who? The antichrists. You have already heard who they are.
If you are not like them, you can recognize them. But anyone who is like them cannot.
“These people come from the world. So they talk about the world, and the world listens to them.”
Who are the people who “talk about the world”?
Notice who is against love.
Look, you have heard the Lord say, “If you forgive people when they wrong you, your Father in heaven will forgive your wrongs too.
But if you do not forgive people when they wrong you, your Father will not forgive your wrongs either.”
This is what the Truth has said. If it is not the Truth speaking, then argue against it.
If you are a Christian and believe Christ, remember that He said, “I am the truth.”
This saying is true. It stands firm.
Now listen to people who “talk about the world.”
“Aren’t you going to get back at him?
Are you going to let him brag that he did this to you?
No! Let him find out that he is dealing with a real man.”
People say things like this every day. Those who say such things “talk about the world, and the world listens to them.”
Only people who love the world say such things. And only people who love the world listen to them.
And you have heard that loving the world and ignoring love is the same as denying that Jesus came in the flesh.

Tell me: did the Lord Himself do that when He was in the flesh? When He was beaten, did He want revenge? When He was hanging on the cross, didn’t He say, “Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they are doing”?
He had all the power, yet He made no threats. So why do you threaten? Why do you swell up with anger, when you are under someone else’s power?
He died because He chose to die, and still He made no threats. You do not even know when you will die—and you make threats?
4. “We are from God.”
Let’s see why. Let’s see if it is for any reason other than love.
“We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us. Whoever is not from God does not listen to us.
This is how we know the spirit of truth and the spirit of error.” That is, whoever listens to us has the spirit of truth. Whoever does not listen to us has the spirit of error.

Let’s see what he advises us to do. And let’s choose to listen to him, since he gives his advice in the spirit of truth. Let’s not listen to antichrists, or to people who love the world, or to the world itself.
If we are born of God, “dear friends,” he goes on. Look back to see where this comes from: “We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us. Whoever is not from God does not listen to us.

This is how we know the spirit of truth and the spirit of error.” Yes, now he makes us listen eagerly. He tells us that whoever knows God listens, but whoever does not know God does not listen. He tells us that this is how we tell the spirit of truth apart from the spirit of error. Well then, let’s see what he is about to advise. What is it that we must listen to him about? “Dear friends, let us love one another.”
Why? Just because a man gives this advice?
“Because love comes from God.”
He has praised love highly by saying that it “comes from God.” But he is going to say even more. Let’s listen eagerly.
So far he has said, “Love comes from God. Everyone who loves is born of God and knows God.
Whoever does not love does not know God.”
Why? “Because God is love” [Love is God].
What more could be said, brothers and sisters?

Suppose nothing else were said to praise love in all the pages of this letter. Suppose nothing at all were said about it in all the other pages of the Scriptures. Suppose this one thing was all that the voice of God’s Spirit told us: “For Love is God.” Then we would not need anything more.
5. Now see that acting against love is acting against God.
No one should say, “When I don’t love my brother, I sin against a human being (notice this!). And sin against a human being is no big deal. As long as I don’t sin against God.”
How can you not be sinning against God when you sin against love?
“Love is God.” Is this something “we” are saying?
If we said, “Love is God,” maybe one of you would be offended and say, What did he just say?
What does he mean, that “Love is God”?
God “gave” love. God handed out love as a gift.
“Love comes from God: Love IS God.”

Look, brothers and sisters, here you have God’s Scriptures. This letter is one of the Bible’s accepted books. It is read aloud in every nation. The whole world accepts its authority. It has built up the whole world.
Here God’s Spirit is telling you, “Love is God.”
Now go against God if you dare, and refuse to love your brother!
6. So what did it mean when it said a moment ago, “Love comes from God,” and now says, “Love IS God”?
God is Father and Son and Holy Spirit. The Son is God from God. The Holy Spirit is God from God. And these three are one God, not three Gods.
The Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God. And the person who loves is the one in whom the Holy Spirit lives. So “Love is God.” But love “IS God” because it is “from God.”
You find both in this letter: “Love comes from God,” and “Love is God.”
The Scripture never says about the Father alone that He is “from God.” So when you hear the phrase “from God,” it means either the Son or the Holy Spirit.
The apostle says, “God’s love is poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit, who is given to us.” So let’s understand that the One who lives in love is the Holy Spirit.

This Holy Spirit is the One whom bad people cannot receive. He is the Fountain the Scripture talks about: “Let the fountain of your water be your very own, and don’t let any stranger share it with you.”
Everyone who does not love God is a stranger, an antichrist.
They may come to church, but they cannot be counted among God’s children. That Fountain of life does not belong to them.
Even a bad person can have baptism. Even a bad person can have the gift of prophecy.
We read that King Saul had the gift of prophecy. He was hunting down holy David, and yet he was filled with the spirit of prophecy and began to prophesy.
Even a bad person can receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood. The Bible says about such people, “Whoever eats and drinks in an unworthy way eats and drinks judgment on himself.”
Even a bad person can carry the name of Christ. In other words, even a bad person can be called a Christian. It is like the people the Bible describes: “They made the name of their God dirty.”
So I say that even a bad person can have all these sacraments. But no one can have love and be a bad person at the same time.
So this is the special gift. This is the “Fountain” that is truly your “own.”
God’s Spirit urges you to drink from this. God’s Spirit urges you to drink from Himself.
7. “This is how God’s love was shown among us.”
Look, we are being urged to love God.
Could we love Him if He had not loved us first?
Even if we were slow to love first, let’s not be slow to love Him back.
He loved us first. And even then, we do not love.

He loved people who did wrong, but He took away their wrongdoing. He loved people who did wrong, but He did not bring them together to keep doing wrong. He loved the sick, but He came to them to make them well.
So “Love is God.”
“This is how God’s love was shown among us: God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we could live through Him.”

The Lord Himself says, “No one can have a greater love than this: to give up his life for his friends.” That is where Christ’s love for us was proven, because He died for us. But how is the Father’s love for us proven?

It is proven because He “sent His only Son” to die for us. The apostle Paul says the same thing: “He did not spare His own Son but handed Him over for all of us. So how could He not also freely give us everything along with Him?”
Look, the Father handed Christ over. Judas handed Him over too. Doesn’t it seem like they did the same kind of thing?
Judas is called a “traditor,” someone who hands over [or, a traitor]. Is God the Father that?
“Never!” you say.
I am not the one saying it. The apostle says it: “He did not spare His own Son but ‘tradidit Eum,’ handed Him over, for all of us.”
The Father handed Him over, and He also handed Himself over.
The same apostle says, “He loved me and handed Himself over for me.”
If the Father handed over the Son, and the Son handed over Himself, what did Judas do?

There was a “traditio” (a handing over) by the Father. There was a “traditio” by the Son. There was a “traditio” by Judas. The action is the same. So what makes them different: the Father handing over the Son, the Son handing over Himself, and Judas the disciple handing over his Master?
Here is the difference: the Father and the Son did it out of love, but Judas did it as a treacherous betrayal.
So you see, what matters is not simply what a person does. What matters is the attitude and the will behind it.
We find God the Father doing the same deed as Judas. Yet we bless the Father, and we hate Judas.
Why do we bless the Father and hate Judas?
We bless love, and we hate wickedness.
What a great gift the human race received when Christ was handed over!
Was Judas thinking about this when he handed Him over?
God was thinking about our salvation, which bought us back. Judas was thinking about the money he would get for selling the Lord.
The Son Himself was thinking about the price He paid for us. Judas was thinking about the price he was paid for selling Him.
So the different intentions make the actions different.

The action is one and the same. But when we measure it by the different intentions, we find that one deserves love and the other deserves condemnation. One deserves glory, and the other deserves to be hated.
That is how powerful love is.
See how love alone tells actions apart. Love alone shows the difference between the things people do.
8. We have said this about cases where the actions look the same.
But sometimes the actions are different. Then we find a person made fierce by love, and another made charming and gentle by wickedness.
A father beats a boy, while a kidnapper hugs a boy.
If you just name the two things, blows and hugs, who would not choose the hugs and refuse the blows?
But if you look at the people doing them, it is love that gives the blows and wickedness that gives the hugs.
See what we are stressing here. People’s actions can only be judged by whether they grow from the root of love.
Many things people do look good, and yet they do not grow from the root of love.
After all, thorn bushes have flowers too. And some actions really do seem rough, even cruel. Yet they are done to train and correct, because love commands it.

So here, once and for all, is one short rule for you: Love, and do what you want. If you stay silent, stay silent out of love. If you cry out, cry out because of love. If you correct someone, correct them out of love. If you go easy on someone, go easy on them out of love. Let the root of love be inside you. Nothing but good can grow from this root.

9. “This is love—this is how God’s love for us was shown: God sent His one and only Son into this world, so that we could live through Him.—This is love: not that we loved God, but that He loved us.” We did not love Him first. He loved us for this purpose: so that we would love Him. “And He sent His Son to be the Atoner for our sins.” The Latin word is “litatorem,” which means one who offers a sacrifice.
He offered a sacrifice for our sins.
Where did He find something to sacrifice?
Where did He find a pure victim to offer?
He found no other. He offered Himself.
“Dear friends, since God loved us this much, we also should love one another.
Peter,” He says, “do you love me?”
And he said, “I love you.”
“Feed my sheep.”
10. “No one has ever seen God.” He is invisible. We must look for Him with our hearts, not with our eyes.
If we wanted to see the sun, we would clean our physical eyes. In the same way, if we want to see God, let’s clean the eye that can see God.
Where is this eye?
Listen to the Gospel: “Blessed are those whose hearts are pure, for they will see God.”
But no one should picture God according to what his eyes crave.

If he does that, he makes up a huge shape for himself. Or he imagines something so enormous it cannot be measured, spreading out in every direction like the light he sees with his physical eyes. He stretches it across field after field of space, making it as big as he possibly can. Or he pictures God as an old man with a dignified look.
Don’t imagine any of these things.
There is something you may picture, if you want to see God: “God is love.”
What kind of face does love have? What shape does it have? How tall is it? What feet does it have? What hands? No one can say.

And yet it does have feet, because they carry people to church. It has hands, because they reach out to the poor. It has eyes, because with them we notice people in need. As the Bible says, “Blessed is the person who pays attention to the needy and the poor.”
It has ears, the ones the Lord speaks of: “Whoever has ears to hear should listen.”
These are not body parts in separate places. The person who has love sees all of it at once with his mind.
Live in it, and it will live in you. Make your home there, and you will become a home.
What do you say, brothers and sisters? Who loves something he cannot see?
So why, when love is praised, do you raise your hands, cheer and applaud?
What have I shown you?
Did I bring out something shining with colors?
Did I put gold and silver in front of you?
Did I dig up jewels from some hidden treasure?
Have I shown your eyes anything like that?
Does my face change while I am speaking?
I am a human being in a body. I look the same as when I came out to you. You look the same as when you came here. Yet love is praised, and you cheer.
You certainly don’t see anything.
But just as you enjoy praising love, enjoy keeping it in your hearts too.
Pay close attention to what I say, brothers and sisters. With God’s help, I am urging all of you toward a great treasure.

Imagine you were shown a beautiful little vase. It has raised designs, it is inlaid with gold, and it is skillfully made. It delights your eyes and pulls at the eager desire of your heart. You admire the artist’s skill, the weight of the silver, and the shine of the metal. Wouldn’t each of you say, “Oh, if only I had that vase!”
But it would do you no good to say it, because you would have no way to get it.
Or if someone really wanted it, he might think about stealing it from someone else’s house.
Love is being praised to you. If you like it, take it and make it yours. You don’t need to rob anyone. You don’t need to think about buying it. You can have it free, at no cost.
Take it and hold it close. There is nothing sweeter.
If it is this wonderful when we only talk about it, what must it be like to actually have it?

11. Brothers and sisters, some of you may want to hold on to love. If so, above all, do not think of it as something weak and lazy. And don’t think love is kept by a kind of gentleness. No, that isn’t gentleness at all. It is just being tame and not caring.
That is not how love is kept.

Don’t think you love your servant just because you never beat him. Don’t think you love your son just because you never discipline him. Don’t think you love your neighbor just because you never correct him. That is not love. It is just weakness.
Let love be eager to correct and to improve. If someone’s behavior is good, enjoy it. If it is bad, let it be fixed and corrected.
Don’t love the wrong that is in a person. Love the person. God made the person, but the person made the wrong himself.
Love what God made. Don’t love what the person made himself.
When you love the person, you take away the wrong. When you value the person, you correct the wrong.
Even if you have to be strict sometimes, let it be because of love, to correct.
That is why love was pictured by the Dove that came down on the Lord.
The Holy Spirit came in the shape of a dove. He is the One through whom love would be poured into us. Why did He come like that?
The dove has no bitter gall. Yet she fights for her young with her beak and wings. Her fierceness has no bitterness in it.
A father is the same way. When he punishes his son, he does it to train him.
As I said, a kidnapper lures a child with bitter sweet-talk so that he can sell him. A father punishes without bitterness so that he can correct.
Be like that toward everyone.

Look, brothers and sisters, here is a great lesson, a great rule. Each of you has children or wants to have them. Or if someone has fully decided not to have children in the body, at least he wants to have spiritual children. What father does not correct his son? What son does not get disciplined by his father?
And yet the father seems fierce with him.
It is the fierceness of love, the fierceness of caring. It is a kind of fierceness without bitterness, like the dove’s and not like the raven’s.
That reminds me, brothers and sisters, to tell you this. The people who have broken love are the ones who caused the split in the church. Just as they hate love itself, they also hate the dove.
But the dove proves them wrong. It comes down from heaven, the heavens open, and it stays on the Lord’s head.
Why does this happen? So that John could hear, “This is the One who baptizes.”
Get away, you robbers! Get away, you invaders of Christ’s property!
On your own properties, where you insist on being the masters, you have dared to put up the ownership signs of the great Owner.
He recognizes His own signs. He claims His own property for Himself.
He does not tear down the signs. Instead He comes in and takes over.
In the same way, when someone comes into the Catholic Church, his baptism is not canceled, so that the commander’s sign is not canceled. But what happens in the Catholic Church?
The sign is recognized. The Owner comes in under His own signs, where the robber was coming in under signs that were not his.
“If we love one another, God lives in us, and His love is made complete in us.
This is how we know that we live in Him and He lives in us: He has given us some of His Spirit.
And we have seen and we are witnesses that the Father sent the Son to be the Savior of the world.
If anyone openly says that Jesus is the Son of God, God lives in him, and he lives in God.
And we have come to know and believe the love God has for us.
God is love. Whoever lives in love lives in God, and God lives in him.”
1. Love is a sweet word, but the deed is even sweeter.

We can’t talk about it all the time. We have lots of things to do, and all kinds of business pull us in different directions. So our tongues don’t have time to talk about love constantly, even though our tongues could do nothing better.
But even if we can’t always talk about it, we can always keep it.
Think of the Alleluia we sing during this season. Are we singing it all the time?
We don’t sing Alleluia for one hour—I’m not even talking about the whole hour. We sing it for barely a few moments of one hour, and then we move on to something else.
As you already know, Alleluia means “Praise the Lord.”
The person who praises God with his tongue can’t do it all the time. But the person who praises God with his life and behavior can do it always.

Acts of mercy, loving feelings, holy devotion, clean and pure living, humble self-control: we should practice these things all the time. We should do them in public and at home, in front of people and in our own rooms, while talking and while silent, while busy and while free. We must always keep them, because all these good qualities I have named are on the inside.
But who could name them all?
It is as if an emperor’s army were stationed inside your mind.

An emperor gets whatever he wants done through his army. In the same way, once the Lord Jesus Christ begins to live in our inner self (that is, in the mind, through faith), He uses these good qualities as His servants.

These good qualities can’t be seen with the eyes. Yet when we name them, people praise them. And they would not be praised unless they were loved. They would not be loved unless they were seen. So if they are only loved when seen, they must be seen with a different eye: the inner sight of the heart. Through these invisible qualities, the parts of the body are set moving where everyone can see. The feet walk, but where do they go? They go wherever the good will moves them, the will that serves the good emperor like a soldier. The hands work, but on what? On whatever love commands, the love that the Holy Spirit breathes into us within.

So the body parts can be seen when they move. But the One who gives them orders from within cannot be seen. Who He is, the One giving orders within, is known almost only to Him, the One who gives the orders, and to the person inside who receives them.
2. Brothers and sisters, you heard this just now when the Gospel was read—at least if you listened not only with the ears of your body but also with the ears of your heart.
What did it say? “Be careful not to do your good deeds in front of people so they will see you.”
Did He mean that we should hide every good thing we do from people’s eyes, and be afraid of being seen?
If you are afraid of people watching, you won’t have anyone copying your example. So you should be seen.
But you must not do it just so that people will see you.
That should not be where your joy ends. That should not be the goal of your happiness—thinking you have gotten the full reward for your good deed once people see you and praise you.
That is worth nothing. When you are praised, think little of yourself. Let the One who works through you be praised in you.
So don’t do good things to be praised yourself. Do them for the praise of the One who gives you the power to do good.
Doing wrong comes from you. Doing right comes from God.
But look at twisted people and how backward they are.
When they do something good, they insist on taking the credit. When they do something bad, they insist on blaming God.
Turn this twisted, backward way of thinking around. It turns things upside down, so to speak. It puts on the bottom what belongs on top, and puts on top what belongs on the bottom.
Do you want to put God on the bottom and yourself on top?
You won’t lift yourself up. You will fall flat on your face, because He is always above.

What then? You do well, and God does badly? No! If you want to speak more truthfully, say this instead: I do badly, He does well. When I do something good, the good comes from Him. Whatever I do on my own is bad.
Admitting this makes the heart strong and lays a firm foundation for love.
If we must hide our good works so people won’t see them, what about what the Lord said in the sermon He preached on the mountain?
In that same place, a little earlier, He also said, “Let your good works shine in front of people.”
And He did not stop there or end there. He added, “And give glory to your Father in heaven.”
And what does the apostle say?
“The churches of Judea that were in Christ did not know my face. They had only heard people say, The man who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy.
And they praised God because of me.”
See how he too, when he became so well known, did not use the good to praise himself. He used it to praise God.
And as for himself—that he once tore the Church apart and was a persecutor, jealous and cruel—he admits this himself. We are not the ones blaming him for it.
Paul is glad for us to talk about his sins, so that the One who healed such a terrible disease may be glorified.
For it was the Doctor’s hand that cut open that huge wound and healed it.
That voice from heaven knocked down the persecutor and raised up the preacher. It killed Saul and brought Paul to life.
Saul was the one who persecuted a holy man. That is where this man got his name, back when he was persecuting the Christians. Later, instead of Saul he became Paul.
What does the name Paulus mean?
It means “little.” So when he was Saul, he was proud and puffed up. When he was Paul, he was humble and little.
That’s why we say, I will see you “paulo post,” which means, after a little while.
Listen to how he was made little: “For I am the least of the apostles.” And in another place he says, “To me, the least of all God’s holy people.”
So among the apostles he was like the hem of a robe. But the Church of the non-Jewish nations touched it, like the woman who had the bleeding illness, and was made well.

3. So, brothers and sisters, this is what I want to say. This is what I am saying. If I could help it, I would never leave this unsaid: Do these good works at one time and those at another, depending on the time, the hour, and the day.

Should you always be talking? Always be silent? Always be eating to refresh your body? Always be fasting? Always be giving bread to the needy? Always be giving clothes to people who have none? Always be visiting the sick? Always be making peace between people who disagree? Always be burying the dead?
No. Now you do this, then you do that.
You start these things, and then they stop. But the thing that commands all the forces inside you like an emperor has no starting point and should never stop.
Let love inside you never take a break. But let the acts of love be done at the right times.
So, as the Bible says, let “brotherly love” go on. Let “brotherly love continue.”
4. But maybe some of you have been wondering all along, while we have been explaining this letter of blessed John to you. Why is it only “brotherly” love that he praises so strongly?
He says, “Whoever loves his brother.” And he says, “We have been given a command to love one another.”
Over and over he talks about brotherly love. But love for God, the love we should have for God, he does not mention nearly as often. Still, he does not leave it out completely.
But about loving an enemy, he says almost nothing in the whole letter.
He preaches love to us with great passion and praises it. Yet he does not tell us to love our enemies. He tells us to love our brothers and sisters.
But just now, when the Gospel was read, we heard, “If you love the people who love you, what reward will you get?
Don’t even the tax collectors do that?”

So how can this be? John the apostle praises brotherly love as something very important for us, to help us become complete in a certain way. But the Lord says it is not enough to love our brothers and sisters. He says we must stretch that love so far that it reaches even our enemies.
Whoever reaches as far as his enemies does not jump over his brothers and sisters.
Like fire, love has to catch hold of what is closest first, and then spread to what is farther away.
A brother is closer to you than some random person.
And a person you don’t know, who is not against you, has more claim on you than an enemy who is against you.
Stretch your love to the people closest to you. But don’t call that stretching. Loving the people close to you is almost the same as loving yourself.
Stretch it to strangers who have done you no harm.
Go past even them. Reach all the way to loving your enemies.
This, at least, is what the Lord commands.
So why has the apostle said nothing here about loving an enemy?

5. Think about every kind of love. There is the kind called fleshly love, which is usually called not “dilectio” but “amor.” (The word “dilectio” is usually used for better things and understood to mean better things.) Yet every kind of love, dear brothers and sisters, includes wishing good things for the ones who are loved.
For we should not love like this, and we are not able to love like this (whether we say “diligere” or “amare”—the Lord used the second word when He said, “Petra, amas me?”
“Peter, do you love me?”). We should not love people the way we hear greedy eaters say, I love thrushes.
Do you ask why he loves them?
So he can kill them and eat them.
He says he loves them. But he loves them so that they will stop existing. He loves them so that he can get rid of them.
And whatever we love as food, we love so that it will be eaten up and we will be refreshed.
Should people be loved like that, so that they get used up?
But there is a kind of friendly goodwill. It makes us want, at some point, to do good to the people we love.
What if there is nothing good we can do for them?
Then the goodwill, the wishing well, is enough by itself for the one who loves.
We should not want people to be miserable just so we can do acts of mercy.
You give bread to the hungry. But it would be better if no one were hungry and you had no one to give bread to.
You give clothes to people who have none. Oh, if only everyone had clothes and there were no such need!
You bury the dead. Oh, if only that life had finally come, where no one will ever die!
You make peace between people who are fighting. Oh, if only it were finally here, that everlasting peace of Jerusalem, where no one will disagree!
All these are services we do because people are in need.
Take away the miserable, and acts of mercy will come to an end.
Acts of mercy will end. But will the fire of love be put out?
You love a happy person with a truer kind of love, because there is no favor you can do for him. That love will be purer and much more genuine.
When you do a kindness for a miserable person, you might want to put yourself above him. You might want him to be under you, since you are the one who helped him.
He was in need, and you gave. And because you gave, you think of yourself as greater than the person who received.
Wish for him to be your equal, so that you can both be under the One Lord, to whom no one can give anything.
6. This is where the proud soul has gone past its limits and, in a way, become greedy.
For, “The root of all evils is greed.” And it is also said, “The beginning of all sin is pride.”
And maybe we ask how these two sayings fit together: “The root of all evils is greed,” and, “The beginning of all sin is pride.”
If pride is the beginning of all sin, then pride is the root of all evils.
Yet it is certainly true that “the root of all evils is greed.”
We find that pride also has greed (or grabbing) in it. For man has gone past his limits. And what is being greedy? It is going beyond what is enough.
Adam fell because of pride. “The beginning of all sin is pride,” it says. Did he fall because of greed?
Who could be greedier than someone for whom God was not enough?
In fact, brothers and sisters, we read that man was made in the image and likeness of God. And what did God say about him?
“Let him have power over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and all the livestock that move on the earth.”
Did He say, Have power over people?
“Have power,” He says. He has given him a natural power. “Have power” over what? “Over the fish of the sea, the birds of the sky, and every creature that moves on the earth.”
Why is this power over these creatures a natural power?
Because man gets this power from the fact that he was made in God’s image.
And in what way was he made in God’s image?

In his intellect, in his mind, in his inner self. He can understand truth. He can tell right from wrong. He knows who made him. He is able to understand his Creator and to praise his Creator. The person who has wisdom has this kind of understanding.

But many people wore away God’s image in themselves through evil desires. By their twisted way of living, they put out the very flame of understanding, so to speak. So the Scripture cried out to them, “Don’t be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding.”
In other words: I have put you above the horse and the mule. I made you in my image. I have given you power over these animals.

Why? Because they don’t have a reasoning mind. But you, with your reasoning mind, can grasp truth, and you understand what is above you. So place yourself under the One who is above you, and the things you were put in charge of will be under you.
But through sin, man abandoned the One he should be under. So now he has been put under the things he should be above.
7. Pay attention to what I say: God, man, animals. Above you is God. Below you are the animals.
Recognize the One above you, so that the creatures below you will recognize you.
That is why, since Daniel recognized God as above him, the lions recognized Daniel as above them.
But if you do not recognize the One above you, you look down on the One who is greater than you, and you end up under what is lower than you.
For example, how was the pride of the Egyptians crushed?
By frogs and flies.
God could have sent lions. But a great man might be scared of a lion.
The prouder they were, the more their wicked necks were broken by small, weak, worthless things.
But the lions recognized Daniel, because he was under God.

So what about the martyrs who were thrown to the wild beasts to fight them, and were torn apart by the teeth of savage animals? Were they not under God? Or were those three men servants of God, but the Maccabees not servants of God?
The fire recognized the three men as God’s servants. It did not burn them or even damage their clothes. So didn’t the fire recognize the Maccabees too?
Yes, it recognized the Maccabees. It did, brothers and sisters, recognize them too.
But by the Lord’s permission, a whipping was needed. He has said in Scripture, “He whips every son He accepts.”
Brothers and sisters, do you think the iron could have pierced deep into the Lord’s body unless He had allowed it? Or that He would have hung nailed to the cross unless He wanted to?
Didn’t His own creation recognize Him?
Or was He giving His faithful people an example of patience?
So you see, God rescued some people in a way everyone could see, and others He did not rescue in a visible way. Yet He rescued all of them spiritually. Spiritually, He abandoned no one.
To the eye, He seemed to abandon some, and He seemed to rescue others.
He rescued some so that you would not think He lacked the power to rescue.
He has proved that He has the power. So when He does not rescue, you should understand that there is a more hidden will at work. Don’t guess that it was too hard for Him.

But what then, brothers and sisters? One day we will escape all these traps of our mortal life. The times of temptation will be over. The river of this world will have flowed past. We will get back that “first robe,” the immortality we lost by sinning. “This body that decays will have put on what cannot decay,” that is, this flesh will be clothed with what cannot decay, “and this body that dies will have put on immortality.” Then we will be God’s children, now made complete, with no more need to be tempted or whipped, and all creatures will recognize us. All things will be placed under us, if here we place ourselves under God.
8. So a Christian should be the kind of person who does not brag that he is above other “people.”
God has given you a place over the animals, meaning that you are better than the animals.
You have this by nature. You will always be better than an animal.
If you want to be better than another person, you will resent him when you see that he is your equal.
You should want everyone to be your equal. And if you are wiser than someone, you should want him to become wise too.

As long as he is slow, he learns from you. As long as he is untaught, he needs you. You are seen as the teacher and he as the student. So you seem to be the greater one, because you are the teacher, and he seems to be the lesser one, because he is the student.
If you don’t want him to be your equal, then you want him to stay a student forever.
But if you want him to stay a student forever, you will be a jealous teacher.
And if you are a jealous teacher, how can you really be a teacher?
Please, don’t teach him your jealousy.
Listen to the apostle speaking from a heart full of love: “I wish everyone were just like me.” In what way did he want everyone to be his equal?
This is how he was greater than everyone: out of love, he wanted all people to be his equals.
So I say, man has gone past his limits. He wanted to grab more than was his. He wanted to be above other people—he who was made to be above the animals. And that is pride.
9. Look at all the great things pride does.
Keep this in your hearts: the things pride does look very much like the things love does. They seem almost equal.
Love feeds the hungry, and so does pride. Love does it so that God will be praised. Pride does it so that pride itself will be praised.
Love gives clothes to people who have none, and so does pride. Love fasts, and so does pride. Love buries the dead, and so does pride.
Love wants to do every kind of good work, and it does them. Pride goes after the very same things. You could say it keeps its horses running hard to keep up.
But love stands in the way and gives no room to pride, which is being driven badly. I don’t mean that pride drives badly. I mean that pride is being driven badly.
How terrible for the person whose chariot driver is pride! He is sure to crash headfirst!

But when good is being done, how can we tell that pride is not what is pushing us on? Who knows? Who can see it? Where is it? We only see the actions. Mercy feeds people, and pride feeds people too. Mercy welcomes strangers, and pride welcomes strangers too. Mercy speaks up for the poor, and pride speaks up for them too.
How can this be? When we look at the actions, we see no difference.

I dare to say something. But it is not me saying it; Paul said it. Love dies. That is, a person who has love declares the name of Christ and suffers as a martyr. Pride also declares His name, and it also suffers as a martyr.
One has love. The other does not have love.

But the person who does not have love should listen to the apostle: “If I give away everything I own to the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but I do not have love, it does me no good at all.”

So the Bible calls us away from the face we show on the outside and points us to what is inside. It calls us away from this outer surface that people show off in front of others, and it points us to what is inside.
Go back to your own conscience and question it.
Don’t look at the flowers blooming on the outside. Look at what root is in the ground.
Is selfish desire rooted there?
Then there may be a show of good deeds, but there cannot be truly good works.
Is love rooted there?
Then don’t be afraid. Nothing evil can grow from that.
A proud person pats you gently. Love is strict.
One gives you clothes. The other hits you.
The proud person gives clothes to please people. Love hits to correct and discipline.
A blow from love is more welcome than a gift from pride.
So come inside, brothers and sisters. In everything you do, look to God, who is your witness.
Ask yourselves whether He sees what attitude you have when you do it.
If your heart does not accuse you of doing it to show off, that’s good. Don’t be afraid.
But when you do good, don’t be afraid that someone else will see you.
Be afraid of doing it just so that you will be praised. Let the other person see it, so that God will be praised.
If you hide it from people’s eyes, you also keep people from copying you. Then you take away from God the praise that belongs to Him.
When you give to the poor, you are giving to two people. Both are hungry. One is hungry for bread, and the other is hungry for righteousness.

You, the one doing the good deed, stand between these two starving people. As the Bible says, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled.” If love is doing the work, then while it helps one of them, it has pity on both. It wants to help both.
One person wants something to eat. The other wants someone to copy.

You feed the first one. Give yourself as an example to the second. Then you have given to both. The first one thanks you because you ended his hunger. The second one copies you because you set him an example.
10. So show mercy, as people with merciful hearts. When you love your enemies, you are also loving your brothers and sisters.
John keeps talking about loving our brothers and sisters. But don’t think that this means he gave no command about loving our enemies.
You love your brothers and sisters. “How,” you ask, “do we love our brothers and sisters?”
Let me ask you why you love an enemy.
Why do you love him?
So that he will be healthy in this life? What if that is not good for him?
So that he will be rich? What if his riches make him blind?
So that he will get married? What if his married life turns out bitter?
So that he will have children? What if they turn out bad?
So the things you seem to wish for your enemy when you love him are uncertain. They are all uncertain.
Wish for him to have eternal life with you. Wish for him to become your brother. Then, when you love him, you are loving a brother.
You don’t love him for what he is now. You love him for what you want him to become.

Dear friends, I told you once before, if I remember right, about a log of wood lying out in the open. A skilled worker saw the log. It was still rough, just as it had been cut in the forest. He liked it, and he wanted to make something out of it.
He did not love it so that it would stay that way forever.
His skill showed him what it would become. His liking was not about what it was. He liked it for the thing he would make out of it, not for the thing it was then.
That is how God loved us sinners.
We say that God loved sinners, because He says, “People who are well do not need the Doctor, but sick people do.”
Did He love us sinners so that we would stay sinners?
Our Carpenter saw us like rough wood from the forest. In His mind He saw the building He would make out of it, not the rough wood it was then.

It is the same when you see your enemy fighting against you. He is raging. He bites with his words. He provokes you with insults. He harasses you with hatred. But you pay attention to this one thing in him: he is a human being.
You see all these things aimed against you, and you see that a man did them. But you also see in him that God made him.
God made him a human being. But his hatred for you is his own doing. His ill will toward you is his own doing.
So what do you say in your mind?
“Lord, be merciful to him. Forgive his sins. Put fear into him. Change him.”
You don’t love him for what he is now. You love him for what you want him to become.
So when you love an enemy, you are loving a brother.
That is why perfect love means loving an enemy. And this perfect love is found in love for our brothers and sisters.
No one should say that the apostle John asked a little less of us, and the Lord Christ asked a little more.
John told us to love our brothers and sisters. Christ told us to love even our enemies.
Notice why Christ told you to love your enemies.
So that they would stay enemies forever?
If that were why He told you, so that they would stay enemies, then you would be hating them, not loving them.
Notice how He Himself loved. He did not want them to keep on persecuting Him as they were. So He said, “Father, forgive them, because they don’t know what they are doing.”
Those He wanted forgiven, He wanted changed. And those He wanted changed, He was willing to turn from enemies into brothers. And He really did make them brothers.

He was killed. He was buried. He rose again. He went up into heaven. He sent the Holy Spirit to His disciples. They began to preach His name boldly. They did miracles in the name of the One who was crucified and killed. The very people who had killed the Lord saw them. And those who had shed His blood in anger came to believe, and so they drank that blood.
11. I have said these things, brothers and sisters, and I have said them at some length. But love needed to be urged on you more strongly, dear friends, and this was the way to do it.
If there is no love in you, then we have said nothing.
But if love is in you, it is as if we have poured oil on a fire.
And in people who did not have it, perhaps our words have lit it.
In one person, the love that was there has grown. In another, love that was not there has begun.
So we have said these things so that you will not be slow to love your enemies.
Is someone raging at you? He rages; you pray. He hates; you feel pity.
It is the fever in his soul that hates you. He will get well, and then he will thank you.
How do doctors love sick people?
Do they love them for being sick?
If they loved them for being sick, they would want them to stay sick forever.
