This is why they love sick people: not so that they will stay sick, but so that they will go from being sick to being well.
And doctors often have to put up with so much from patients who are out of their minds!
What insults they hear! Very often the patients even hit them.
The doctor fights the fever and forgives the person.
What shall I say, brothers and sisters? Does he love his enemy?
No, he hates his enemy, which is the disease. That is what he hates. But he loves the person who hits him. He hates the fever.
Who or what is hitting him? The disease, the sickness, the fever.
He takes away the thing that is fighting him, so that what remains is the person who will thank him.
You should do the same. If your enemy hates you, and hates you unfairly, know that desire for the things of the world is ruling him. That is why he hates you.
If you hate him too, then you are paying back evil with evil.
What good does it do to pay back evil with evil?
I was weeping over one sick man who hated you. Now I will be weeping over you too, if you hate as well.
But he attacks your property. He takes some of the things you own here on earth. So you hate him, because he squeezes you in here on earth.
Don’t let yourself be squeezed. Move yourself up to heaven. There your heart will be in a place with plenty of room, so that you won’t feel squeezed in your hope of eternal life.
Think about what he is taking from you. He could not take even these things unless he was allowed to by the One who “whips every son He welcomes.”
This enemy of yours is, in a way, a tool in God’s hands for healing you.

If God knows it is good for you to be robbed by him, God allows it. If He knows it is good for you to be hit, He allows him to hit you. God is taking care of you through him. So wish for him to be made well.
12. “No one has ever seen God.”
Look, dear friends: “If we love each other, God will live in us, and His love will be made perfect in us.”
Start to love, and you will be made perfect.
Have you started to love?
Then God has started to live in you. Love Him who has started to live in you, so that by living in you more fully He may make you perfect.
“This is how we know that we live in Him and He lives in us: He has given us some of His Spirit.”
That’s good! Thanks be to God!
We come to know that He lives in us.
But how do we come to know this very fact, that we really do know He lives in us?
Because John himself has said it: “Because He has given us some of His Spirit.”
But how do we know that He has given us some of His Spirit?
This very thing, that He has given you some of His Spirit, how do you come to know it?
Ask your own heart, deep inside. If it is full of love, you have the Spirit of God.
How do we know that this is how you know the Spirit of God lives in you?
“Because God’s love has been poured into our hearts by the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.”
13. “And we have seen, and we are witnesses, that God has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world.”
Calm your minds, you who are sick. Such a great Doctor has come. Are you still going to give up hope?
The diseases were terrible. The wounds could not be cured. The sickness was hopeless.
Do you notice how bad your sickness is, but not notice that the Doctor is all-powerful?
You feel hopeless, but He is all-powerful. His witnesses are the people who were healed first and who tell others about the Doctor. Yet even they are healed in hope more than in reality.
That is what the apostle says: “For we are saved by hope.”
So we have started to be made well by faith. But our healing will be complete “when what decays has put on what cannot decay, and what dies has put on what cannot die.”
This is hope, not the reality.
But whoever is glad in hope will also hold on to the reality. And whoever does not have the hope will not be able to reach the reality.
14. “Whoever declares that Jesus is the Son of God, God lives in him and he lives in God.”
We can say it in a few words now. “Whoever declares”: not in words but in actions, not with the tongue but with the life.
Many people declare it with their words but deny it with their actions. “And we have known and believed the love that God has in us.”
And again, how have you come to know this?
“Love is God.” He already said it earlier. Look, he says it again.
Love could not be praised to you any more highly than by being called God.
Maybe you were ready to look down on a gift from God.
But will you look down on God?
“Love is God. Whoever lives in love lives in God, and God lives in him.”
Each one lives in the other: the One who holds, and the one who is held.
You live in God, but so that you may be held. God lives in you, but so that He may hold you and keep you from falling.
Don’t imagine that you become God’s house in the same way that your house holds up your body. If the house you live in falls out from under you, you fall. But if you pull away, God does not fall.
When you leave Him, He is not any less. When you come back to Him, He is not any greater.

You are healed, but you give Him nothing. You are made clean, you are made new, you are set straight. He is medicine for the sick, a straight ruler for what is crooked, light for those in darkness, and a home for those who are abandoned.
So everything is given to you. Be careful not to imagine that God gains anything when you come to Him. No, He does not even gain a slave.
Will God really be left without servants if you don’t want to serve, or if nobody wants to?
God does not need servants. The servants need God. That is why the psalm says, “I said to the Lord, You are my God.”
He is the true Lord.
And what does the psalm say?
“For You don’t need my good things.”
But you need the good you get from your servant.
Your servant needs the good he gets from you, so that you will feed him. And you need the good you get from your servant, so that he will help you.
You can’t draw water for yourself. You can’t cook for yourself. You can’t run ahead of your horse. You can’t take care of your animal.
You see that you need the good you get from your servant. You need his help.
So you are not a true master, because you need someone below you.
The true Lord is the One who wants nothing from us. And how terrible for us if we do not look for Him!
He wants nothing from us. Yet He looked for us when we were not looking for Him.
One sheep had wandered off. He found it and carried it back on His shoulders, full of joy.
Did the Shepherd need the sheep? Or did the sheep need the Shepherd? The more I love to talk about love, the less I want this letter to end.
No one is more passionate in praising love.
Nothing sweeter is preached to you. Nothing healthier is drunk by you. But this is true only if you make God’s gift strong in you by living a godly life.

Don’t be ungrateful for His great grace. He had one only Son, but He did not want Him to be the only Son. He wanted Him to have brothers. So He adopted as His own those who would share eternal life with Him.
“This is how love is made perfect in us, so that we can be confident on the day of judgment: because as He is, so are we in this world.
There is no fear in love. But perfect love drives out fear, because fear brings torment.
Whoever is afraid has not been made perfect in love.
Let us love Him, because He loved us first.
If someone says, ‘I love God,’ but hates his brother, he is a liar. If someone does not love his brother, whom he can see, how can he love God, whom he cannot see?
And this is the command we have from Him: whoever loves God should love his brother too.”
1. Dear friends, you remember that we still have to deal with the last part of the apostle John’s letters and explain it to you, as the Lord allows.
We have not forgotten this debt. And you should not forget your right to collect it.

This same love is praised in this letter above everything else, almost as the only thing. And this love makes us very faithful in paying what we owe. It also makes you very sweet in asking for what you are owed.

I said “very sweet in asking,” because where there is no love, the person who demands payment is bitter. But where there is love, the one who asks is sweet. And the one who is asked may have to work hard, but love makes that work feel like almost no work at all. It makes it light.

Look at animals that cannot speak or reason. Their love is not spiritual; it is physical and natural. Even so, the mother gives herself to her young with great affection when they want the milk that is theirs. However hard the little one pushes at her to nurse, that is still better for the mother than if it would not nurse or ask for what love owes it.

We often see big calves pushing their heads into the cow’s udder so hard that they almost lift the mother off the ground. Yet she does not kick them away. In fact, if her calf is not there to nurse, she moos to call it to come and drink.

The apostle speaks of spiritual love when he says, “I became little among you, like a nurse caring for her little ones.” If we have that kind of love, we love you all the more when you ask us for what we owe you.
We don’t like it when people are sluggish, because we worry about those who are listless.
But we had to stop reading straight through this letter for a while. Certain set readings came in between. They had to be read on their holy days and preached on.
Now let’s go back to where we were interrupted. Holy brothers and sisters, listen with full attention to what remains.
I don’t know if love could be praised any more wonderfully than by saying, “Love is God.”
It is short praise, but mighty praise. It is short to say, but mighty in meaning!
How quickly you can say, “Love is God!”
This is short too. If you count it, it is one thing. If you weigh it, how great it is!
“Love is God,” he says, “and whoever lives in love lives in God, and God lives in him.”
Let God be your home, and be a home for God yourself. Live in God, and let God live in you.
God lives in you so that He can hold you. You live in God so that you will not fall. The apostle says this about this same love: “Love never falls.”
How could someone fall when God is holding him?
2. “This is how our love is made perfect in us, so that we can be confident on the day of judgment: because as He is, so are we in this world.”
He tells us how each person can test himself. He can see how much love has grown in him, or rather how much he has grown in love.
If love is God, then God cannot grow or shrink. So when we say love is growing in you, it only means that you are growing in love.
So ask yourself how much you have grown in love. Listen to what your heart answers you. Then you will know how far you have come.
He promised to show us how we can know Him. And he said, “This is how love is made perfect in us.”
Ask: how? “So that we can be confident on the day of judgment.”
Whoever is confident on the day of judgment has perfect love in him.
What does it mean to be confident on the day of judgment?
It means not being afraid that the day of judgment will come.
Some people do not believe there will be a day of judgment. They cannot be confident about a day they don’t believe will come.
Let’s leave them aside. May God wake them up so that they may live. Why should we talk about the dead?
They don’t believe there will be a day of judgment. They don’t fear it or want it, because they don’t believe in it.
Now someone has started to believe in a day of judgment. If he has started to believe, he has also started to be afraid.
But he is still afraid. He is not yet confident about the day of judgment. So love has not yet been made perfect in him.
But does that mean we should give up hope?
You can see the beginning in him. So why do you give up hope for the end?
“What beginning do I see?” you ask.
That very fear. Listen to the Scripture: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”

So he has started to fear the day of judgment. Let his fear lead him to correct himself. Let him be on guard against his enemies, which are his sins. Let him start to come alive again on the inside. Let him put to death the parts of him that belong to the earth. As the apostle says, “Put to death your parts that belong to the earth.”
By “parts that belong to the earth” he means spiritual evil. He goes on to explain it: “Greed, impurity,” and the other things he lists there.
The more this person who fears the day of judgment puts to death his earthly parts, the more his heavenly parts rise up and grow strong.
And the heavenly parts are all good works.
As the heavenly parts rise up, he begins to want the very thing he used to fear.
He used to be afraid that Christ would come and find him ungodly, someone He would have to condemn. Now he longs for Christ to come, because Christ will find him godly, someone He can crown.
Now he has started to long for Christ’s coming. His pure soul longs for the Bridegroom’s embrace, so it turns away from the adulterer. Inside, it becomes a virgin through faith, hope and love.
Now this person is confident about the day of judgment. When he prays, “Your kingdom come,” he is not fighting against himself.
Someone who is afraid of God’s kingdom coming is afraid that his prayer will be answered.
How can we say he is praying if he is afraid that his prayer will be answered?
But someone who prays with the confidence of love wants Him to come right now.
Someone in the Psalms spoke about this same longing: “And You, Lord, how long?
Turn back, Lord, and rescue my soul.”
He groaned because he was being made to wait so long.
Some people patiently accept dying. But some who are perfect patiently put up with living.
What do I mean?

Think of someone who still wants this life. When the day of his death comes, he patiently accepts death. He fights against himself so that he can follow God’s will. In his mind he wants what God chooses, not what human will chooses. Because he wants this present life, he pulls back from death. But still he takes hold of patience and courage, so that he can face death calmly. He dies patiently.
But think of someone who wants, as the apostle says, “to be set free and be with Christ.” That person does not die patiently. He lives patiently, and he dies gladly.
Look at the apostle living patiently. Here he does not love life; he patiently puts up with it.
“To be set free,” he says, “and to be with Christ is far better. But staying in the body is necessary for your sake.”
So, brothers and sisters, make an effort. Settle it deep inside yourselves that this will be your concern: to long for the day of judgment.
The only way love is proved to be perfect is when a person has started to long for that day.
But the one who longs for it is the one who is confident about it. His conscience is not afraid, because his love is perfect and sincere.
3. “This is how His love is made perfect in us, so that we can be confident on the day of judgment.”
Why will we be confident?
“Because as He is, so are we also in this world.”
You have heard the reason for your confidence: “Because as He is,” says the apostle, “so are we also in this world.”
Doesn’t it seem like he said something impossible?
Is it possible for a human being to be like God?
I have already explained to you that “as” does not always mean “equal to.” Sometimes it means “somewhat like.”
Think about how you say, “My picture has ears just as I do.”
Is it exactly the same? And yet you still say “just as.”
So if we were made in God’s image, why are we not like God?
Not equal to Him, but like Him in our own measure.
So where does our confidence on the day of judgment come from?
“Because as He is, so are we also in this world.”
We must connect this to the same love and understand what it means.
The Lord says in the Gospel, “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Don’t the tax collectors do this too?”
So what does He want us to do?
“But I tell you, love your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you.”
So if He tells us to love our enemies, where does He find an example to show us?
From God Himself. He says, “So that you may be children of your Father in heaven.”
How does God do this?
He loves His enemies. He is the One “who makes His sun rise on the good and the bad, and sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous.”

This is the perfection God invites us to: that we love our enemies as He loved His. And this is our confidence on the day of judgment, that “as He is, so are we also in this world.” He loves His enemies by making His sun rise on the good and the bad, and by sending rain on the righteous and the unrighteous. We cannot give them sun and rain. But we can give them our tears when we pray for them.
4. Now let’s see what he says about this same confidence.
How can we tell that love is perfect?
“There is no fear in love.”
Then what do we say about someone who has started to fear the day of judgment?
If his love were perfect, he would not be afraid.
Perfect love would make him perfectly righteous, and he would have nothing to fear. In fact, he would have something to long for: that evil would pass away and God’s kingdom would come.
So “there is no fear in love.”
But in what kind of love?
Not in love that has only just started. Then in what kind?
“But perfect love,” he says, “drives out fear.”
So let fear make the beginning, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.”
You could say that fear gets a place ready for love.
But once love starts to live there, the fear that got the place ready is driven out.
As love grows, fear shrinks. The more love comes inside, the more fear is driven out.
More love, less fear. Less love, more fear.
But if there is no fear at all, love has no way to come in.

Think of sewing. The thread is pulled in by the bristle. The bristle goes in first, but unless it comes out again, the thread cannot take its place. In the same way, fear first fills the mind. But fear does not stay there, because it only comes in to bring love in.
Once the mind feels safe, what joy we have, both in this world and in the world to come!
Even in this world, who can hurt us when we are full of love?
See how the apostle cheers about this very love: “Who can separate us from the love of Christ? Can trouble, or hardship, or persecution, or hunger, or having no clothes, or danger, or the sword?”
And Peter says, “Who will harm you if you follow what is good?—There is no fear in love. But perfect love drives out fear, because fear brings torment.”
Knowing that we have sinned torments the heart. We have not yet been made right with God.
Something in it itches and stings.
So what does the psalm say about this same perfect righteousness?
“You turned my mourning into joy for me. You took off my sackcloth and dressed me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to You and I will not be stung.”
What does “so that I will not be stung” mean?
It means that there will be nothing left to prick my conscience.
Fear pricks. But don’t be afraid. Love comes in, and she heals the wound that fear makes.
The fear of God wounds the way a doctor’s knife does. It cuts away the rotten part, and it seems to make the wound bigger.
Look: when the rot was in the body, the wound was smaller, but it was dangerous. Then comes the knife. Before, the wound hurt less than it hurts now, while the doctor is cutting it.
It hurts more while he is operating on it than if he left it alone. It hurts more during the healing, but only so that it will never hurt again once it is healed.
So let fear fill your heart, so that it can bring love in. Let the scar come after the doctor’s knife.
He is such a great Healer that the scars can’t even be seen. Just put yourself in His hands.
If you have no fear, you cannot be made right with God.
The Scriptures say it plainly: “Whoever is without fear cannot be made right with God.”
So fear must come in first, so that love can come through it.
Fear is the operation. Love is the good health.
“But whoever is afraid has not been made perfect in love.”
Why? “Because fear brings torment,” just as the surgeon’s knife brings torment when it cuts.
5. But there is another saying that seems to contradict this one, unless someone understands it properly.
In one place in the Psalms it says, “The fear of the Lord is pure, lasting forever.”
He shows us a fear that lasts forever, but a pure fear.
But if the psalm shows us a fear that lasts forever, does this letter perhaps contradict it when it says, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear”?
Let’s ask both of these sayings of God what they mean.
There is one Spirit, even though there are two books, two mouths, and two tongues.
This was said through John’s mouth, and that through David’s mouth. But don’t think there is more than one Spirit.
If one breath can fill the two pipes of a double flute, can’t one Spirit fill two hearts and move two tongues?
And if two pipes filled by one breath play in tune together, can two tongues filled by the Spirit, the Breath of God, be out of tune?
So they are in tune there. There is harmony. But it takes someone who knows how to listen.

Look: this Spirit of God breathed into two hearts and filled them. He moved two tongues. From one tongue we have heard, “There is no fear in love. But perfect love drives out fear.” From the other we have heard, “The fear of the Lord is pure, lasting forever.”
How can that be? The notes seem to clash.
No, they don’t. Wake up your ears. Listen to the tune.
There is a reason why the word “pure” is added in one place and not in the other. It is because there is one fear that is called pure, and there is another fear that is not called pure.
Let’s look at the difference between these two kinds of fear. Then we will understand how the flutes play in harmony.
How should we understand them? How can we tell them apart?
Listen, dear friends. Some people fear God because they don’t want to be thrown into hell. They are afraid they might burn with the devil in everlasting fire.
This is the fear that brings love in. But it comes in so that it can leave again.
If you still fear God because of punishment, you do not yet love the God you fear in this way.
You don’t long for the good things. You are just afraid of the bad things.
But because you are afraid of the bad things, you correct yourself and start to long for the good things.
Once you have started to long for the good, the pure fear will be in you.
What is pure fear?
It is the fear of losing those good things themselves.
Pay attention! Fearing God because He might throw you into hell with the devil is one thing. Fearing God because He might leave you is something else.

The fear that makes you afraid of being thrown into hell with the devil is not yet pure. It does not come from loving God, but from being afraid of punishment. But when you fear God because you don’t want His presence to leave you, you hold on to Him. You long to enjoy God Himself.

6. The best way to explain the difference between these two fears is to picture two married women. One fear is the kind love drives out. The other is pure and lasts forever. Imagine that one of the wives is willing to be unfaithful to her husband. She enjoys doing wrong. She is only afraid that her husband will condemn her.
She is afraid of her husband. But the reason she is afraid of him is that she still loves doing wrong.
To this woman, having her husband around is not welcome. It is a burden. And if she happens to be living wickedly, she is afraid of her husband, because he might come home.
People who are afraid of the coming day of judgment are like her.
Now imagine that the other wife loves her husband. She feels that she owes him pure embraces. She does not dirty herself with the filth of unfaithfulness. She wants her husband to be with her.
So how can we tell these two fears apart?
One woman is afraid, and the other is afraid too.
Ask them, and they seem to give the same answer. Ask the first one, “Are you afraid of your husband?” She answers, “Yes, I am.”
Ask the other one if she is afraid of her husband. She answers, “Yes, I am afraid of him.”
The words are the same, but the hearts are different.
Now ask them, “Why?”
One says, “I’m afraid of my husband, because he might come home.” The other says, “I’m afraid of my husband, because he might leave me.”
One says, “I’m afraid of being condemned.” The other says, “I’m afraid of being abandoned.”
Let the same thing happen in the minds of Christians. Then you will find a fear that love drives out, and another fear that is pure and lasts forever.
7. So first, let’s talk to people who fear God the way a woman who enjoys doing wrong fears her husband. She is afraid he will condemn her. Let’s speak to people like that first.

Listen, soul. You fear God because you are afraid He will condemn you. That is just like the woman who enjoys doing wrong. She fears her husband because he might condemn her. You don’t approve of that woman. So don’t approve of yourself either.

If you have a wife, would you want her to fear you like that, just so you won’t condemn her? Would you want her to enjoy doing wrong and be held back only by the weight of her fear of you, instead of hating the wrong itself?
No. You would want her to be pure and faithful because she loves you, not because she is afraid of you.
So be toward God the way you would want your wife to be toward you.
And if you don’t have a wife yet but want one, that is the kind of wife you would want.
But wait, what are we saying, brothers and sisters?

Think about that woman whose fear of her husband is really a fear of being condemned by him. Maybe she doesn’t cheat on him because she is afraid he will somehow find out and take her life. But a husband can be fooled and kept in the dark. After all, he is only human, just like she is, the one who can fool him.
She fears a man she can hide from. So don’t you fear the face of your true Husband, which is always watching you?
“The Lord sets His face against people who do evil.”

She sees that her husband is away, and maybe she is tempted by the pleasure of cheating. But she still tells herself, “I won’t do it. He is away, yes. But it’s hard to stop him from finding out somehow.”

She holds herself back so that a mortal man won’t find out. Yet he might never find out. He might even be fooled, so that he thinks a bad woman is good and thinks an unfaithful wife is faithful. So don’t you fear the eyes of the One no one can fool? Don’t you fear the presence of the One you can never get away from?
Pray that God will look at you and turn His face away from your sins. Pray, “Turn Your face away from my sins.”
But how can you expect Him to turn His face away from your sins if you won’t turn your own face away from them?
The same voice says in the Psalm, “For I admit my wrongdoing, and my sin is always in front of me.”
Admit it, and He forgives.

8. We have spoken to the soul that still has the kind of fear that does not last forever, the fear that love shuts out and throws out. Now let’s speak to the soul that already has the pure fear that lasts forever.
Do you think we will find that soul so we can speak to it? Do you think it is here in this congregation? Is it up here where the clergy sit? Is it anywhere on earth?
It must be here somewhere. It is just hidden.
Right now it is winter. But inside the root, the green life is still there.
Maybe we can get that soul to listen.
But wherever that soul is, I wish I could find it! Then, instead of it listening to me, I could listen to it!
It should be teaching me, not learning from me!

It is a holy soul, a soul on fire, longing for God’s kingdom. I am not the one who speaks to that soul. God Himself speaks to it. He comforts it while it patiently puts up with living here on earth. He says: “You want Me to come right now. I know you wish I would come right now. I know what you are like. You can wait for My coming without fear. I know waiting is hard for you. But wait a little longer. Hold on. I am coming, and I am coming soon.”
But to the soul that loves, time moves slowly.
Listen to her sing. She is like a lily among the thorns. Listen to her sigh and say, “I will sing, and I will understand the blameless way. When will You come to me?”
But in the blameless way she has no reason to be afraid, because “perfect love throws fear out.”
And when He has come and she is in His arms, she still has fear. But it is the fear of someone who feels safe.
What is she afraid of?
She will watch herself and guard against her own wrongdoing so that she doesn’t sin again. She is not afraid of being thrown into the fire. She is afraid of being left by Him.
And what will there be in her? The “pure fear that lasts forever.”
We have heard two flutes playing the same tune.
One speaks of fear, and the other speaks of fear too. But the first speaks of the fear a soul has of being condemned. The second speaks of the fear a soul has of being left alone.
The first is the fear that love throws out. The second is the fear that lasts forever.
9. “Let us love, because He loved us first.”
How could we love at all, unless He had loved us first?
By loving, we became His friends. But He loved us when we were His enemies, so that we could become His friends.
He loved us first, and He gave us the gift of loving Him.
We did not love Him yet. Loving is what makes us beautiful.
Suppose an ugly, unattractive man loves a beautiful woman. What can he do?
Or suppose a woman is ugly, unattractive and dark-skinned, and she loves a handsome man. What can she do?
Can she become beautiful by loving?
Can he become handsome by loving?
He loves a beautiful woman. But when he looks at himself in a mirror, he is too ashamed to lift his face toward the lovely woman he is in love with.
What can he do to become handsome?
Should he wait for good looks to come?
No. While he waits, he only gets older, and that makes him even less attractive.

So there is nothing he can do. There is no advice to give him except this: he should hold himself back and not dare to love someone so far above him. Or if he does love her and wants to marry her, let him love her purity, not just her pretty face.
But our soul, my brothers and sisters, is ugly because of sin. By loving God it becomes beautiful.
What a love that must be, that makes the one who loves beautiful!
But God is always beautiful. He is never ugly, and He never changes.
The One who is always beautiful loved us first. And what were we when He loved us? Nothing but dirty and ugly.
But He did not love us so He could leave us dirty. No, He loved us to change us, to make us beautiful instead of ugly.
How do we become beautiful?
By loving the One who is always beautiful.
As love grows in you, your beauty grows too. Love itself is the beauty of the soul.
“Let us love, because He loved us first.”
Listen to the apostle Paul: “But God showed His love in us: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” The good died for the bad. The beautiful died for the ugly.
How do we know Jesus is beautiful?
“You are more beautiful than any of the sons of men. Grace pours from Your lips.”
Why is that? Look again at why He is beautiful: “More beautiful than any of the sons of men.” It is because “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

But when He took on a human body, He took on your ugliness, so to speak. That means He took on your mortality, the fact that you die. He did this to fit Himself to you and become like you, so He could stir you up to love the beauty inside.
So where in Scripture do we find that Jesus was plain and ugly? We have already found Him beautiful, “more beautiful than any of the sons of men.” So where do we find Him ugly too?
Ask Isaiah: “We saw Him, and He had no beauty or attractiveness.”
Now here are two flutes that seem to play notes that clash. But one Spirit breathes into both of them.
One says, “More beautiful than any of the sons of men.” The other, in Isaiah, says, “We saw Him, and He had no beauty or attractiveness.”
One Spirit fills both flutes. They do not clash at all.
Don’t close your ears. Use your understanding.
Let’s ask the apostle Paul to explain to us how these two flutes play in harmony.
Let him play us the first note: “More beautiful than any of the sons of men.—Who, being in the form of God, did not think it was robbery to be equal with God.”

Let him also play us the second note: “We saw Him, and He had no beauty or attractiveness.—He gave up His high standing. He took the form of a servant. He was made like human beings, and people found Him looking just like a man.
He had no beauty or attractiveness,” so that He could give you beauty and attractiveness.
What kind of beauty? What kind of attractiveness?
The kind of loving that comes from real, selfless love. So that as you love, you run, and as you run, you love.
Now you are beautiful. But don’t keep staring at yourself, or you might lose what you were given. Let your eyes rest on the One who made you beautiful.
Be beautiful only for this reason: so that He will love you.
But aim everything at Him. Run to Him. Look for His embrace. Be afraid of ever leaving Him. Then you will have the pure fear that lasts forever.
“Let us love, because He loved us first.”
10. “If anyone says, ‘I love God.’”
Which God? And why do we love?
“Because He loved us first,” and He gave us the ability to love.
He loved us when we were ungodly, to make us godly. He loved us when we were wicked, to make us good. He loved us when we were sick, to make us well.
Ask anyone you like. Let each person tell you whether he loves God.
He will shout it out and declare, “I love Him! God knows I do.”
But there is another question to ask.
“If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and yet hates his brother, he is a liar.”
How can you prove that he is a liar?
Listen: “If someone doesn’t love his brother whom he can see, how can he love God whom he can’t see?”
What does that mean, then? Does someone who loves his brother also love God?
He has to love God. He cannot help loving the One who is Love itself.
Can anyone love his brother and not love Love?
He has to love Love.
What then? If he loves Love, does that mean he loves God?
Yes, it certainly does.
By loving Love, he loves God.
Or have you forgotten what you said a little while ago, “Love is God”?
If “Love is God,” then whoever loves Love loves God.
So love your brother, and you can be sure.
You cannot say, “I love my brother, but I don’t love God.”
If you say “I love God” but don’t love your brother, you are lying. In the same way, if you say “I love my brother” but think you don’t love God, you are fooling yourself.
If you love your brother, you have to love Love itself. But “Love is God.” So whoever loves his brother has to love God.
But if you don’t love the brother you can see, how can you love God, whom you can’t see?
Why can’t he see God?
Because he doesn’t have Love itself.
He can’t see God because he doesn’t have love. And he doesn’t have love because he doesn’t love his brother.
So the reason he can’t see God is that he doesn’t have Love.

If he has Love, he sees God, because “Love is God.” And love keeps cleaning that inner eye more and more, so that it can see God, the One who never changes. He will always rejoice in God’s presence. He will enjoy Him forever when he is together with the angels.
Only let him keep running now, so that at last he can be glad in his true home.

He must not fall in love with the journey or with the road. Let everything taste bitter except the One who calls us, until we hold on to Him tightly. Then we can say what the Psalm says: “You have destroyed all who leave You to chase after other lovers.” Who are these people who chase other lovers? The people who walk away from God and love the world. But what will you do? The Psalm goes on to say: “But for me, it is good to cling to God.”
All my good is to cling to God, and to do it freely, for nothing in return.
Suppose you ask him, “Why do you cling to God?” And he answers, “So that He will give me—” Give you what?
He is the One who made heaven and earth. What more is He going to give you?
You are already clinging to Him! Find something better than Him, and He will give it to you.
11. “If someone doesn’t love his brother whom he can see, how can he love God whom he can’t see?
And this is the command we have from Him: the person who loves God should love his brother as well.”
What a wonderful thing you said, “I love God”—while you hate your brother!
You murderer, how can you love God?
Didn’t you hear earlier in this same letter, “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer”?
“Yes, but I really do love God, even though I hate my brother.”
No, you really do not love God if you hate your brother.
And now I will prove it another way.
This same apostle said, “He gave us a command to love one another.”
How can anyone say you love Him when you hate His command?
Who would ever say, “I love the emperor, but I hate his laws”?
The emperor can tell whether you love him by this: whether his laws are kept all through the provinces.
So what is our Emperor’s law?
“I give you a new command: love one another.”
So you say you love Christ? Then keep His command, and love your brother.
But if you don’t love your brother, how can anyone say you love the One whose command you look down on?
Brothers and sisters, I never get tired of talking about love in the name of the Lord.
The more you have an endless hunger for this love, the more we hope love itself is growing in you. We hope it is driving out fear, so that only that pure fear remains, the fear that lasts forever.
Let’s put up with the world. Let’s put up with troubles. Let’s put up with the traps of temptation that make us stumble.
Let’s not leave the road. Let’s hold on to the unity of the Church. Let’s hold on to Christ. Let’s hold on to love.

Let’s not be torn away from the members of His Bride, and let’s not be torn away from the faith. Then we can be proud and glad when He comes. And we will live safely in Him, now by faith and later by sight. He has given us such a great down payment on this: the gift of the Holy Spirit.
“Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ is born of God. And everyone who loves the Father also loves the One who is born of Him.
This is how we know that we love God’s children: because we love God and do what He commands.
For this is what loving God is: keeping His commands.”

1. Those of you who were here yesterday probably remember how far we got in going through this letter. We had reached this: “If someone doesn’t love his brother whom he can see, how can he love God whom he can’t see?
And this is the command we have from Him: the person who loves God should love his brother as well.”
That is as far as we got.
So let’s see what comes next.
“Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God.”
Who is it that doesn’t believe that Jesus is the Christ?
The person who doesn’t live the way Christ commanded.
Lots of people say, “I believe.” But faith without actions does not save.
And what faith does is love. As the apostle Paul says, “Faith that works through love.”
Before you believed, your works were either nothing at all, or, if they looked good, they were worth nothing.

If you had no good works, you were like a man with no feet, or with sore feet that can’t walk. If your works looked good before you believed, you were running, yes. But you were running off the road. So you got lost instead of reaching the finish line.
So we need to do two things: run, and run on the right road.
Someone who runs off the road is running for nothing. Or really, he is just wearing himself out.
The more he runs off the road, the more lost he gets.
What is the road we run on?
Christ told us, “I am the Way.”
What is the home we are running to?
“I am the Truth.”
You run by Him, you run to Him, and you rest in Him.
But so that we could run by Him, He came all the way to us. We were far away, like foreigners in a distant country.
And being far away wasn’t the only problem. We were also so weak that we couldn’t even move.
He came like a Doctor to the sick. He stretched Himself out like a Road to reach those who were in a distant country.
Let’s be saved by Him. Let’s walk in Him.

This is what it means to “believe that Jesus is the Christ.” It means believing the way real Christians believe, Christians not just in name, but in their actions and their lives. It does not mean believing the way the devils believe.
For as the Scripture tells us, “The devils also believe, and they tremble.”
What more could the devils believe? They even said, “We know who You are: the Son of God.”
Peter said the same thing the devils said.
The Lord asked His disciples who He was and who people said He was. They answered, “Some people say You are John the Baptist. Some say You are Elijah. Others say Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.
He said to them, ‘But who do you say I am?’
And Peter answered, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’”
And then the Lord said to him, “Simon son of Jonah, how blessed you are! It wasn’t flesh and blood that showed you this. It was My Father in heaven.”
Look at the praise that comes after this faith.
“You are Peter, and on this rock I will build My Church.”
What does “On this rock I will build My Church” mean?
It means on this faith. On what was just said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.
On this rock,” He says, “I will build My Church.”
What great praise! So Peter says, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” But the devils also say, “We know who You are: the Son of God, the Holy One of God.”
Peter said this, and the devils said it too. The words were the same, but the heart behind them was not.
So how can we tell that Peter said it with love?
Because a Christian’s faith comes with love, but a devil’s faith has no love.
How is it without love? Peter said it because he wanted to hold on to Christ. The devils said it because they wanted Christ to go away from them.
Before they said, “We know who You are: the Son of God,” they said, “What do You want with us?
Why have You come to destroy us before the time?”
So it is one thing to confess Christ so you can hold on to Christ. It is a very different thing to confess Christ so you can push Christ away.
So you see, when John says here, “Everyone who believes,” he means a faith that is truly your own. He doesn’t mean a faith that simply agrees with what many others say.
So, brothers and sisters, don’t let any heretics tell you, “We believe too.”
That is why I gave you the example of the devils. I don’t want you to be happy just with the words “I believe.” I want you to look closely at how people actually live.
2. So let’s see what it means to believe in Christ, what it means to believe that Jesus is the Christ.
John goes on: “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God.”
But what does it mean to believe that?
“And everyone who loves the Father also loves the One who is born of Him.”
Right away John joined love to faith, because faith without love is worth nothing.
Faith with love is a Christian’s faith. Faith without love is a devil’s faith. But people who don’t believe at all are worse than the devils. They are even more foolish than the devils.
Some people refuse to believe in Christ. In that way, they are not even as good as the devils.

Another person does believe in Christ, but hates Christ. He confesses his faith because he is afraid of being punished, not because he loves the crown of reward. The devils were afraid of being punished too.

Add love to this faith, so that it becomes the kind of faith the apostle Paul talks about, “faith that works through love.” Then you have found a Christian. You have found a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem, a fellow citizen of the angels, a traveler sighing for home along the way. Join up with him. He is your travel companion. Run with him, if you really are one too.
“Everyone who loves the Father also loves the One who is born of Him.”
Who is the One who “fathered”? The Father.
Who is the One who “is born”? The Son.
So what is John saying?
“Everyone who loves the Father loves the Son.”
3. “This is how we know that we love the sons of God.”
What does this mean, brothers and sisters?

Just a moment ago John was talking about the Son of God, not the sons of God. Here one Christ was set in front of us to think about. We were told, “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God. And everyone who loves the One who fathered,” meaning the Father, “also loves the One who is born of Him,” meaning the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.
Then John goes on: “This is how we know that we love the sons of God.” It sounds as if he was about to say, “This is how we know that we love the Son of God.”

Just before, he was talking about the Son of God, but now he says “the sons of God.” Why? Because the sons of God are the Body of God’s only Son. He is the Head and we are the members, so together it is one Son of God.

So whoever loves the sons of God loves the Son of God. And whoever loves the Son of God loves the Father. No one can love the Father without loving the Son. And whoever loves the sons also loves the Son of God.
Which sons of God?
The members of the Son of God.
And by loving, a person becomes a member himself. Through love he becomes part of the structure of Christ’s body. So there will be one Christ, loving Himself.
When the members of a body love one another, the body is loving itself.
“When one member is in pain, every member hurts along with it. When one member receives honor, every member shares the joy.”
And then Paul goes on to say, “Now you are Christ’s body, and you are its members.”
A little earlier John was talking about loving your brothers and sisters. He said, “If someone doesn’t love his brother whom he can see, how can he love God whom he can’t see?”
But if you love your brother, could it be that you love your brother and don’t love Christ?
How could that be, when you are loving members of Christ?
So when you love members of Christ, you love Christ. When you love Christ, you love the Son of God. When you love the Son of God, you love the Father too.
So love can’t be cut up into separate pieces.
Pick one to love, and the rest come along with you.
Suppose you say, “I love only God, God the Father.”
You are lying. If you love, you don’t love Him alone. If you love the Father, you love the Son too.

“All right,” you say, “I love the Father, and I love the Son. But that’s all. I love God the Father and God the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, who went up into heaven and sits at the Father’s right hand. He is the Word through whom everything was made, and ‘the Word became flesh and lived in us.’ That’s all I love.”
You are lying. If you love the Head, you also love the members. And if you don’t love the members, you don’t love the Head either.
Doesn’t it make you tremble to hear what the Head said from heaven for the sake of His members: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting ME?”
He called the person who persecuted His members His own persecutor. And He calls the person who loves His members His own lover.
And you know who His members are, brothers and sisters. They are none other than the Church of God.
“This is how we know that we love the sons of God: when we love God.”
How can that be? Aren’t the sons of God one thing and God Himself something else?
But whoever loves God loves His commands.
And what are God’s commands?
“I give you a new command: love one another.”

Let no one make excuses by saying he has a different love, that he loves one thing instead of another. This love works one way only. This love is bound together into one. So it makes everything that holds on to it into one. It is like fire that melts things down into one.
It is like gold. The lump is melted and becomes a single piece.
But unless the heat of love is applied, many things can never be melted down into one.
“When we love God,” that is how “we know that we love the sons of God.”
4. And how do we know that we love the sons of God?
By this: “when we love God and do what He commands.”
Here we sigh, because it seems so hard to do what God commands.
Listen to what comes next. Tell me, what makes your loving such hard work?
Loving greed does. What you love costs you hard work. But there is no hard work in loving God.
Greed will order you to work hard, face dangers, go through terrible hardships and troubles. And you will do what it tells you.
What for? So that you can have enough to fill your money chest, and lose your peace of mind.
Maybe you felt safer before you had it than you have ever felt since you started having it.
Look at what greed has ordered you to do.
You have filled your house, and now you are terrified of robbers. You have gotten gold, and you have lost your sleep.
Look at what greed has ordered you to do.
It said, “Do it,” and you did.
What does God order you to do?
“Love Me.” You love gold, so you will look for gold, and maybe you won’t find it. But whoever looks for Me, I am already with him.
You will love honor, and maybe you won’t get it. But who ever loved Me and did not reach Me?
God says to you: You want to get yourself a patron or a powerful friend. So you try to win his favor by going through someone lower down.
But God says to you, “Love Me. You don’t win My favor by going through someone else. Your love itself brings Me close to you.”
Brothers and sisters, what could be sweeter than this love?
There was a good reason you heard this in the Psalm just now: “Wicked people told me about pleasures, but nothing like Your law, O Lord.”
What is God’s Law?
God’s command.
What is God’s command?
That “new command.” It is called new because it makes people new: “I give you a new command: love one another.”
Listen, and you will see that this is God’s law.
The apostle says, “Help carry one another’s heavy loads. That is how you will fulfill the law of Christ.”
This, yes, this is the goal and completion of everything we do: love.
Love is the finish line. This is what we run for. This is what we run toward. When we reach it, we will rest.
5. You heard in the Psalm, “I have seen the end of all perfection.”
He said, “I have seen the end of all perfection.” What had he seen?

Do we think he climbed to the top of some very high, pointed mountain and looked out and saw the whole earth and the circle of the round world? Is that why he said, “I have seen the end of all perfection”?

If that is something to praise, then let’s ask the Lord for really sharp physical eyes. Then all we would need is some extremely high mountain on earth, so that from its top we could see the end of all perfection.
You don’t need to go far. Look, I’m telling you, it is right here. Climb the mountain and see the end.
Christ is the Mountain. Come to Christ, and from there you will see the end of all perfection.
What is this end?

Ask Paul. He says, “The end of the command is love, coming from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith that is not fake.” And in another place he says, “Love is the fullness,” or the fulfilling, “of the law.”
What is more finished and complete than “fullness”?
You see, brothers and sisters, the apostle uses the word “end” here as a word of praise.
Don’t think of an end that means using something up. Think of an end that means completing something.
When someone says, “I have finished my bread,” he means one thing. When he says, “I have finished my coat,” he means something else.
I finish the bread by eating it. I finish the coat by making it.

In both cases the word is “end” or “finish.” But the bread is finished by being used up, and the coat is finished by being made. The bread is finished so that it is gone. The coat is finished so that it is complete.
So take the word “end” in this sense too when the Psalm is read and you hear the title, “On the end, a Psalm of David.”
You hear this all the time in the Psalms, so you should understand what you are hearing.
What does “On the end” mean? “For Christ is the end of the law for everyone who believes.”
And what does “Christ is the end” mean?
It means this: Christ is God, and “the end of the command is love,” and “Love is God.” For the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are One.
There He is your End. In another place He is your Way.
Don’t get stuck on the road and never reach the end.
Whatever else you come to along the way, go past it until you reach the end.
What is the end?
“It is good for me to hold on tight to God.”
Have you taken firm hold of God? Then you have finished the road. You will stay in your true home.
Pay close attention! Someone goes after money. Don’t let money be your end. Pass it by, like a traveler in a foreign land.
But if you love it, greed will tangle you up. Greed will be like chains on your feet. You won’t be able to move forward anymore.
So pass this by too. Look for the end.
You want good health. Still, don’t stop there.
What is good health, anyway? Death ends it. Sickness weakens it. It is a weak, mortal thing that doesn’t last.
Yes, go after good health, so that sickness doesn’t get in the way of your good works. But that is exactly why health is not the end. You want it for the sake of something else.
Anything you want for the sake of something else is not the end. Anything you love for its own sake, freely, is the end.
You go after honors. Maybe you want them so you can do something, so you can get something done and please God that way. But don’t love the honor itself, or you will stop there.
Do you want praise? If you want God’s praise, that’s good. If you want praise for yourself, that’s bad. You are stopping short on the road.
But look, people love you and praise you. Don’t be happy when they praise you for yourself. Let yourself be praised in the Lord, so that you can sing, “My soul will be praised in the Lord.”
You give a good speech, and people praise it.
Don’t let it be praised as if it were yours. The end is not there.
If you make that your end, it will be the end of you. But not an end where you are made complete. It will be an end where you are used up.
So don’t let your speech be praised as if it came from you, as if it were yours.
Then how should it be praised? The way the Psalm says: “In God I will praise the speech. In God I will praise the word.”
If you do this, what comes next in that Psalm will happen to you: “I have put my hope in God. I will not be afraid of what people can do to me.”
When everything that is yours is praised in God, you don’t need to fear losing your praise, because God never fails.
So pass this by too.
6. See, brothers and sisters, how many things we pass by that are not the end.
We use these things along the way. It is like stopping to rest and eat at the rest stops on a journey, and then moving on.
So where is the end?
“Beloved ones, we are sons of God, but what we will be has not yet been made clear.” That is said right here in this letter.
So we are still on the road. Wherever we get to, we still have to keep going, until we reach some end.
“We know that when He shows Himself, we will be like Him, because we will see Him just as He is.
That is the end. There we will praise God forever. There we will sing Alleluia always, without ever stopping.
So this is the end he talked about in the Psalm: “I have seen the end of all perfection.” And it is as if someone asked him, “What is this end you have seen?”
He answers, “Your command, which is very wide.”
This is the end: how wide the command is.
The wideness of the command is love, because where there is love, nothing feels cramped.
The apostle was in this wide, roomy place when he said, “We have opened our mouths to you, Corinthians. Our hearts are wide open. We haven’t closed you out of them.”
This is what it means when it says, “Your command is very wide.”
What is this wide command?
“I give you a new command: love one another.”
So love is never cramped.
Do you want to avoid feeling cramped here on earth?
Then live in that wide, roomy place.

Whatever people do to you, they can’t squeeze you in. That is because you love what people can’t hurt. You love God. You love your brothers and sisters. You love God’s law. You love God’s Church. And it will last forever.
You work hard here on earth, but you will come to the joy that was promised.
Who can take away what you love?
If no one can take away what you love, you can sleep safely. Or better, you can stay awake safely, so that you don’t fall asleep and lose what you love.
It is said for a good reason, “Light up my eyes, so that I never fall asleep in death.”
People who close their eyes to love fall asleep in the cravings of bodily pleasures.
So stay awake! Here are those pleasures: eating, drinking, living it up in luxury, playing games, going hunting. All kinds of evil follow these empty shows.
Don’t we know these things are pleasures? Who can deny that they are enjoyable?
But God’s law is loved even more.
Shout back at the people who try to tempt you: “Wicked people have told me about pleasures, but nothing like Your law, O Lord.”
This joy lasts. It doesn’t only last as the goal you can reach. It also calls you back when you run away.
7. “For this is the love of God: that we keep His commandments.”
You have already heard, “All the law and the prophets hang on these two commandments.”
See how He doesn’t want you to spread yourself thin over lots and lots of pages: “All the law and the prophets hang on these two commandments.”
Which two commandments?
“Love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.
And love your neighbor as yourself.
All the law and the prophets hang on these two commandments.”
So you see which commandments this whole letter is talking about.
So hold on to love, and let your minds be at rest.
Why are you afraid that you might do harm to someone?
Who harms a person he loves?
Just love. It is impossible to love without doing good.
But maybe you correct someone?
Kindness does that, not harshness.
But maybe you give him a beating?
You do it to train him. Your loving kindness won’t let you leave him without discipline.
And in fact, somehow the results turn out different, even opposite. Sometimes hatred acts charming, and love acts fierce.

Someone hates his enemy but pretends to be his friend. He sees him doing something wrong, and he praises him. He wants him to rush headlong. He wants him to go blindly over the cliff of his cravings and maybe never come back. So he praises him, for “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul.” He rubs him with the oil of flattery. See? He hates him, and he praises him.

Someone else sees his friend doing the same kind of thing. He calls him back. If his friend won’t listen, he even uses harsh words. He scolds. He argues. Sometimes it comes to this: you even have to argue!
See? Hatred acts sweet and gentle, and love argues!
Don’t just look at words that seem kind, or at a correction that seems harsh. Look at the source they come from. Look for the root they grow from.
One person is gentle and smooth so that he can deceive. The other argues so that he can correct.
So, brothers and sisters, we can’t make your hearts bigger. Ask God for the gift of loving one another.

Love everyone, even your enemies. Don’t love them because they are your brothers. Love them so that they may become your brothers. Then you will always burn with love for your brothers. You will love the one who has already become your brother. And you will love your enemy, so that by being loved he may become your brother.
Whenever you love a brother, you love a friend.
He is already with you. He is already joined to you in unity, yes, in catholic unity.
If you are living rightly, you love a brother who was once an enemy.
But suppose you love someone who doesn’t believe in Christ yet. Or maybe he believes, but only the way demons believe. You scold him for his emptiness.
Keep loving him, and love him like a brother. He isn’t a brother yet. But you love him so that he may become one.
So all our love is love for our brothers. It is for Christians, for all His members.

My brothers and sisters, think of the training that love gives. Think of its strength, its flowers, its fruit, its beauty, and its sweetness. Think of its food, its drink, its nourishment, and its embrace. You can never get too much of it.
If it gives us so much joy while we are far from home, how glad we will be when we reach our own homeland!
8. So let’s run, my brothers and sisters. Let’s run and love Christ.
Which Christ? Jesus Christ.
Who is He? The Word of God.
And how did He come to the sick?
“The Word became flesh and lived in us.”
So what Scripture predicted has come true: “Christ had to suffer and rise again from the dead on the third day.”
Where is His body?
Where are His members working hard?
Where do you need to be so that you are under your Head?
“And that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in His name through all nations, starting at Jerusalem.”
That is where your love should spread.
Christ says it, and the Psalm says it too, that is, the Spirit of God: “Your commandment is extremely broad.” And yet someone wants love to be shut up in Africa!
If you want to love Christ, spread your love over the whole earth. Christ’s members are all over the earth.
If you love only a part, you are divided. If you are divided, you are not in the body. If you are not in the body, you are not under the Head.
What good does it do you to believe and also to insult Him?
You worship Him in the Head, but you insult Him in the Body.
He loves His Body.
You may have cut yourself off from His Body. But the Head has not cut itself off from its Body.
Your Head calls out to you from above: “It is useless for you to honor Me. It is useless for you to honor Me.”

It is just as if a man wanted to kiss your head while stepping on your feet. Maybe he is wearing boots with nails, and he crushes your feet while he holds your head and kisses it. Wouldn’t you cry out, right in the middle of his kind words? Wouldn’t you say, “What are you doing, man? You are stepping on me!”
You wouldn’t say, “You are stepping on my head.” After all, he honored your head. But the head would cry out more for the parts being stepped on than for itself because it was honored.
Doesn’t the head itself cry out, “I don’t want your honor. Stop stepping on me”?
Now say it, if you can: “How have I stepped on you?” Say this to the head: “I wanted to kiss you. I wanted to hug you.”
But you fool, don’t you see? What you want to hug is joined to what you are stepping on. There is a unity that holds the whole body together.
Up above you honor me, but down below you step on me.
The part you step on hurts more than the part you honor is glad.
How does the tongue cry out?
It says, “It hurts me.” It doesn’t say, “It hurts my foot.” It says, “It hurts me.”
Tongue, who touched you? Who hit you? Who poked you? Who pricked you?
“No one. But I am joined to the parts that are being stepped on.”
“How could I not feel pain, when I am not separate from them?”

9. So our Lord Jesus Christ went up to heaven on the fortieth day. As He went, He entrusted His Body to us, where it would go on lying. He had a reason for this. He saw that many would honor Him because He had gone up to heaven. And He saw that their honor is useless if they trample on His members here on earth.
Someone might go wrong and worship the Head in heaven while trampling on the feet on earth. So that no one would do that, He told us where His members would be.
When He was about to go up, He spoke His last words on earth. After those words He never spoke on earth again.
The Head, about to go up to heaven, entrusted His members on earth to us, and then He left.
From then on, you don’t find Christ speaking on earth. You find Him speaking, but from heaven.
And why did He speak even from heaven?
Because His members on earth were being trampled on.
He spoke from above to Saul, the persecutor: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?”
“I have gone up to heaven, but I still lie on earth. Here I sit at the Father’s right hand. But there I am still hungry and thirsty, and I am a stranger.”
So how did He entrust His Body to us when He was about to go up to heaven?
The disciples asked Him, “Lord, will You show Yourself now? And when will the kingdom of Israel come?”

He was just about to leave, and He answered, “It is not for you to know the time the Father has kept in His own power. But you will receive strength when the Holy Spirit comes on you, and you will be My witnesses.”
See where His Body is spread out. See where He does not want to be trampled on: “You will be My witnesses to Jerusalem, and to Judea, and even to the whole earth.”
“Look where I lie, I who am going up!
I go up because I am the Head. My Body is still lying below.”
Where is it lying? All over the earth.
“Don’t strike it. Don’t hurt it. Don’t trample on it.” These are Christ’s last words as He was about to go into heaven.

Think of a sick man wasting away in bed at home. He is worn out by his illness and close to death. His soul is almost ready to leave his lips. Maybe he is worried about something dear to him, something he loves very much. It comes to his mind, and he calls his heirs. He says to them, “Please, do this.”
In a way, he holds his soul back by force, so that it won’t leave before those words are settled.
He speaks those last words, then he breathes his last, and his body is carried to the grave.
How do his heirs remember the last words of that dying man?
Suppose someone stood up and told them, “Don’t do it.” What would they say?
“What? Shouldn’t I do what my father told me with his very last breath? Those were the last words I heard from him as he was leaving this life.
I may ignore other things he said, but his last words have a stronger hold on me. After that I never saw him again. I never heard him speak again.”

Brothers and sisters, think about this with Christian hearts. A man’s words, spoken as he was about to go to the grave, are so sweet, so precious, and so important to his heirs. Then how should we value the last words of Christ? He spoke them not as He was about to go back to the grave, but as He was about to go up to heaven!

When a man has lived and died, his soul is taken off to other places, and his body is buried in the ground. It makes no difference to him whether his words are carried out or not. He now has something else to do, or something else to suffer. Either he is rejoicing in Abraham’s bosom, or he is in eternal fire, longing for a drop of water. Meanwhile, his body lies in the grave without feeling anything. And yet people still keep the last words of the dying man.
So what can people expect if they don’t keep the last words of the One who sits in heaven? He sees from above whether His words are despised or not.
These are the words of the One who said, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?” He keeps a record for the judgment of everything He sees His members suffer.
10. “But what have we done?” they say.
“We are the ones being persecuted, not the persecutors.”
You are the persecutors, you miserable people.
First of all, you have divided the Church.
The sword of the tongue is stronger than a sword of steel.
Hagar, Sarah’s servant, was proud. Her mistress treated her harshly because of her pride.
That was discipline, not punishment.
So when Hagar ran away from her mistress, what did the angel say to her?
“Go back to your mistress.”
So, you worldly soul, you are like a proud slave woman. Suppose you have suffered some trouble to discipline you. Why are you raging?
“Go back to your mistress.” Hold on to the peace of the Church.
Look, we bring out the Gospels. We read where the Church is spread out. People argue against us and call us “Betrayers!”
Betrayers of what? Christ entrusts His Church to us, and you don’t believe it. So should I believe you when you insult my parents?
Do you want me to believe what you say about “betrayers”?
First, believe Christ yourself.
What is worth believing?
Christ is God, and you are a man. Which one should be believed first?
Christ has spread His Church over the whole earth. If I say it, you may look down on me. But the Gospel says it, so watch out.
What does the Gospel say?
“Christ had to suffer and rise again from the dead on the third day. And repentance and forgiveness of sins had to be preached in His name.”
Where there is forgiveness of sins, there is the Church.

How is that the Church? Because it was said to her, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven. Whatever you set free on earth will be set free in heaven. And whatever you tie up on earth will be tied up in heaven.”
Where is this forgiveness of sins spread?
“Through all nations, starting at Jerusalem.”

So believe Christ! But you know very well that if you believe Christ, you will have nothing to say about “betrayers.” That is why you want me to believe you when you speak evil of my parents. You would rather do that than believe for yourself what Christ predicted!
1. All believers know about the wedding of the king’s son and his feast. The Lord’s Table is spread, and it is open to all who want to come.
But each person needs to watch how he comes to it, even when no one forbids him to come.
The Holy Scriptures teach us that the Lord has two feasts. Both the good and the evil come to one of them. The evil do not come to the other.
The feast we just heard about in the Gospel reading has both good and evil guests.
All who made excuses to stay away from this feast are evil. But not everyone who came in is good.
So I am speaking to you who are the good guests at this feast. You keep these words in mind: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment on himself.”
I am speaking to all of you who are like this. Do not look for the good outside. Put up with the evil inside.
2. I am sure you want to know, dear friends, who I meant when I said they should not look for the good outside, and should put up with the evil inside.
If everyone inside is evil, who am I speaking to?
If everyone inside is good, who did I tell them to put up with as evil?
So first, with the Lord’s help, let me get out of this difficulty as well as I can.
If you think of “good” in the full and strict sense, no one is good except God alone.
The Lord says it very plainly: “Why do you call Me good? No one is good but One, and that is God.”
Then how can that wedding feast have good and bad guests, if “no one is good but God alone”?
First of all, you should know that in a certain sense we are all evil.
Yes, in a certain sense we are surely all evil. But there is no sense in which we are all good.
Can we compare ourselves with the Apostles? The Lord Himself said to them, “If you, then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children…”
If we look at the Scriptures, there was only one evil man among the twelve Apostles. The Lord spoke about him in one place when He said, “You are clean, but not all of you.”
But when He spoke to all of them together, He said, “If you, who are evil…”
Peter heard this. John heard this. Andrew heard this. All the rest of the eleven Apostles heard it.
What did they hear?
“If you, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask Him?”
When they heard that they were evil, they lost hope. But when they heard that God in heaven was their Father, they took heart again.
“You, who are evil.” What do evil people deserve? Only punishment.
“How much more will your Father in heaven…”
What do children deserve? Only a reward.
The word “evil” brings the fear of punishment. The word “children” brings the hope of being heirs.
3. So in one way they were evil, and in another way they were good.
The same people were told, “You, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children.” And right away these words were added: “How much more will your Father in heaven…”
So He is the Father of evil people, but not of those who will be left that way. He is the Doctor of those who will be healed.
So in a certain way they were evil.

And yet I do not think those guests of the Master of the house at the King’s wedding belonged with the “bad” in the words, “they invited good and bad.” The bad, as we heard, were shut out, in the person of the one man who was found without a wedding garment.
In a certain way, I say again, they were bad, and yet they were good. And in a certain way they were good, and yet they were bad.
Listen to John tell in what way they were bad: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
See in what way they were bad: they had sin.
In what way were they good?
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”

You have just heard me explain, from the Holy Scriptures I believe, that the same people are good in one way and bad in another. Suppose we wanted to read the words “they invited good and bad” in this sense, as meaning the same people, both good and bad at once. We are not allowed to read them that way. The reason is the one man who was found “without a wedding garment.” He was not just “thrown out” and kept from that feast. He was condemned to the punishment of everlasting darkness.

4. But someone will say, “What about one man? Is it so strange or so important if one person in the crowd ‘without a wedding garment’ slipped in without the servants of the Master of the house noticing?
Could anyone say, because of that one man, ‘they invited good and bad’?”
So pay attention, my brothers, and understand.
That one man stood for one whole group, because there were many of them.
Here some careful listener may answer me: “I do not want to hear your guesses. I want you to prove to me that this one man stood for many.”
With the Lord’s help, I will prove it clearly. And I will not have to look far to prove it.
God will help me with His own words in this passage. Through my preaching He will give you a clear proof.
“The Master of the house came in to see the guests.”

See, my brothers, the servants’ job was only to invite the good and the bad and bring them in. Notice that it does not say the servants looked over the guests, found among them a man without a wedding garment, and spoke to him.
That is not written.
The Master of the house saw him. The Master of the house found him out. The Master of the house inspected him. The Master of the house set him apart.
It would not have been right to skip over this.
But I have set out to prove something else: that this one man stands for many.
So “the Master of the house came in to see the guests, and He found there a man who was not wearing a wedding garment.
And He said to him, Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?
And the man had nothing to say.”
The One who questioned him was someone he could not give a false answer to.
The garment He was looking for is in the heart, not on the body. If it were worn on the outside, it could not have been hidden even from the servants.
Where must this wedding garment be put on? Hear it in these words: “Let Your priests be clothed with righteousness.”
The Apostle speaks of this garment: “If indeed we will be found clothed, and not naked.”
So the servants did not notice him, but the Lord found him out.
When he is questioned, he has nothing to say. He is tied up, thrown out, and condemned—one man for many.
I have said, Lord, that You teach us that in this You are warning everyone.
So remember with me, my brothers, the words you have heard. You will quickly see and decide that this one man was many.
It is true that the Lord questioned only one man. To one man He said, “Friend, how did you get in here?”
Only one man had nothing to say. And about that same man it was said, “Tie him hand and foot, and throw him into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”
Why? “For many are called, but few are chosen.”
How can anyone argue against the truth when it is shown this clearly?
“Throw him,” He says, “into the outer darkness.”
“Him”—surely that one man. And about him the Lord says, “For many are called, but few are chosen.”
So it is the few who are not thrown out.
It is true there was only one man “who did not have the wedding garment.
Throw him out.” But why is he thrown out?
“For many are called, but few are chosen.”
Leave the few alone. Throw out the many.
It is true that there was only one man.
Yet without a doubt that one man was many. And more than that, those many far outnumbered the good.
The good are many too. But compared with the bad, they are few.
In a harvest there is a lot of wheat. But compare it with the chaff, and the grains are few.
The same people are many when you look at them by themselves. Compared with the bad, they are few.
How can we prove that by themselves they are many?
“Many will come from the east and from the west.”
Where will they come to?
To that feast which both good and bad people enter.
But then He spoke of another feast and added, “and will sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.”
That is the feast the bad will not come near.
Let us receive worthily the feast we have now, so that we may reach the other one.
So the same people are many and also few. By themselves they are many. Compared with the bad, they are few.
So what does the Lord say?
He found one man, and He said, “Let the many be thrown out, and let the few remain.”
The words “many are called, but few are chosen” simply show us clearly which people at this present feast are counted fit to be brought to that other feast. No bad people will come there.
5. So what does this mean?
I do not want any of you who come to the Lord’s Table in this life to be among the many who will be shut out. I want you to be among the few who will be kept.
How can you reach this?
Take “the wedding garment.”
You will say, “Explain this ‘wedding garment’ to us.”

Without a doubt, it is the garment that only the good have. They are the ones who will be left at the feast and kept for that other feast, where no bad person comes. The grace of the Lord will bring them safely there. These are the ones who have “the wedding garment.”
So, my brothers, let us look among the believers for those who have something that bad people do not have. That will be “the wedding garment.”
If we talk about the sacraments, you can see that the bad and the good share them.
Is it Baptism? It is true that without Baptism no one reaches God. But not everyone who has Baptism reaches Him.
So I cannot take Baptism—I mean the Sacrament itself—to be “the wedding garment.” I see this garment in the good, and I see it in the bad.
Maybe it is the Altar, or what is received at the Altar.
But no. We see that many eat and “eat and drink judgment on themselves.”
Then what is it?
Is it fasting? The wicked fast too.
Is it hurrying together to church?
The wicked hurry there too.
Finally, is it miracles?
Both good and bad people perform them. And sometimes good people do not perform them at all.

Look at the people of long ago. Pharaoh’s magicians worked miracles, but the Israelites did not. Among the Israelites, only Moses and Aaron worked them. The rest did not; they watched, they were afraid, and they believed.
Were Pharaoh’s magicians, who did miracles, better men than the people of Israel, who could not do them? Yet Israel was the people of God.
In the Church itself, listen to the Apostle: “Are all prophets?
Do all have gifts of healing?
Do all speak in tongues?”
6. So what is that “wedding garment”?
This is the wedding garment. The Apostle says, “The goal of the commandment is love that comes from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith that is real.”
This is “the wedding garment.”
Not just any kind of love. Very often people who share a guilty conscience seem to love one another.
