Some people rob together. Together they love the harmful arts of sorcery and the theater. They shout together at the chariot races or the wild-beast fights. Such people often love one another. But they do not have “love that comes from a pure heart, a good conscience, and faith that is real.
The wedding garment” is love like this.
“If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels but do not have love, I have become like sounding brass and a tinkling cymbal.”
Tongues have come in alone, and they are told, “How did you get in here without a wedding garment?”
He said, “If I have the gift of prophecy, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.”
See, these are the miracles of people who very often do not have “the wedding garment.”
He says, “If I have all these, but do not have Christ, I am nothing.”
So is “the gift of prophecy” nothing? Is “the knowledge of mysteries” nothing?
It is not that these things are nothing. But if I have them “and do not have love, I am nothing.”
How many good things are worth nothing without this one good thing!

So suppose I do not have love. I may give generously to the poor. I may even confess Christ’s Name to the point of blood and fire. Yet these things may be done just out of a love of glory. Then they are empty.

They may be done out of a love of glory and be empty, instead of coming from the rich love of a godly heart. So he names them all plainly too—and you, listen to them: “If I give away all my goods to help the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but do not have love, it does me no good.”
So this is “the wedding garment.”
Examine yourselves. If you have it, you do not need to be afraid at the Lord’s Feast.
In one and the same person there are two things: love and desire.
If love is not yet born in you, let it be born. And if it is born, let it be fed, cared for, and made to grow.

As for desire, it cannot be completely put out in this life. “For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” As long as desire is in us, we are not without sin. So let love grow and desire shrink. Then one day love will be made perfect and desire will be used up.
Put on “the wedding garment.” I am speaking to you who do not have it yet.
You are already inside. You already come to the Feast. But you still do not have the garment that honors the Bridegroom. “You are still seeking your own things, not the things of Jesus Christ.”
“The wedding garment” is worn to honor the union—the union of the Bridegroom with the Bride.
You know the Bridegroom. It is Christ.
You know the Bride. It is the Church.
Honor the Bride. Honor the Bridegroom.
If you give them both the honor they deserve, you will be their children.
So grow in this.
Love the Lord, and in this way learn to love yourselves. Then, when you have loved yourselves by loving the Lord, you can safely love your neighbor as yourselves.
When I find a man who does not love himself, how can I trust him with his neighbor, whom he should love as himself?
You will say, “Who is there who does not love himself?”
Who? Look: “Whoever loves wickedness hates his own soul.”
Does a man love himself if he loves his body and hates his soul? That hurts him. It hurts both his body and his soul.
And who loves his own soul?
The one who loves God with all his heart and with all his mind.
I would trust such a person with his neighbor right away.
“Love your neighbor as yourselves.”
7. Someone may ask, “Who is my neighbor?”
Every person is your neighbor.
Did we not all have the same two parents?
Animals of every kind are neighbors to one another: dove to dove, leopard to leopard, asp to asp, sheep to sheep. So is a human being not a neighbor to another human being?
Remember how creation was put in order.
God spoke, and the waters produced swimming creatures: great whales, fish, birds, and other such things.
Did all the birds come from one bird?
Did all vultures come from one vulture?
Did all doves come from one dove?
Did all snakes come from one snake? Or all gilt-head fish from one gilt-head? Or all sheep from one sheep?
No. The earth certainly produced all these kinds together.
But when it came to human beings, the earth did not produce man.

One father was made for us. Not even two, a father and a mother. I say it again: one father was made for us, not even two, a father and a mother. The one mother came from the one father. The one father came from no one; God made him. And the one mother came from him.
So notice what our race is like. We all flowed from one spring. And because that one turned bitter, we all went from being a good olive tree to being a wild olive tree.
And so grace came too.
One man brought us into sin and death. Yet we are still one race, still neighbors to one another, not just alike but related to each other.
One came against one. Against the one who scattered came the One who gathers.
So against the one who kills stands the One who gives life.
“For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.”
Everyone who is born from the first man dies. In the same way, everyone who believes in Christ is made alive.
That is, as long as he has “the wedding garment,” and is invited as someone who will stay and not be thrown out.
8. So, my brothers, have love.
I have explained that this is the garment, the “wedding garment.”
Faith is praised. Clearly it is praised. But the Apostle shows what kind of faith this is.
Some people boasted about their faith but did not live good lives. The Apostle James rebukes them and says, “You believe there is one God. You do well. The devils also believe, and they tremble.”
Remember with me why Peter was praised and why he was called blessed.
Was it because he said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God”?
The One who called him blessed was not looking at the sound of the words. He was looking at the feeling in his heart.
Do you want to know that Peter’s blessing did not come from these words?
The devils said the same thing.
“We know who You are, the Son of God.”
Peter confessed that He was “the Son of God.” The devils confessed that He was “the Son of God.”
“Tell them apart, my lord. Tell the difference between the two.”
I do make a clear difference.
Peter spoke out of love. The devils spoke out of fear.
And again Peter says, “I am with You, even to death.”
The devils say, “What do we have to do with You?”
So you who have come to the feast, do not boast about faith alone.
Look closely at what kind of faith this is. Then “the wedding garment” will be seen in you.
Let the Apostle show the difference and teach us: “Neither circumcision is worth anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith.”
Tell us, what kind of faith? Don’t even the devils believe and tremble?
I will tell you, he says. Listen, now I will show the difference: “But faith that works through love.”
What faith, then? What kind?
“Faith that works through love.”
He says, “If I have all knowledge and all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing.”
Have faith with love. You cannot have love without faith.
This is my warning, this is my appeal, this is what I teach you in the Lord’s name, dear friends: have faith with love. For it is possible to have faith without love.
I am not urging you to have faith, but love.
You cannot have love without faith—I mean love for God and for your neighbor. Where could it come from without faith?
How can someone love God if he does not believe in God?
How can the fool love God, the one “who says in his heart, There is no God”?
It is possible for you to believe that Christ has come and still not love Christ.
But it is not possible for you to love Christ and yet say that Christ has not come.
9. So have faith with love.
This is the “wedding garment.”
You who love Christ, love one another. Love your friends. Love your enemies.
Do not let this be hard for you.
What do you lose by it, when you gain so much?
What? Do you ask God for your enemy to die, as if it were a great favor?
That is not “the wedding garment.”
Think of the Bridegroom Himself, hanging on the Cross for you and praying to His Father for His enemies. “Father,” He says, “forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”
You have seen the Bridegroom speak like this. Now look at the friend of the Bridegroom, a guest “with the wedding garment.”
Look at blessed Stephen. See how he rebukes the Jews, as if in anger and resentment: “You stubborn people, uncircumcised in heart and ears! You have resisted the Holy Spirit.
Which of the Prophets did your fathers not kill?”
You have heard how harsh his words are.
And right away you are ready to speak against anyone. I wish it were against someone who offends God, and not someone who offends you.
Someone offends God, and you do not rebuke him. He offends you, and you shout. Where is that “wedding garment”?
So you have heard how harsh Stephen was. Now hear how he loved.
He offended the people he was rebuking, and they stoned him.

His furious persecutors attacked him from every side. Their hands and the blows of the stones crushed him and bruised him to death. As this happened, he first said, “Lord Jesus Christ, receive my spirit.”

He prayed for himself standing up. Then he knelt down for those who were stoning him and said, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them. Let me die in my body, but do not let these people die in their souls.
And when he had said this, he fell asleep.”
After these words he said nothing more. He spoke them and departed. His last prayer was for his enemies.
Learn from this to have “the wedding garment.”
So you too, kneel down and strike your forehead on the ground. As you are about to come to the Lord’s Table, the Feast of the Holy Scriptures, do not say, “Oh, if only my enemy would die!
Lord, if I have earned anything from You, kill my enemy.”
If you do say this, are you not afraid He might answer you, “If I chose to kill your enemy, I would kill you first.
What! Are you boasting because you have now been invited here?
Just think what you were a little while ago.
Did you not blaspheme Me? Did you not mock Me? Did you not want to wipe My Name off the earth?
Yet now you praise yourself because you have been invited here!
If I had killed you when you were My enemy, how could I have made you My friend?
So why do you use your wicked prayers to teach Me to do what I did not do to you?”
No, instead God says to you, “Let Me teach you to imitate Me.
When I was hanging on the Cross, I said, ‘Forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.’
I taught this lesson to My brave soldier.
Be My recruit against the devil.
There is no other way for you to fight and never be defeated, except by praying for your enemies.
Yet by all means ask for this. Yes, ask for this very thing: ask that you may go after your enemy. But ask wisely. Be clear about what you are asking for.
Look, a man is your enemy. Answer Me: what is it in him that is against you?
Is he against you because he is a man?
No. Then what? Because he is evil.
As a man, as the one I made, he is not against you.”
He says to you, “I did not make man evil. He became evil by disobeying; he obeyed the devil instead of God.
What he has made himself is what is against you. He is your enemy because he is evil, not because he is a man.
I hear two words, ‘man’ and ‘evil.’ One is the name of his nature. The other is the name of his sin. I heal the sin, and I keep the nature.”

So your God says to you, “Look, I do take revenge for you. I do kill your enemy. I take away what makes him evil, and I keep what makes him a man. Now if I make him a good man, have I not killed your enemy and made him your friend?”
So keep asking for what you are asking. But do not ask that the people will die. Ask that their hostility will die.
If you pray that the man will die, it is one wicked man praying against another. And when you say, “Kill the wicked one,” God answers you, “Which of you?”
10. So widen your love. Do not limit it to your wives and children.
Even animals and sparrows have that kind of love.

You know how sparrows and swallows love their mates. They hatch their eggs together and feed their young together. They do it out of a kind of free and natural kindness, and they expect nothing in return.
The sparrow does not say, “I will feed my young so that when I grow old, they will feed me.”
He has no such thought. He loves them and feeds them because he loves them. He shows a parent’s affection and expects nothing back.
I know, and I am sure, that you love your children in the same way.
“For children should not save up for their parents, but parents for their children.”
In fact, many of you use this as an excuse for your greed. You say you are getting things for your children and saving them up for them.
But I say: widen your love. Let this love grow. Loving your wives and children is not yet that “wedding garment.”
Have faith toward God.
First love God. Reach out to God. And draw to God everyone you can.
There is your enemy. Let him be drawn to God.
There is a son, a wife, a servant. Let them all be drawn to God.
There is a stranger. Let him be drawn to God.
There is an enemy. Let him be drawn to God.
Draw, keep drawing your enemy. As you draw him, he will stop being your enemy.

In this way let love move forward. Let it be fed, so that it may be made perfect. In this way let “the wedding garment” be put on. And in this way, as we grow, let God’s image, in which we were created, be engraved in us again.
For sin bruised it and wore it away.
How is it bruised? How is it worn away?
When it is rubbed against the earth?
And what does “when it is rubbed against the earth” mean?
When it is worn down by earthly desires.
For “though man walks in this image, he is troubled in vain.”
In God’s image we look for truth, not emptiness.
So by loving the truth, let the image in which we were created be engraved again. And let our Caesar be paid His own tax.
You have heard this in the Lord’s answer when the Jews tested Him. He said, “Why are you testing Me, you hypocrites? Show Me the tax money”—that is, the stamp and the inscription of the image.
Show me what you pay, what you get ready, what is demanded from you.
And “they showed Him a denarius,” and “He asked whose image and inscription it had.”
They answered, “Caesar’s.” So Caesar looks for his own image.
Caesar does not want to lose what he ordered to be made. And surely God does not want to lose what He has made.
My brothers, Caesar did not make the money. The masters of the mint make it. The workers have their orders. He gives his commands to his officials.
His image was stamped on the money. Caesar’s image was on the money.
And yet he demands what others have stamped. He puts it in his treasury. He will not let anyone refuse it to him.
Christ’s coin is man.
In man is Christ’s image, Christ’s Name, Christ’s gifts, and Christ’s rules of duty.

1. The blessed Apostle wanted to show that the Prophets had foretold a time when all the nations would believe in Christ. So he quoted this passage, where it is written, “And it will happen that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

In earlier times, only the Israelites called on the name of the Lord who made heaven and earth. The other nations called on idols that could not speak or hear, and those idols did not hear them. Or they called on demons, and the demons did hear them—but only to harm them.
“But when the right time had fully come,” what had been foretold came true: “And it will happen that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”

Some Jews, even some who believed in Christ, did not want the Gentiles to have the Gospel. They said the Gospel should not be preached to people who were not circumcised. So the Apostle Paul used this passage against them: “And it will happen that everyone who calls on the Name of the Lord will be saved.” Then, to convince the people who did not want the Gospel preached to the Gentiles, he went straight on to say, “But how can they call on Him if they have not believed in Him? And how can they believe in Him if they have not heard of Him? And how can they hear without someone preaching? And how can anyone preach unless they are sent?”

He said, “How can they call on Him if they have not believed in Him?” That is why you did not learn the Lord’s Prayer first and the Creed afterward. You learned the Creed first, so that you would know what to believe. Then you learned the Prayer, so that you would know whom to call on.
So the Creed is about faith, and the Lord’s Prayer is about prayer. That is because it is the person who believes who is heard when he calls.
2. But many people ask for things they should not ask for, because they do not know what is good for them.
So a person who prays must watch out for two things. He must not ask for what he should not ask for. And he must not ask it from someone he should not ask.
Nothing must be asked from the devil, from idols, or from evil spirits.

Whatever we need to ask, we must ask it from Him: from the Lord our God Jesus Christ, from God the Father of the Prophets and Apostles and Martyrs, from the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from God who made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them.
But we must be careful not to ask Him for things we should not ask for.
We ought to ask for life. But if you ask for it from idols that cannot speak or hear, what good does it do you?
In the same way, if you ask God the Father in heaven for your enemies to die, what good does it do you?
Have you not heard or read the Psalm that foretells the terrible, damned end of Judas the traitor? Have you not heard how the prophecy said about him, “Let his prayer be turned into sin”?
So if you get up and pray for bad things to happen to your enemies, your “prayer will be turned into sin.”
3. You have read in the Holy Psalms how the one who speaks there seems to call down many curses on his enemies.
Surely, someone might say, the one who speaks in the Psalms is a righteous man. So why does he wish evil on his enemies like that?

He does not wish it. He sees it coming. It is a prophecy from someone telling what will happen in the future, not a curse he wants to come true. The prophets knew by the Spirit who was going to suffer evil and who was going to receive good. And when they prophesied, they spoke as if they wanted what they saw coming.
But how can you know? The person you are asking evil for today might become a better person than you tomorrow.
But you will say, “I know he is a wicked man.”
Fine. Then you must know that you are wicked too.
Maybe you set yourself up to judge another person’s heart, which you do not really know. But you do know one thing about yourself: you are wicked.
Do you not hear the Apostle say, “I used to be a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man. But I was shown mercy, because I did it in ignorance and unbelief”?

When the Apostle Paul was persecuting the Christians, he tied them up wherever he found them. He dragged them to the Chief Priests to be questioned and punished. So what do you think, brothers and sisters? Did the Church pray against him, or for him?

The Church of God had learned from her Lord. As He hung on the Cross, He said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” So surely the Church prayed for Paul (or rather Saul, as he was still called then). She prayed that what later happened in him would happen.

For he says, “But the churches of Judea that are in Christ did not know me by sight. They had only heard that the man who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy. And they praised God because of me.” Why did they praise God? Only because they had asked God for this before it happened.
4. So first of all our Lord cut out “much speaking.” He did not want you to bring a flood of words to God, as if your many words could teach Him something.
So when you pray, you need devotion, not lots of words.
“For your Father knows what you need before you ask Him.”
So do not be eager to use many words, because He knows what you need.
But someone might say here: If He knows what we need, why should we use even a few words? Why should we pray at all?
He already knows. So let Him just give us what He knows we need.
Yes, but He wants you to pray. He wants to give to your longing, so that you will not take His gifts lightly. After all, He is the one who put this deep longing in us.
So the words our Lord Jesus Christ taught us in His prayer are the rule and measure for our desires.
You must not ask for anything except what is written there.
5. “So this is what you should say,” He says: “Our Father, who is in heaven.”
Here you see that you have started to have God as your Father.
You will have Him as your Father when you are born again.
Even now, before you are born, you have been conceived from His seed. You are about to be brought to birth in the baptismal font, which is like the Church’s womb.
“Our Father, who is in heaven.”
So remember that you have a Father in heaven.
Remember that you were born from your father Adam to die. And remember that you are going to be born again from God the Father to live.
And whatever you say, say it in your hearts.
Only let your prayer come from deep, sincere longing, and the One who hears prayer will answer it with power.
“May Your name be kept holy.”
Why do you ask for God’s name to be kept holy?
It is already holy. So why do you ask for something that is already holy?
And when you ask for His name to be kept holy, aren’t you praying to Him for His sake, and not for your own?
No. If you understand it correctly, you are asking for yourself.
What you are asking is this: that His name, which is always holy in itself, will be kept holy in you.
What does “be kept holy” mean?
It means “be treated as holy,” and not be looked down on.
So you see, the good you wish for, you are wishing for yourself.
For if you look down on God’s name, it will be bad for you, not for God.
6. “May Your kingdom come.”
Who are we talking to? Won’t God’s kingdom come even if we do not ask for it?
We are speaking about the kingdom that will come after the end of the world.
For God always has a kingdom. The whole creation serves Him, so He is never without a kingdom.
So what kingdom are you wishing for?
The one written about in the Gospel: “Come, you who are blessed by My Father. Receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you since the world began.”
That is the kingdom we mean when we say, “May Your kingdom come.”
We pray that it will come in us. We pray that we will be found in it.
It will certainly come. But what good will it do you if it finds you standing on the left side?
So here again you are wishing good for yourself. You are praying for yourself.
This is what you long for. This is the desire in your prayer: that you will live in such a way that you will have a share in God’s kingdom, which will be given to all the saints.
So when you say, “May Your kingdom come,” you are praying for yourself, that you will live a good life.
Let us have a share in Your kingdom. Let what is coming to Your saints and righteous people come to us too.
7. “May Your will be done.”
What? If you do not say this, won’t God do His will anyway?
Remember what you said in the Creed: “I believe in God the Father Almighty.”
If He is Almighty, why do you pray for His will to be done?
So what does “May Your will be done” mean?
It means: may it be done in me, so that I do not fight against Your will.
So here again you are praying for yourself, not for God.
For God’s will is going to be done in you, even if it is not done by you.

He will say to some, “Come, you who are blessed by My Father. Receive the kingdom prepared for you since the world began.” In them God’s will will be done: the saints and righteous will receive the kingdom. And He will say to others, “Go away into the everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” In them too God’s will will be done: the wicked will be condemned to everlasting fire.
But for His will to be done by you is something different.
So there is a good reason why you pray for His will to be done in you. It is so that things will go well for you.
Whether things go well or badly for you, His will is still going to be done in you. But oh, how I wish it would be done by you as well!
So why do I say, “May Your will be done in heaven and on earth,” and not, “May Your will be done by heaven and earth”?
Because what is done by you is really done in you by Him.
Nothing is ever done by you unless He Himself does it in you.
Sometimes He does things in you that are not done by you. But nothing is ever done by you unless He does it in you.
8. But what does “in heaven and on earth” mean, or “as in heaven, so on earth”?
The Angels do Your will. May we do it too.
“May Your will be done as in heaven, so on earth.”
The mind is heaven, and the flesh is earth.
Maybe you say with the Apostle (if you really do say it), “With my mind I serve God’s law, but with my flesh I serve the law of sin.” Then God’s will is being done in heaven, but not yet on earth.

But a day is coming when the flesh will agree with the mind, and “death will be swallowed up in victory.” Then no bodily cravings will be left for the mind to fight against. The struggle on earth will be gone, and the war in the heart will be over. And this will be gone too, which Scripture describes: “The flesh fights against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh. They are opposed to each other, so that you cannot do the things you want to do.” When this war is over, I say, and all sinful desire has been changed into love, nothing will be left in the body to oppose the spirit. There will be nothing to tame, nothing to hold back with a bridle, nothing to stamp down. Everything will move together in harmony toward righteousness, and God’s will will be done in heaven and on earth.
“May Your will be done in heaven and on earth.”
When we pray for this, we are wishing for perfection.
“May Your will be done as in heaven, so on earth.”
In the Church, the spiritual people are heaven, and the worldly people are earth.
So “May Your will be done as in heaven, so on earth” means this: as the spiritual people serve You, may the worldly people also be changed and serve You too.
“May Your will be done as in heaven, so on earth.”
There is also another, very spiritual meaning.
For we are told to pray for our enemies.
The Church is heaven, and the enemies of the Church are earth.
So what does “May Your will be done as in heaven, so on earth” mean?
May our enemies believe in You, just as we believe! May they become our friends and stop being our enemies!
They are earth, and that is why they are against us. May they become heaven, and then they will be with us.
9. “Give us today our daily bread.”
Here it is clear that we are praying for ourselves.
When you say, “May Your name be kept holy,” it takes some explaining to show that you are praying for yourself and not for God.

When you say, “May Your will be done,” this too needs explaining. Otherwise you might think you are wishing something good for God in this prayer, that His will would be done, instead of praying for yourself.
When you say, “May Your kingdom come,” this also must be explained. Otherwise you might think you are wishing something good for God in this prayer, that He would reign.
But from this point to the end of the Prayer, it is plain that we are praying to God for ourselves.
When you say, “Give us today our daily bread,” you admit that you are God’s beggar.
But do not be ashamed of this. No matter how rich someone is on earth, he is still God’s beggar.
The beggar stands in front of the rich man’s house. But the rich man himself stands at the door of the great Rich One.
People come to the rich man with requests, and he goes to God with his own requests.
If he were not in need, he would not knock on God’s ears in prayer.
And what does the rich man need?
I dare to say it: the rich man needs even his daily bread.
How is it that he has plenty of everything? Where did it come from, except that God gave it to him?
What would he have if God took His hand away?
Haven’t many people gone to sleep rich and woken up as beggars?
And if he does not go without, that is because of God’s mercy, not his own power.

10. Dear friends, think about this bread that fills our bodies and gives our flesh new strength each day. God gives this bread not only to people who praise Him, but also to people who insult Him. He is the one “who makes His sun rise on bad people and good people, and sends rain on those who do right and those who do wrong.”
You praise Him, and He feeds you. You insult Him, and He still feeds you.
He is waiting for you to turn from your sin. But if you refuse to change, He will condemn you.

So both good and bad people receive this bread from God. Do you think, then, that there is no other bread that the children ask for? The Lord spoke of it in the Gospel when He said, “It is not fitting to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”
Yes, there certainly is.
So what is that bread? And why is it called daily?
Because it is just as necessary as the other bread. We cannot live without it, just as we cannot live without bread.
It is shameless to ask God for riches. It is not shameless to ask for daily bread.
What feeds pride is one thing. What keeps us alive is something else.
This bread that can be seen and touched is given to both good and bad people. But there is also a daily bread that the children pray for.
That bread is the word of God, which is given out to us day by day.
Our bread is daily bread. It keeps alive not our bodies, but our souls.
We need it, because even now we are workers in the vineyard. It is our food, not our pay.
The man who hires a worker for his vineyard owes him two things: food, so that he does not faint, and his pay, so that he can be glad.
So our daily food here on earth is the word of God, which is always being given out in the churches. Our pay after the work is done is called eternal life.

Or again, by our daily bread you may understand what the faithful receive—what you will receive after you are baptized. Then it makes good sense for us to ask, “Give us today our daily bread.” We are asking to live in such a way that we are never cut off from the Holy Altar.
11. “And forgive us our debts, as we forgive those who owe us.”
Here again we do not need to explain that we are praying for ourselves.
We are begging for our debts to be forgiven.
For we are in debt—not in money, but in sins.
Maybe you are thinking right now, “And you too?”
We answer, “Yes, we too.”
“What? Holy Bishops, are you in debt too?”
“Yes, we are in debt too.”
“Surely not you, my lord!”
“Don’t say such a thing! Don’t be so unfair to yourself.”
I am not being unfair to myself. I am telling the truth. We are in debt: “If we say we have no sin, we are fooling ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
We have been baptized, and yet we are still in debt.
It is not that something was left over that was not forgiven us in Baptism. It is that as we live, we keep picking up things that need to be forgiven every day.
People who are baptized and then die right away come up out of the font with no debt. They leave the world without any debt.
But people who are baptized and go on living pick up stains of sin, because they are weak and mortal. It is like a leaking ship. These sins do not sink the ship, but it still needs to be pumped out.
Otherwise, water will leak in little by little until the whole ship sinks.
Praying this prayer is like using the pump.
But we should not only pray. We should also give to the poor. When the pump is used to keep a ship from sinking, both voices and hands are at work.
We work with our voices when we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us.”
And we work with our hands when we do this: “Share your bread with the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house.
Hide your gift to the poor in a poor man’s heart, and it will plead for you before the Lord.”
12. All our sins were forgiven in the “washing of new birth.” Even so, we would be in serious trouble if we were not also given the daily cleansing of the Holy Prayer.

Giving to the poor and praying wash sins away. Only we must not commit the kind of sins that would force us to be cut off from our daily Bread. Let us all avoid debts like that, which bring a severe and certain condemnation.
Do not call yourselves righteous, as if you had no reason to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us.”

Maybe you stay away from idol worship, from the comforts astrologers offer, and from the cures of magicians. Maybe you stay away from the lies of false teachers and the splits caused by people who break away from the Church. Maybe you stay away from murder, adultery and sexual immorality, from stealing and robbery, from lying in court, and from all the other sins I do not name. Those sins have ruinous results. Anyone who commits them must be cut off from the altar. He is bound on earth in such a way that he is also bound in heaven, which puts him in great and deadly danger—unless he is set free again on earth in such a way that he is also set free in heaven. But even after we set all these sins aside, there are still plenty of ways a person can sin.
A person sins by enjoying looking at something he should not look at.
But who can control how quickly the eye moves?
In fact, people say the eye got its very name from its quickness.
Who can hold back the ear or the eye?

You can shut your eyes whenever you want, and they close in a moment. But you can only close your ears with some effort. You have to lift your hand and reach them. And if someone holds your hand, your ears stay open. Then you cannot shut them against insults, dirty talk, flattery, or tempting words.
And when you hear things you should not hear, even if you do not do them, don’t you sin with your ear? Don’t you enjoy hearing something bad?
How many great sins the deadly tongue commits!
Yes, sometimes they are sins so serious that a person is cut off from the altar because of them.
All speaking against God comes from the tongue. And many careless words are spoken that are not right.

But suppose your hand does nothing wrong, your feet do not run to anything evil, and your eyes do not look at anything immodest. Suppose your ears do not listen with pleasure to filthy talk, and your tongue does not speak indecent words. Even so, tell me: who can control his thoughts?
How often we pray, my brothers and sisters, while our thoughts are somewhere else! It is as if we forget who we are standing before, or who we are bowing down before!
If all these things are gathered together against us, will they fail to crush us just because they are small faults?
What does it matter whether we are crushed by lead or by sand?
Lead is one solid lump. Sand is tiny grains. But there are so many grains that they crush you.
In the same way, your sins are small.
Don’t you see how rivers fill up and land is flooded and ruined by small drops?
The drops are small, but there are many of them.
13. So let us say it every day, and say it sincerely from the heart, and do what we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us.”
It is a promise, a covenant, an agreement that we make with God.
The Lord your God says to you, “Forgive, and I will forgive.”

You have not forgiven. So it is you, not I, who keeps your sins held against you. My dearly loved children, I beg you, listen to me. I know what is good for you in the Lord’s Prayer, and most of all in this line of it: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us.”
You are about to be baptized. Forgive everything. Whatever anyone has in his heart against anyone else, let him forgive it from his heart.

Come in like that, and be sure of this: all your sins are forgiven. That includes the original sin you received when you were born from your parents, going back to Adam—the sin that is the reason you run with babies to the Savior’s grace. It also includes all the sins you have committed later in your lives, by word, deed, or thought. All of them are forgiven. And you will come out of the water as if from standing before your Lord, with every debt surely cancelled.
14. Now, because of those daily sins I have talked about, you need to say in that daily prayer that cleanses us, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us.” So what will you do?
You have enemies. For who can live on this earth without them?
Be careful: love them.
Your enemy can never hurt you by his violence as much as you hurt yourself if you do not love him.

He may damage your property, or your flocks, or your house, or your male servant, or your female servant, or your son, or your wife. At the most, if he is given that much power, he may harm your body.
But can he harm your soul the way you can harm it yourself?
Dear friends, I beg you, reach forward to this perfection.
But am I the one who has given you the power to do this?
No, He alone has given it—the One to whom you say, “May Your will be done as in heaven, so on earth.”
But do not think it is impossible.
I know—I have seen it for myself—that there are Christians who really do love their enemies.
If you think it is impossible, you will not do it.
So first believe that it can be done. Then pray for God’s will to be done in you.
After all, what good does your neighbor’s evil do you?
If there were no evil in him, he would not even be your enemy.
So wish him well. Wish that he would stop his evil, and then he will not be your enemy anymore.
It is not the human being in him that is your enemy. It is his sin.
Is he your enemy because he has a soul and a body?
In that way he is just like you. You have a soul, and so does he. You have a body, and so does he.
He is made of the same stuff as you. You were both made from the same earth and given life by the same Lord.
In all this he is just like you. So see him as your brother.
The first couple, Adam and Eve, were our parents—one our father, the other our mother. So we are brothers and sisters.
But let us leave aside our first beginnings.
God is our Father, and the Church is our Mother. So we are brothers and sisters.
But you will say, “My enemy is a pagan, a Jew, or a heretic.” I spoke about them a little while ago, when I explained the words, “May Your will be done as in heaven, so on earth.”
O Church, your enemy is the pagan, the Jew, the heretic. He is the earth.
If you are heaven, call on your Father in heaven and pray for your enemies. Saul was once an enemy of the Church like that. People prayed for him, and he became her friend.
He did not just stop persecuting her. He worked hard to help her.
And yet, to be honest, people did pray against him. But they prayed against his wickedness, not against his human nature.
So let your prayer be against your enemy’s wickedness. Pray that his wickedness will die and that he will live.
If your enemy died, it might seem that you had lost an enemy. But you would not have gained a friend.
But if his wickedness dies, you lose an enemy and gain a friend at the same time.
15. But you are still saying, “Who can do this? Who has ever done it?”
May God make it happen in your hearts!
I know as well as you do that only a few people do it. Those who do are great and spiritual people.
All the faithful in the Church who come to the altar and receive the Body and Blood of Christ—are they all like that?
And yet they all say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us.”
What if God answered them, “Why do you ask Me to do what I have promised, when you do not do what I have commanded?”
What have I promised?
“To forgive your debts.”
What have I commanded?
“That you also forgive those who owe you.”
How can you do this if you do not love your enemies?
So what should we do, brothers and sisters?
Has Christ’s flock shrunk down to so few?
Suppose only those who love their enemies should say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us.” Then I do not know what to do. I do not know what to say.
Should I tell you, “If you do not love your enemies, do not pray”? I do not dare say that. No—pray instead that you will love them.
But should I tell you, “If you do not love your enemies, do not say in the Lord’s Prayer, ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us’”?
Suppose I told you, “Do not say these words.”
If you do not say them, your debts are not forgiven. And if you do say them but do not live by them, your debts are not forgiven either.
So for them to be forgiven, you must both say the prayer and live by it.
16. I see a reason to comfort not just a few people, but the whole crowd of Christians. And I know you are eager to hear it.
Christ has said, “Forgive, so that you will be forgiven.”
And what do you say in the Prayer we have been talking about?
“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us.”
In other words: Lord, forgive us in the same way that we forgive.
This is what you are saying: “O Father, who is in heaven, forgive our debts in the same way that we also forgive those who owe us.”
This is what you must do. If you do not do it, you will be lost.
When your enemy asks you to forgive him, forgive him right away.
Is that too much for you to do?
It may be a lot to love your enemy while he is attacking you. But is it a lot to love someone who is humbly begging you for mercy?
What do you have to say?
Before, he was violent, and so you hated him.
I wish you had not hated him even then. I wish that while you were suffering his violence, you had remembered the Lord saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”
I would have wished very much that even when your enemy was attacking you, you had paid attention to the Lord your God saying this.
But maybe you will say: He did it, but He did it because He is the Lord, the Christ, the Son of God, the Only Son, the Word who became flesh.
But what can I do? I am a weak and sinful person.
If your Lord is too high an example for you, then think about your fellow servant.
Holy Stephen was being stoned. While they were throwing stones at him, he knelt down and prayed for his enemies. He said, “Lord, do not put this sin on their account.”
They were throwing stones, not asking to be forgiven. Yet he prayed for them.
I wish you were like him. Reach forward.
Why are you always dragging your heart along the ground?
Listen: “Lift up your heart.” Reach forward. Love your enemies.
If you cannot love him while he is attacking you, at least love him when he asks you to forgive him.
Love the person who says to you, “Brother, I have sinned. Forgive me.”
If you do not forgive him then, I am not just saying that you wipe this prayer out of your heart. I am saying that you yourself will be wiped out of God’s book.
17. But if at least then you forgive him, or let go of the hatred in your heart—remember, it is hatred in the heart that I am telling you to give up, not proper discipline.
“But what if the person who asks me to forgive him is someone I ought to punish?”
Do as you see fit. For I assume you love your child even when you punish him.
You ignore his cries when you discipline him with the rod, because you are saving his inheritance for him.
So this is what I am saying: when your enemy asks you to forgive him, let go of all hatred in your heart.
But maybe you will say, “He is lying. He is only pretending.”
You who judge another person’s heart, tell me what your own father is thinking. Tell me what you yourself were thinking yesterday.
He is asking and begging you to forgive him. So forgive him—by all means, forgive him.
If you will not forgive him, you are hurting yourself, not him. He knows what to do.
You do not want to forgive your own fellow servant. So he will go to your Lord and say to Him, “Lord, I begged my fellow servant to forgive me, and he would not. Please, You forgive me.”
Doesn’t the Lord have the power to cancel His servant’s debts?
So that man receives forgiveness from his Lord and goes away free, while you stay tied up.

Tied up how? The time for prayer will come. The time must come when you have to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us.” And the Lord will answer you: You wicked servant! When you owed Me such a huge debt, you asked Me, and I forgave you. “Ought you not to have felt pity for your fellow servant, the way I felt pity for you?”
These words come from the Gospel, not from my own heart.
But if someone asks you and you forgive the one who begs for pardon, then you can say this prayer.
And even if you are not yet strong enough to love him while he is attacking you, you can still pray this prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us.”
Let us move on to the rest.
18. “And do not lead us into temptation.”
We say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us,” because of our past sins. We cannot undo them and make it as if they had never been done.
You can work hard not to do again what you did before. But how can you make it so that what you have done was never done?
For the things that have already been done, this line of the prayer helps you: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive those who owe us.”
But what will you do about the sins you might fall into later?
“Do not lead us into temptation, but rescue us from evil.”
“Do not lead us into temptation, but rescue us from evil”—that is, from temptation itself.

19. Now the first three requests—“May Your name be kept holy, may Your kingdom come, may Your will be done as in heaven, so on earth”—are about eternal life. God’s name should always be kept holy in us. We should always be in His kingdom. We should always do His will.
This will go on forever.
But “daily bread” is needed now.
Everything else we pray for from this point on has to do with what we need in this present life.
We need daily bread in this life. We need our debts forgiven in this life.
For when we reach the other life, all debts will come to an end.
In this life there is temptation. In this life the voyage is dangerous. In this life something is always sneaking in through the cracks of our weaknesses, and it has to be pumped out.
But when we are made equal to the Angels of God, we will no longer need to say and pray to God to forgive our debts, because there will be none.

So here in this life we need “daily bread.” Here we need the prayer that our “debts will be forgiven.” Here we pray that we will “not come into temptation,” because in that other life temptation does not come in. Here we pray that we will be “rescued from evil,” because in that life there will be no evil, only eternal and lasting good.
1. Yesterday the holy Gospel warned us not to ignore the sins of our brothers and sisters. It said: “If your brother sins against you, correct him when it is just the two of you.
If he listens to you, you have won your brother back.
But if he refuses to listen to you, take two or three others with you. Then every word can be confirmed by two or three witnesses.
If he will not listen to them either, tell it to the Church.
And if he will not listen to the Church, treat him like a heathen and a tax collector.”
Today the passage that comes next, which we heard read, is about the same subject.
When the Lord Jesus had said this to Peter, Peter went on to ask his Master how often he should forgive a brother who had sinned against him. He asked if seven times would be enough.
“The Lord answered him: Not just seven times, but seventy times seven.”
Then He added a parable that is full of terror. “The kingdom of heaven is like the master of a house who settled accounts with his servants. Among them he found one who owed ten thousand talents.

The master ordered that everything the man had, his whole family, and the man himself be sold to pay the debt. Then the servant fell down at his master’s feet.” He begged for more time, and he was let off the whole debt.
As we have heard, “His master felt sorry for him and forgave him the whole debt.”

That man was now free from his debt, but he was a slave to evil. After he left his master, he found someone who owed him money. That man did not owe him ten thousand talents, the amount he himself had been forgiven. He owed him a hundred denarii. And “he grabbed him by the throat and began to drag him, saying, Pay me what you owe.”
Then the man begged his fellow servant, just as that servant had begged his master. But he did not find his fellow servant to be the kind of man that servant had found his master to be.
He would not forgive him the debt. He would not even give him more time.
He was very violent and dragged him off to make him pay. And he himself had only just been set free from his own debt to his master!

The other servants were upset. They “went and told their master what had happened.” The master called his servant in and said to him, “You wicked servant! You owed me such a huge debt, and I felt sorry for you and forgave you all of it.
Shouldn’t you have had mercy on your fellow servant, just as I had mercy on you?”
And he ordered that everything he had forgiven him must be paid.
2. So He told this parable to teach us. With this warning He wanted to keep us from being lost.
He said, “My heavenly Father will do the same to you if each of you does not forgive his brother his sins from your heart.”
You see, brothers and sisters, this is clear. The warning is useful. We must by all means obey it, for our own good, so that we do what we have been told.
Every person owes a debt to God. And every person also has some brother who owes a debt to him.
Who does not owe God a debt? Only someone in whom no sin can be found.
And who has no brother in debt to him? Only someone no one has ever sinned against.
Do you think you can find anyone in the human race who does not owe his brother something because of some sin?
So every person is a debtor, and yet he also has debtors of his own.
So the righteous God gives you a rule for how to treat the person who owes you. He will follow the same rule with those who owe Him.
There are two works of mercy that set us free. The Lord Himself stated them briefly in the Gospel: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven. Give, and it will be given to you.”
“Forgive, and you will be forgiven” is about pardoning.
“Give, and it will be given to you” is about doing good to others.
About pardoning: you want your own sin to be pardoned, and you have someone else you can pardon.
About doing good: a beggar asks you for something, and you yourself are God’s beggar.

When we pray, we are all God’s beggars. We stand, or rather we lie face down, at the door of the great Master of the house. We groan and plead because we want to receive something. And that something is God Himself.
What does the beggar ask you for?
Bread. And what do you ask God for, if not Christ? He says, “I am the living Bread that came down from heaven.”
Do you want to be forgiven?
Then forgive. “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”
Do you want to receive? “Give, and it will be given to you.”
3. But now listen. Even in such a clear command, I may raise a difficulty.
When someone asks for pardon, the one who should grant it owes it to him. But this question of forgiveness may puzzle us, just as it puzzled Peter.
“How often should I forgive?
Is up to seven times enough?”
“It is not enough,” says the Lord. “I do not tell you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”
Now count how many times your brother has sinned against you.
If you can reach the seventy-eighth wrong, and get past the seventy times seven, then go ahead and take revenge.
Is this really what He means? Is it really true that if he sins “seventy times seven,” you must forgive him, but if he sins seventy-eight times, you are then allowed not to forgive?
No, I dare to say that even if he sins seventy-eight times, you must forgive.
Yes, as I said, if he sins seventy-eight times, forgive.
And if he sins a hundred times, forgive.
But why should I name one number after another?
In a word: as often as he sins, forgive him.
Have I then taken it on myself to go beyond the limit my Lord set?
He set the limit of forgiveness at the number seventy-seven. Do I dare to jump over that limit?
No. I have not dared to go beyond it at all.
I have heard the Lord Himself speaking through His Apostle, and there no limit or number is set.
He says, “Forgive one another if anyone has a quarrel against someone, just as God in Christ has forgiven you.”
That is the rule.
Suppose Christ forgave your sins only “seventy times and seven.” Suppose He pardoned up to that point and refused to pardon any more. Then you may set the same limit and refuse to forgive beyond it.
But if Christ has found thousands upon thousands of sins and has still forgiven them all, then do not hold back your mercy. Instead, ask forgiveness for that great number.
The Lord did not say “seventy times seven” without a reason. There is no wrong at all that you should not forgive.
Look at this servant in the parable. He was a debtor who turned out to have a debtor of his own. He owed ten thousand talents.
I think ten thousand talents means at least ten thousand sins.
I will not even say how one single talent can include all sins.
But how much did the other servant owe him?
He owed a hundred denarii.
Isn’t that more than “seventy-seven”?
And yet the Lord was angry because he did not forgive him.
A hundred is more than “seventy-seven.” And besides, a hundred denarii may be worth a thousand coins called “asses.”
But what was that compared with ten thousand talents?
4. So if we want to be forgiven, let us be ready to forgive every wrong done to us.
Think about our sins. Count what we do by our actions, by our eyes, by our ears, by our thoughts, and by countless stirrings. I am not sure we even sleep without owing a talent.
That is why we beg every day. Every day we knock at God’s ears in prayer. Every day we bow down and say, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.”
Which of your debts?
All of them, or only some?
You will answer, “All of them.”
Then do the same with the person who owes you.
This is the rule you set. This is the condition you name. This is the promise and agreement you speak of when you pray, “Forgive us, as we forgive our debtors.”
5. So, brothers and sisters, what does “seventy times seven” mean?
Listen, because it is a great mystery, a wonderful sacred sign.

When the Lord was baptized, the Gospel writer Saint Luke recorded His family line at that point. He listed the generations in proper order, one after another, down to the generation in which Christ was born.
Matthew starts with Abraham and goes down to Joseph. But Luke counts upward.
Why does one count downward and the other upward?
Because Matthew set out the family line by which Christ came down to us. So he started his count at Christ’s birth and counted downward.
But Luke starts counting at Christ’s baptism, and that is where the going up begins. So he counts upward. And in his count he reaches seventy-seven generations.
With whom did he begin his count?
Notice with whom. He started counting from Christ and went all the way up to Adam. Adam was the first sinner, and he fathered us bound with the chain of sin.
He counted up to Adam, and that makes seventy-seven generations. From Christ to Adam, and from Adam to Christ, there are these seventy-seven generations.
So if no generation was left out, then no wrong is left out of what we must forgive.
That is why he counted seventy-seven generations, the same number the Lord used about forgiving sins. He began counting from the baptism, where all sins are forgiven.
6. Brothers and sisters, see an even greater mystery in this.
The number seventy-seven holds a mystery about the forgiveness of sins.
That is how many generations there are from Christ to Adam.
So look a little more carefully for the secret meaning of this number. Search out its hidden meaning. Knock more carefully, so that it will be opened to you.
Righteousness means keeping the Law of God. That is true.
The Law is given in ten commandments.
That is why the servant in the parable “owed ten thousand talents.”
These are the famous Ten Commandments, written by the finger of God and given to the people by Moses, the servant of God.
So he “owed ten thousand talents.” This stands for all sins, based on the number of the Law.
And the other servant “owed a hundred denarii.” This also comes from the same number.
A hundred times a hundred is ten thousand, and ten times ten is a hundred.
One “owed ten thousand talents,” and the other owed ten times ten denarii.
Neither number moves away from the number of the law. In both numbers you will find every kind of sin included.

Both men are debtors. Both plead and beg for pardon. But the wicked, ungrateful servant would not repay what he had received. He would not show the mercy that had been shown to him, though he did not deserve it.

7. So think about this, brothers and sisters. Everyone starts from Baptism. He goes out free, and the “ten thousand talents” are forgiven him. And when he goes out, he will soon find some fellow servant who owes him something.
So let him notice what sin really is. The number eleven stands for breaking the law.
The law is ten; sin is eleven.
The law is shown by ten, and sin by eleven.
Why is sin shown by eleven?
Because to get to eleven, you have to go past ten.
The law sets the proper limit, and going past it is sin.
When you go past ten, you come to eleven.
This deep mystery was pictured when the command was given to build the tabernacle.
Many things there are listed by number, and they hold a great mystery.
Among other things, the curtains made of haircloth were to be not ten but eleven. That is because haircloth stands for confessing our sins.
What more do you need?
Do you want to know how all sins are contained in the number “seventy-seven”?
Seven usually stands for something whole. In seven days the cycle of time is complete. When the seventh day is over, it goes back to the first, so that the same cycle can go on.
Whole ages pass by in cycles like this. Yet they never move away from the number seven.
So He was speaking of all sins when He said “seventy times seven.” Multiply that eleven by seven, and you get seventy-seven.
That is why He wants all sins forgiven. He marked them out by the number “seventy-seven.”
So let no one hold on to anything to his own harm by refusing to forgive. Otherwise it will be held against him when he prays.
For God says, “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”
I have forgiven you first. You at least should forgive after that.
If you will not forgive, I will call you back. I will put on you again everything I had forgiven you.
The Truth does not lie. Christ does not deceive, and He is not deceived. At the end of the parable He said, “Your Father in heaven will do the same to you.”
You have found a Father. Imitate your Father.
If you will not imitate Him, you are working to lose your inheritance.
So “My heavenly Father will do the same to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother his sins from your heart.”
Do not say “I forgive” with your tongue while putting off forgiving in your heart. By His threat of vengeance, God shows you what your punishment will be.
God knows where you are speaking from.
People can hear your voice. God looks into your conscience.
If you say, “I forgive,” then forgive.
It is better to be harsh in your words and forgive in your heart than to be gentle in your words and unforgiving in your heart.
8. Now unruly boys will beg us. They hate being beaten, and they object like this when we want to punish them.
“I have sinned, but forgive me.”
All right, I forgave him, and he sins again.
“Forgive me,” he cries, and I forgave him.
He sins a third time.
“Forgive me,” he cries, and a third time I forgave him.
Now, the fourth time, let him be beaten.
And he will say, “What? Have I worn you out up to seventy-seven times?”
If objections like this put strict discipline to sleep, then once discipline is gone, wickedness will run wild without punishment.
So what should we do?
Let us correct with words, and if needed, with the lash. But let us also forgive the sin and throw the memory of it out of our hearts.
That is why the Lord added, “from your heart.” Even when we discipline out of love, gentleness should not leave our heart.
What is as kind and gentle as a surgeon with his knife?
The person who is to be cut cries out, but he is cut. The person who is to be cauterized cries out, but he is cauterized.
This is not cruelty. That surgeon’s treatment must never be called cruelty.
He is cruel to the wounded part so that the patient can be healed. If the wound is handled softly, the man is lost.

So this is my advice, my brothers and sisters. Let us love our brothers and sisters, no matter how they have sinned against us. Let us not let our love for them leave our hearts. And when it is needed, let us discipline them. Otherwise, if discipline becomes slack, wickedness will grow, and we will begin to be accused on God’s behalf. For we have heard it read: “Rebuke those who sin in front of everyone, so that others also may fear.”
Certainly, if you tell the different times apart, which is the only right way, and solve the question like that, then everything is true.
If the sin is secret, rebuke it in secret.
If the sin is public and open, rebuke it in public so that the sinner may be changed, and “so that others also may fear.”
1. We just heard the holy Gospel being read. It has given us a warning about the forgiveness of sins.
Now my sermon must give you a warning about this same subject.
We are servants of the word. It is not our own word, but the word of our God and Lord. No one serves Him without receiving glory, and no one despises Him without being punished.

He is the Lord our God. While He remained with the Father, He made us. Then He Himself was made for our sake, and He made us new. This Lord our God, Jesus Christ Himself, tells us what we have just heard in the Gospel.
“If your brother sins against you,” He says, “rebuke him. If he repents, forgive him. And if he sins against you seven times in a day, and comes and says, I repent, forgive him.”
He does not want “seven times in a day” to mean anything other than “as often as it happens.” Otherwise your brother might sin eight times, and you would refuse to forgive him.
So what does “seven times” mean?
It means always, as often as he sins and repents.
One psalm says, “Seven times a day I will praise You.” That means the same thing as another psalm that says, “His praise will always be in my mouth.”
There is a very strong reason why seven times stands for always. All of time moves around in a circle of seven days that come and then come back again.
2. So whoever you are, if your thoughts are set on Christ and you want to receive what He has promised, do not be slow to do what He has commanded.
What has He promised?
“Eternal life.” And what has He commanded?
That you forgive your brother.
It is as if He said to you, “You are a human being. Forgive another human being, so that I, who am God, may come to you.”

For now I will pass over, or rather pass by for a while, God’s even greater promises. In them our Creator promises to make us equal to His angels, so that we may live forever with Him, in Him, and through Him. Leaving that aside for now, don’t you want to receive from your God the very thing you are commanded to give your brother?
I say it again: this very thing you are commanded to give your brother, don’t you want to receive it from your Lord?
Tell me if you don’t want it. Then don’t give it.
What does this mean? It means you should forgive the person who asks you, if you need to be forgiven yourself.
But if you have nothing that needs to be forgiven, then, I dare to say, refuse to forgive.
But I should not even say this.
Even if you have nothing that needs to be forgiven, forgive.
3. You are about to say to me, “But I am not God. I am a human being, a sinner.”
Thank God that you admit you have sins.
So forgive, so that your sins may be forgiven.
Yet the Lord our God Himself urges us to imitate Him.

First of all, God Himself, Christ, urges us. The Apostle Peter said about Him, “Christ suffered for us. He left you an example, so that you would follow in His steps. He did no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth.”
He truly had no sin. Yet He died for our sins and shed His blood so that sins could be forgiven.
For our sake He took on Himself what He did not deserve, so that He could set us free from what we did deserve.
He did not deserve death, and we did not deserve life.
Why? Because we were sinners.
He did not deserve death, and we did not deserve life. He received what He did not deserve. He gave what we did not deserve.

But we are speaking about the forgiveness of sins. So that you do not think it is too high a thing to imitate Christ, listen to the Apostle. He says, “Forgive one another, just as God in Christ has forgiven you.”
“So imitate God.”
These are the Apostle’s words, not mine.
Is it really proud to imitate God?
Listen to the Apostle: “Imitate God, as dearly loved children.”
You are called a child. If you refuse to imitate Him, why do you want His inheritance?
4. I would say this even if you had no sin that you wanted to have forgiven.

But as things are, whoever you are, you are a human being. Even if you are righteous, you are a human being. Whether you are a layperson, a monk, a member of the clergy, a bishop, or an apostle, you are a human being.
Listen to what the Apostle says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.”
This is the famous John, who was also an Evangelist. The Lord Christ loved him more than all the others, and he lay against His chest. He is the one who says, “If we say.”
He did not say, “If you say that you have no sin.” He said, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
He included himself in the guilt, so that he would also be included in the pardon.
“If we say.”
Think about who is saying this: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.
But if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all wickedness.”
How does He cleanse us?
By forgiving. He does this not because He finds nothing to punish, but because He finds something to forgive.
So, brothers, if we have sins, let us forgive those who ask us.
Let us not hold on to hostility in our hearts against anyone.
Holding on to hostility corrupts our hearts more than anything else.
5. So I want you to forgive, because I find you asking for forgiveness.

You are being asked, so forgive. You are being asked, and you yourself will ask. You are being asked, so forgive. You will ask to be forgiven. For look, the time of prayer will come. I will hold you to the words you will have to say.
You will say, “Our Father, who is in heaven.”
For you will not be one of the children if you do not say, “Our Father.”
So you will say, “Our Father, who is in heaven.”
Go on: “May Your name be held holy.”
Keep going: “May Your kingdom come.”
Go on further: “May Your will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.”
Look at what you add next: “Give us today our daily bread.”
Where are your riches?
So you are a beggar.
But for now, since this is the point I am talking about, say what comes after “Give us today our daily bread.”
Say what follows: “Forgive us our debts.”
Now you have come to the words I am talking about: “Forgive us our debts.”
By what right? By what agreement? On what condition? On what clear terms?
“As we also forgive those who owe us.”
Not forgiving is only a small part of it. You do even more: you lie to God.
The condition is set. The law is fixed.
“Forgive as I forgive.”
So He does not forgive unless you forgive.
“Forgive as I forgive.”
You want to be forgiven when you ask. So forgive the person who asks you.

The One who is an expert in heaven’s laws gave us the words of these prayers. He does not trick you. Ask in the exact words of His heavenly voice. Say, “Forgive us, as we also forgive,” and do what you say.
Whoever lies in his prayers loses the benefit he is asking for. Whoever lies in his prayers loses his case and also receives his punishment.
If someone lies to the emperor, he is proven guilty of his lie when he comes. But when you lie in prayer, your own prayer proves you guilty.
For God does not look for a witness against you to prove you guilty.
The One who gave you the words of the prayers is your Advocate. If you lie, He is a witness against you. If you do not change your ways, He will be your Judge.
So say it, and do it too.
If you do not say it, you will not get what you ask for, because you are asking against the law. But if you say it and do not do it, you will also be guilty of lying.
There is no way to escape that line except by doing what we say.
Can we erase this line from our prayer?
Do you want the words “Forgive us our debts” to stay, and us to erase what follows, “As we also forgive those who owe us”?
You must not erase it, or you yourself will be erased first.
So in this prayer you say, “Give,” and you say, “Forgive.” You say this so that you may receive what you do not have, and be forgiven for the wrong you have done.
So if you want to receive, give. If you want to be forgiven, forgive.
That is a short summary.
Listen to Christ Himself in another place: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven.”
What will you forgive?
The sins others have committed against you.
What will you be forgiven?
The sins you yourselves have committed.
“Forgive.” “Give, and what you desire will be given to you”: eternal life.
Support the poor man’s life in this world. Sustain the poor man’s present life. And for such a small, earthly seed you will receive a harvest of eternal life. Amen.

1. We have just heard the holy readings as they were read. They warn us to gather a supply of virtues and to make a Christian heart strong against the stumbling blocks that were predicted to come. And this warning comes from the Lord’s mercy.
Scripture says, “For what is man, except that You remember him?”

The Lord says, “Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks!” The Truth Himself says so. He alarms us and warns us. He does not want us to be caught off guard. Surely He does not want to make us lose all hope.

Scripture gives us advice, encouragement and teaching against this “woe,” that is, against this evil that we should fear, dread and guard against. It does this in the place where it says, “Those who love Your law have great peace, and nothing makes them stumble.”
He has shown us an enemy to guard against. But He has also made sure to show us a wall to protect us.
When you heard, “Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks,” you were thinking about where you could go outside the world, so that stumbling blocks could not reach you.
So where will you go outside the world to avoid stumbling blocks, unless you flee to Him who made the world?
And how can we flee to Him who made the world, unless we listen to His law, which is preached everywhere?
And listening to it is only a small thing, unless we love it.
When the Bible makes you safe against stumbling blocks, it does not say, “Those who hear Your law have great peace.”
For it is not the people who hear the law who are right in God’s sight.
But “those who do what the law says will be made right with God,” and “faith works by love.” So it says, “Those who love Your law have great peace, and nothing makes them stumble.”
The passage we sang in its place today agrees with this too: “But the meek will inherit the earth, and they will delight in plenty of peace.”
That is because “those who love Your law have great peace.”
These “meek” people are the ones who “love the law of God.”
For Scripture says, “Blessed is the man You correct, O Lord, and teach from Your law. You do this to give him rest from the days of trouble, until the pit is dug for the sinner.”

These words of Scripture seem so different. Yet they flow together and meet in one meaning. Whatever you hear from that very rich fountain, if you accept it and live in loving harmony with the truth, you will be filled with peace at once. You will glow with love, and you will be made strong against stumbling blocks.
2. So it is our task to see, or seek, or learn how we must be “meek.” The words I just quoted from the Scriptures guide us to find what we are looking for.
So, dear friends, pay attention for a little while. This is a serious matter we are dealing with: how we can be meek. We need this when life is hard.
But the hard things that happen in this life are not what we call stumbling blocks. Listen to what “stumbling blocks” really are.
For example, a man may face some hard necessity, and he is weighed down by the pressure of trouble.
Being weighed down by the pressure of trouble is not a stumbling block.
Even the Martyrs were pressed by this kind of pressure, but they were not crushed.
Watch out for a stumbling block. But do not worry so much about the pressure of trouble.
Pressure presses on you. A stumbling block crushes you.
So what is the difference between the two?
Under the pressure of trouble, you got ready to keep up your patience, to hold firm, not to give up your faith, and not to agree to sin.

If you keep this up, or have kept it up, the trouble that presses on you will not make you fall. That pressure of trouble will do what an olive press does. It does not destroy the olive. It squeezes out the oil.
In short, if you give praise to God while this trouble presses on you, that press will be so useful to you! It squeezes such good oil out of you!
The Apostles sat in chains under a press like this. And in that press they sang a hymn to God.
What precious oil was squeezed and pressed out of them!

Job sat on the dunghill under a heavy press. He had no resources, no help, no possessions, no children. He was full, but only of worms, as far as his outward body was concerned. But he was also full of God inside. So he praised God, and that press was not a “stumbling block” to him.
So where was the “stumbling block”?
It came when his wife came to him and said, “Say something against God, and die.”
Everything had been taken from him by the devil. But an Eve was left to this man who was being tested. She was not there to comfort her husband, but to tempt him.
So you can see where the stumbling block was.
She made his miseries seem even worse, and her own miseries along with his. And she began to persuade him to speak evil against God.

But he was “meek,” because “God had taught him from His law and given him rest from the days of trouble.” He had “great peace” in his heart, because he “loved the law of God, and nothing made him stumble.”
She was a stumbling block, but not to him.
In short, look at the meek man. Look at a man taught in the law of God. I mean the eternal law of God.

In Job’s time, the law written on tablets had not yet been given to the Jews. But the eternal law still remained in the hearts of godly people. The law given to the people was copied from that eternal law.
By the law of God he had “been given rest from the days of trouble,” and he “had great peace because he loved the law of God.” So see how “meek” he is, and what he answers.
From this, learn what I want to find out: who the meek are.
He says, “You are talking the way one of the foolish women talks.
If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, should we not bear the bad?”
3. We have seen from an example who the meek are. Now let us try, if we can, to describe them in words.
The meek are people who, in all their good deeds and in everything they do well, are pleased by nothing but God. And in all the evil things they suffer, they are not displeased with God.
Now, brothers and sisters, pay attention to this rule, this pattern. Let us stretch ourselves toward it. Let us seek to grow so that we may fill it.
What good is it that we plant and water, unless God makes it grow?
“The one who plants is nothing, and the one who waters is nothing. It is God who makes it grow.”

Listen, whoever you are who wants to be “meek.” You want “rest from the days of trouble.” You “love the law of God.” You want there to be “no stumbling block for you.” You want to “have great peace.” You want to “possess the earth and delight in plenty of peace.” Listen, whoever you are who wants to be “meek.”
Whatever good you do, do not be pleased with yourself.
“For God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
So whatever good you do, let nothing but God please you. Whatever evil you suffer, do not let God displease you.
What more do you need?
Do this, and you will live.
The days of trouble will not overwhelm you. You will escape what is said: “Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks.”
Which world has woe because of stumbling blocks? The world of which it is said, “And the world did not know Him.”
Not the world of which it is said, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to Himself.”
There is an evil world, and there is a good world. The evil world is all the evil people in this world. The good world is all the good people in this world.
We often see this with a field.
This field is full. Full of what?
Of wheat. Yet we also say, and say truly, “This field is full of chaff.”
It is the same with a tree. It is full of fruit.
Someone else says it is full of leaves.
The one who says it is full of fruit is right. And the one who says it is full of leaves is right too.
All the leaves have not taken away the room for the fruit. And all the fruit has not pushed out the many leaves.
It is full of both. But the wind searches out the one, and the farmer gathers in the other.
So when you hear, “Woe to the world because of stumbling blocks,” do not be afraid. “Love the law of God, and nothing will make you stumble.”
4. But suppose your wife comes to you and advises you to do something evil.
You love her as a wife should be loved. She is one of your members.
You have just heard the Gospel: “But if your eye makes you stumble, if your hand makes you stumble, if your foot makes you stumble, cut them off and throw them away from you.”

Someone may be dear to you. Someone may be highly respected by you. Let him stay highly respected by you, and stay your beloved member, only as long as he does not begin to make you stumble. That means: as long as he does not advise you to do something evil.
Now listen, and see that this is what “stumbling block” means.
I have given the example of Job and his wife. But the word “stumbling block” was not used there.
Listen to the Gospel. When the Lord foretold His suffering, Peter began to persuade Him not to suffer.
“Get behind Me, Satan! You are a stumbling block to Me.”
Here the Lord, who has given you an example of how to live, has clearly taught you two things: what a “stumbling block” is, and how to avoid one.
A little while before, He had said to Peter, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah.” So He had shown that Peter was His member.
But when Peter begins to be a stumbling block, He cuts off the member. Only, He restored the member and put it back in its place.
So the person who begins to persuade you to do something evil will be a “stumbling block” to you.
And here, dear friends, be careful. Most of the time this does not happen through an evil will. It happens through a good will that is mistaken.
Your friend who loves you, and whom you love in return—your father, your brother, your child, your wife—sees you in a bad situation. And he wants you to do something evil.
What do I mean by “sees you in a bad situation”?
He sees you under some pressure of trouble.
